Chronic UTIs affect millions in the UK - these women are out to end the stigma

BBC News Wed, 21 Oct 2026 23:03:59 GMT

"The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok.

For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for.

In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection.

What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle.

"It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London.

The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to 1.7 million women in the UK. Men and children are also affected.

Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs.

A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs.

"I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response".

"It's very validating."

A chronic UTI, which has no official medical definition, is an infection with persistent symptoms - even after a standard course of antibiotics. It can be caused by bacteria entering the lining of your bladder.

The condition can be unpredictable, but at its worst is "completely debilitating", says Adrianne, describing "the most excruciating abdominal pain, like shooting, spasming pain."

"You need a wee all the time, but it's like weeing lava."

"It's a very claustrophobic feeling, of I'm trapped in this body that is betraying me and is in pain," she adds.

Even on a good day she struggles to leave the house as she worries about having a flare-up.

While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust.

Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted.

Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely.

Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them".

"There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds.

Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok.

She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management.

As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks.

"People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says.

Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case."

Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition.

Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment."

But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm.

"I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says.

While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery".

US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Picket Fences, Mash and Alien, dies aged 93

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 20:33:31 GMT

US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences, and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says.

Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives."

In a six-decade career, he took on film and television roles, appearing in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers.

His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose, and create change."

The mustachioed star of several 20th century hit films was born on 25 August 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles.

He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later re-teamed with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt.

Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman.

The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later.

He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects.

"It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien,'" Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to Reuters news agency.

"Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other."

Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley.

During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads.

He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias.

As Commander Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise in the blockbuster.

On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences.

The procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for SAG Awards in 1995 and 1996, and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995.

Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09.

He had a six-episode stint on Cheers playing Rebecca Howe's crush-worthy boss Evan Drake.

In a statement, Skerritt's family said that he leaves behind a "legacy that reaches far beyond the screen"

A deep believer in the power of storytelling, Skerritt helped found the TheFilmSchool in Seattle and co-founded the Red Badge Project, which helps veterans work through PTSD, anxiety and depression by writing and sharing their experiences.

Inspired in part by his experience filming A River Runs Through It, he also believed in protecting the natural world.

He created the documentary series Reflections of the River about America's rivers and supported river conservation.

Trump says NBA star LeBron James disrespected US anthem and demands apology

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 20:04:27 GMT

President Donald Trump has said basketball star LeBron James disrespected the US by not being still while the national anthem was sung.

James, who now plays for the Philadelphia 76ers, appeared to be practising a golf swing and basketball shots as the anthem was being performed ahead of the season-opening match against the New York Knicks on Wednesday.

"While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country!," Trump posted on social media. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag."

James has not responded to the president's latest comments but the pair have criticised each other in the past.

James can be seen in a video making the motion of a golf swing as a performer sings the Star-Spangled Banner at New York's Madison Square Garden.

His teammates, who are lined up next to him on the court, mostly remain standing with minimal movement.

"I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump added, referring to James. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"

The BBC has contacted James for a response through the 76ers and has also asked the team to comment.

The US anthem is played or performed at the start of most professional sports games. Players and spectators are expected to stand for it, if they can, and refrain from moving around. Some people sing along.

This tradition has become a political flash-point before. In 2016, former American football player Colin Kaepernick sat down and later knelt on one knee during the anthem as a demonstration against police brutality and racism in the US.

Trump criticised Kaepernick and later took credit when the athlete could not find a team to play for. Years later, he softened his stance saying Kaepernick should "get another shot" to play in the NFL.

The president has had a longstanding feud with James, who has publicly endorsed or campaigned for Trump's political opponents since the 2016 presidential election

In 2018, Trump suggested James was not intelligent after the athlete said he "would never sit across" from him.

That same year, James accused Trump of giving racists "an opportunity to be out and outspoken without fear".

He has also suggested that Trump's rhetoric led to a mob storming the US Capitol in 2021 to stop the certification of the result of the 2020 election, which former President Joe Biden won. James had endorsed Biden.

In July, when asked to choose between James and Michael Jordan as the all-time greatest basketball player in history, Trump said he preferred Jordan.

"I only like people that like me," Trump said.

James, 41, is the highest point scorer in the history of the National Basketball Association league with more than 40,000 points. He has had a long career and has won the NBA championship with every team he has played for.

In July,⁠ he signed a two-year contract with Philadelphia which is widely expected to be his last as a professional player.

Lockerbie bombing accused loses bid to have case thrown out

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:30:56 GMT

A Libyan man accused of building the bomb that brought down an American airliner over Lockerbie nearly 38 years ago has lost his bid to have the case thrown out of court.

Abu Agila Mas'ud al-Marimi had claimed he was the victim of an illegal rendition when he was transferred into US custody from Libya in 2022.

A US district court judge has ruled that the manner of his removal should not prevent his trial going ahead in Washington in January.

Marimi has denied playing a key role in the attack on Pan Am 103, which killed 270 people on 21 December 1988.

His attempt to have the case dismissed was made public through documents lodged with the court in Washington.

Marimi's lawyers said he was violently abducted from his home in Tripoli in 2022 by armed members of a militia, "in a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the middle of the night".

They alleged that weeks later, after being held without access to lawyers in a detention centre, he was handed over to FBI agents at an airport in Misrata and flown to the United States.

Marimi argued the case should be dismissed because the United States had invaded his constitutional rights and violated extradition agreements between the US and Libya.

Court transcripts obtained by BBC Scotland News have revealed that trial judge Dabney Friedrich rejected the defence motion.

She referred to a longstanding American legal doctrine, which stipulates that a court's right to hold a trial is not impaired if the suspect has been the subject of a forceful abduction.

"This rule rests on the principle that due process of law is satisfied when one present in court is convicted of a crime after a fair trial and in accordance with constitutional procedural safeguards," said the judge.

"Put differently, there's nothing in the Constitution that requires a court to permit a guilty person rightfully convicted to escape justice because he was brought to trial against his will."

In her ruling, the judge said there were two exceptions to that doctrine.

One would apply if Marimi had been brought before the court through the US government's "deliberate, unnecessary and unreasonable invasion" of his constitutional rights.

For that exception to be triggered, the challenged conduct had to be carried out by, or at the direction of, US officials.

The judge said Marimi's allegations "at best suggest that US government officials exerted pressure on Libyan officials to facilitate a rendition, not that US government officials directed or controlled the challenged conduct."

The second exception to the doctrine would apply if the US government had violated an extradition agreement which was the only way a suspect could be transferred between the two countries.

The judge said the US government had invoked two conventions to secure Marimi's appearance in a US court.

"Neither the Montreal Convention nor the Terrorists Bombing Convention provides that it is the only way by which one country may gain custody of a national of another country for the purposes of prosecution," she said.

"Accordingly, Libya was free to transfer Mr Al-Marimi to the United States using any method it chose."

The defence and prosecution have fought a series of legal battles in the approach to Marimi's trial, which is now scheduled to get underway on 19 January after three postponements.

In another ruling, the judge rejected a defence motion to suppress a confession alleged to have been made by Marimi when he was in custody in Libya in 2012.

According to the FBI, Marimi admitted building the bomb which destroyed Pan Am 103 in an operation carried out by the Libyan intelligence service.

Marimi has claimed the confession was false and was made under duress.

The only previous criminal trial related to the Lockerbie bombing took place between May 2000 and January 2001, when three Scottish judges convicted Libyan intelligence agent Abdulbasset al-Megrahi of playing a key role in the plot.

Megrahi was jailed for life but released on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government in 2009 after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer. He died three years later at home in Tripoli.

Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:54:51 GMT

The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark".

Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to.

Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie".

In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended."

She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.

Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy.

Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms.

On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right."

Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution."

She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward".

At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind."

In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms.

"As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said.

It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool.

Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue.

Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:52:45 GMT

Harry Brook hit the fastest 200 in the history of one-day internationals

Just under a year ago, Harry Brook was left wondering if he would be sacked as England white-ball captain and what damage he had done to his international career.

What a turnaround in 12 months. From whacked in Wellington to the run-fest in Rawalpindi, Brook is undeniably England's most important cricketer and probably the best multi-format batter in the world.

Brook's 202 in England's defeat against Sri Lanka was an astonishing display of stroke-making. There can be no higher praise than to compare Brook's dismantling of the Sri Lankan attack to the sort of innings once played by South African genius AB de Villiers.

It was the first double hundred scored by an Englishman in an ODI, passing England's previous best individual score of 182 by Ben Stokes against New Zealand in 2023. In reaching 200 in 114 balls, Brook registered the fastest double ton by anyone in an ODI, bettering the 117 deliveries of India's Shubman Gill against West Indies only last month.

Brook has joined one of international cricket's most exclusive clubs. In completing the set of a hundred in a T20, double hundred in an ODI and triple century in a Test, Brook has matched the previously unique treble of West Indies' legend Chris Gayle.

In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played.

For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side.

Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown.

Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook – he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades.

In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate.

Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026.

The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband.

This video can not be played

'That's life' - captain Brook on England defeat

Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter – that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January.

He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision.

There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket.

Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article".

"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said.

In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer.

As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos – he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers.

As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level".

Harry Brook hit 21 fours and 10 sixes against Sri Lanka

The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament.

Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022.

Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport.

To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan.

In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won.

Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what seemed an impregnable position, their bowling and fielding falling apart amid a growing realisation they were in danger of failing to defend a target of 430.

There was some mitigation. Dew made the ball incredibly slippery, while their attack was weakened by the absence of the rested Jofra Archer and benched Adil Rashid.

Nevertheless, the bowling was awful, particularly Sam Curran, who conceded 103 from nine overs to return the worst figures by an England bowler in an ODI. It was an error by Brook to continue to show faith in the left-armer, while not using the full allocation of 10 overs from either Josh Tongue or Gus Atkinson.

It is one of the first major missteps of Brook's captaincy career and the sort of performance that shows England still have some way to go to be seen as serious World Cup contenders.

Now, England will have to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final, to be played on 31 October, exactly 12 months on from Brook's horror show in Wellington.

Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:46:58 GMT

Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says.

Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and with flooding expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

"How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?" he said.

"Those are the sorts of everyday challenges and threats that we could well face. And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit."

The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.

Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.

The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.

It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".

It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.

Last month, Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the powerful natural climate phenomenon El Niño will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.

Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.

The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".

It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil".

The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

What next for Australia after chastening defeat by South Africa?

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:25:22 GMT

Australia were beaten by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha

Second Test, Gqeberha (day five of five)

South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81

Australia 99 & 295: Head 121; Rabada 4-77, Mulder 3-64

South Africa won by an innings and 31 runs

Scorecard

Some Test defeats feel more consequential than others.

Some can be brushed aside as a bad day. Others point to issues that run deep. For Australia, this capitulation on the Cape feels like the latter.

In losing to South Africa by an innings and 31 runs, Australia surrendered their lead in the series with one match to play.

There was fight on day five: Travis Head scored 121 and nightwatchman Scott Boland survived for 166 balls to take the match into the final session, but Pat Cummins' side still had to follow-on for only the third time this century and lost in little more than three days' play around the rain.

The momentum built in Durban has been swept away.

"It is not just this Test," said former Australia bowler Jason Gillespie on ABC Grandstand.

"We are talking about the batting and a lack of options and performance. Something will change."

It is, of course, little more than a week since South Africa were the ones facing these questions.

They made three changes after Australia won the first Test in Durban.

Eyes are now on the tourists' selectors and this series coming before contests against New Zealand, India and England only adds extra intrigue.

A stony-faced Australia coach Andrew McDonald refused to be drawn on potential changes on Wednesday, but hardly gave ringing endorsements of his batters.

"I can't defend that," McDonald said of Australia's first-innings collapse to 99 all out.

Attracting the most attention is number three Marnus Labuschagne, who has gone 47 innings without an international century to equal the Australia record.

His inexplicable second-innings dismissal, when he hit spinner Simon Harmer to long-on for 39 as Australia tried to save the Test, was the fourth time he has fallen in the thirties in six innings since the Ashes.

"Some of the hardest part of batting at number three is getting in," said Cummins, when asked to guarantee whether Labuschagne will keep his place.

"He is doing that. We need to turn those 30s into bigger scores. He knows that."

In that run of wasted starts, Labuschagne has been bowled missing a flick to leg, missed another to be pinned lbw, drove a spinner straight to cover and whacked another to long-on.

"I got the feeling last night Andrew McDonald was getting very impatient," former Australia batter Phil Jaques said on ABC.

"He wants a response from the batting group and Pat Cummins does as well."

Labuschagne was once the top-ranked batter in the world but averages 25.34 across his past 25 Tests

Amid all of the doubts, this Australia set-up has a history of backing its established players.

When Labuschagne was dropped for a Test against West Indies last year, he was recalled on the back of good domestic form at the start of the Ashes months later.

Former openers Usman Khawaja and David Warner were both backed through difficult times.

Still, after scores of eight and nought this week, on the back of another duck in Durban, opener Nic Maddinson is now under immense pressure for his place.

"It is hard to see how Maddinson will survive to Cape Town," said Gillespie.

Dropping the 34-year-old would also bring the attention on to Australia's selectors.

Maddinson was recalled to open in this series after a 10-year absence, despite primarily being a middle-order player.

"You would have to question the process of what happened in that selection room," Jaques said.

"I feel for Nic. He is a good player and good fella but he hasn't had a great couple of Test matches."

Maddinson was caught behind off the bowling of Kagiso Rabada in both innings of the second Test

In being recalled for this series, Maddinson became the ninth different batter to open for Australia since David Warner retired in 2024.

Like England in the days after Andrew Strauss, it is a problem proving tricky to solve.

If Australia do drop Maddinson, one solution would be to return to a batter who has filled the role before - Matt Renshaw.

Renshaw made 190 in the first Test but opened against Bangladesh last month before being moved to number five for this series.

Renshaw's promotion would create a space in the middle order. Cameron Green and Josh Inglis are fit again. Either could retake that place.

Spin-bowling all-rounder Cooper Connolly is another option. The 23-year-old made his Test debut earlier this year but has only played 12 other first-class matches.

All-rounder Beau Webster is another incumbent under pressure, having gone seven innings without a fifty with scores of eight and 18 in Gqeberha. He is yet to make a century in his 12 Tests.

"Cooper Connolly will come in, possibly at the expense of Webster," predicted Gillespie.

"Labuschagne keeps his spot, Renshaw moves to the top and a batter comes in the middle order - whether Green or Inglis."

It all leaves Australia scrambling, having looked certain winners of this series when South Africa were 110-6 in their first innings.

Their best performer on the final day was Boland, who defended resolutely for more than three hours before being bowled by the impressive South Africa all-rounder Wiaan Mulder after taking five wickets in the first innings.

The performance of Boland restarts another debate; how do you get the 37-year-old, pace trio Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, plus spinner Nathan Lyon into the same XI?

Lyon was the one to miss out here but Cape Town, where the series decider begins on Tuesday, is expected to turn.

"Boland has to play," said Gillespie. "He was Australia's best seam bowler.

"I don't think it is a lock Lyon could play. You have [left-arm spinner] Matt Kuhnemann here and South Africa basically have all right-handed batsmen.

"It is going to be a long selection discussion."

From holding all of the cards, Australia are now fielding all of the questions.

'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:21:42 GMT

Clavicular, a social media influencer who promotes the "looksmaxxing" trend of young men maximising their attractiveness, has pleaded not guilty to criminal charges including rape.

The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged in September with felony rape, drugging an individual for sexual intercourse and procuring alcohol for someone under the age of 21.

The charges stem from an incident in 2025 when he is accused of assaulting a 17-year-old girl at his family's Massachusetts home.

Peters has denied the allegations and said the encounter was consensual. On Thursday, he was granted $10,000 bail, ordered not to contact or post about his accuser, and to surrender his passport.

A woman told police that on 23 May 2025, Peters ordered her an Uber to his family's house in Chatham where they were drinking alcohol while filming a livestream before he allegedly raped her, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.

The police officer who took the report said he believed she was unable to consent due to her age and the level of intoxication she exhibited in the livestream, CBS reported.

Clavicular has more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and has garnered media attention for extreme measures he has taken for "looksmaxxing".

He has admitted to using a hammer on his face and jawline and taking a number of steroids, injections, and other drugs to achieve bodily perfection. He also gives advice on appearing masculine and performs stunts to shock followers.

In Florida earlier this year, he was charged after filming himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator. He pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public.

In March, he was arrested on suspicion of battery after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities said in July that they did not intend to file charges.

After Thursday's hearing, Peters posted a photo of himself in the black suit and black tie he wore to court, while holding his dog which he also brought to court.

His next hearing will be on 24 November, when the judge will decide if there is enough evidence for the case to move forward.

Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:14:04 GMT

A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period, during which both sides are legally required to exchange information with each other on their case.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.

The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.

Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.

Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.

Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:12:51 GMT

Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.

Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.

There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.

Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.

"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.

She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".

The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".

"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.

Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".

"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.

But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.

He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected had been received and was being acted on.

Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.

"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.

"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."

Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.

He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.

"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.

He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.

PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.

It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.

When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.

It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.

According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.

And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.

Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.

"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.

Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.

While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.

The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.

But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.

In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.

"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.

"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."

Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.

"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".

"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.

From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.

She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess".

"She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".

The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her.

"I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police.

"She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."

She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go.

"She kind of put it behind her."

Statements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand.

Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'.

"She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey.

"She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."

Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."

The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted.

"I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times.

"I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."

He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.

The woman's former boyfriend also gave evidence, telling the court she was "very upset" whenever she talked about her encounter with Brand, and that "she characterised it as an assault... she called it rape".

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC cross-examined the woman's former boyfriend and read parts of the statement he gave in June 2025, in which he said the woman had "come round" to having anal sex.

When asked if he had said that, the witness replied: "Yes."

The witness added the woman had "surrendered to the idea".

"If I was being attacked, you either fight back or surrendered, it doesn't negate the attack," he added.

Judge Mr Justice Bennathan sent the jury away until Monday morning, at the end of Thursday's evidence.

He told the jurors that "we aim to finish the prosecution case on Monday", adding the defence case would not begin before Tuesday morning.

The rising French star whose dad won Rugby World Cup with England

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:21:57 GMT

Felix Balshaw has climbed more than 500 places in the ATP rankings since the start of 2026

Accents quickly reveal a lot about a person.

So speaking to Leeds-born Felix Balshaw - the 20-year-old son of England Rugby World Cup winner Iain - it soon becomes clear why he is representing France on his climb up the professional tennis ladder.

There is no mistaking a strong Gallic twang as Balshaw, who celebrated the first ATP Tour victory of his career this week, discusses his journey.

Balshaw was born in West Yorkshire while his father played for Premiership club Leeds Tykes, before the family moved to Biarritz when Iain - an electrifying full-back/wing who scored three tries in England's iconic 2003 campaign - joined the cross-channel exodus to the French Top 14.

The Balshaws have remained in the luxurious Basque coastal city, known for its Belle Epoque architecture, Atlantic seafront casinos and world-class surfing.

"We came down in Biarritz in 2009 and we just loved the place," said Felix, who broke into the world's top 200 last month for the first time.

"I grew up in France and, as each day went by, I felt more and more French.

"Since I've been little, from when I started playing in Tennis Europe juniors, I have always had the French flag by my name."

Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50

Balshaw pledging allegiance to his adopted country is understandable given the limited contact with his birthland.

Trips back across the English Channel have been "very rare" for the Balshaw children, largely restricted to Christmas family gatherings.

Their maternal grandmother lives in Bath, although Felix has never visited his father's hometown of Blackburn.

But the world number 178 is fully aware his dad will forever be ingrained in the fabric of English sporting history.

The then Bath player scored three tries in the pool stage of England's historic 2003 World Cup campaign, helping secure a 20-17 victory over Australia in the final when he came on as a second-half substitute.

On the eve of the biggest match of his career - facing fellow Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the Lyon Open second round - Felix tried to draw inspiration from watching highlights of his father playing in 2003.

"I just had a massive smile [watching] because I can say 'this is my dad'," he said.

"When he was at Biarritz I was always stood in a little corner in the stands with the rugby gang. It was very, very inspirational to watch him.

"As a father he's tough, but it's always important that he has a lot of experience in rugby, so he's got a lot of stuff to teach me.

"He's always been a great, great part of my life. He's always had my back."

Iain Balshaw won 35 caps for England and played three times for the Lions on the 2001 tour to Australia

Balshaw started playing tennis at the age of four, but unsurprisingly also had a talent for rugby.

At 13, he needed to make a choice about which sport he wanted to pursue more seriously with the prospect of a professional career looming.

"When I was little, and your father is a rugby champion, of course you always want to follow in his steps and do the same journey as him," Balshaw said.

"But I just felt that rugby was not going to be my sport.

"Tennis, I guess, is more difficult for me than rugby because it's an individual sport, but there was a little more fire in me [playing tennis].

"That meant it was the right choice to choose tennis."

Balshaw is essentially an inverted Arthur Fery - the French-born British number one who became a household name with a stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

The pair actually met for the first time at this week's ATP 250 event in Lyon, where Balshaw beat Portuguese world number 56 Jaime Faria for his maiden win at tour level.

Possessing a Roger Federer-style one-handed backhand, and a Thor-inspired hammer celebration, Balshaw announced his arrival in some style.

Next week Balshaw will rise into the world's top 180, having starting the 2026 season ranked 718th.

His success will no doubt catch the attention of Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) chiefs, who are desperate to increase the pool of British players at the elite level.

Was Balshaw ever approached by the LTA to represent the country of his birth?

And was there ever a conversation with his parents about who he should represent?

"Maybe my parents are hiding stuff and I don't know, but I have never been personally contacted by the LTA," Felix said.

"I think for [my parents] the most important thing is if I'm happy, they'll be happy as well."

Fernandes to stay captain as Rooney calls Man Utd players babies

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:19:30 GMT

Fernandes criticised Carrick's tactics in the defeat by Como on Wednesday

Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

The United skipper criticised Carrick's tactics for the game, then said it was up to the United head coach and his backroom team, not the players, to spot any issues and change them.

It was seen by many externally as a challenge to Carrick's authority, just eight days after United defender Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox and the club's summer recruitment.

Inside Old Trafford, there is sympathy for Fernandes for the position he found himself in.

The Portugal midfielder did 10 post-match interviews in Como, despite being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee midway through the second half.

While there is disappointment at some of his comments, it is acknowledged Fernandes' annoyance was understandable given the manner of the loss, which was one of the worst in United's European history.

It remains to be seen whether Fernandes will be picked for Sunday's Premier League encounter with Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Carrick will be asked about the situation when he holds his pre-game news conference at 13:30 BST on Friday.

Fernandes has home burgled while in Italy with Man Utd

Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by performances

Wayne Rooney (right) with former Manchester United team-mate Michael Carrick at the club's Carrington training ground

Former Manchester United striker Wayne Rooney said he was in "shock" and "disbelief" at the performance against Como and he is as "worried as I've been for a long time" at the situation at Old Trafford.

And, while he understands the questioning of Carrick, a close personal friend of the former England and United skipper, Rooney also called the players "selfish" and said "they're like babies" in the wake of the controversial comments from both Martinez and Fernandes.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast. "That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their team-mates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves. If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Fernandes' form has dipped markedly from last season, when he was named PFA and FWA Player of the Year and broke the Premier League record for assists in a single season.

"He [Fernandes] is putting pressure on someone else because he doesn't want to face it," added Rooney.

"If he looks at himself in the mirror, if Martinez and all of them looked at themselves in the mirror, they'll find what's looking back at them is them, and that's not good enough. They need to show more."

Rooney has also called on the Manchester United board to provide clarity on the future of Carrick, who he believes needs to "come out fighting".

Carrick will be in charge for Sunday's visit of Bournemouth despite intense speculation he is on the brink of dismissal following United's worst run of form since 2015-16.

"I was in that situation [at Plymouth and Birmingham City] and I can only say now, looking back and reflecting, if I was in Michael Carrick's position now, I'd come out fighting," said Rooney.

"There's no more Mr Nice Guy. There are certain things you've got to do to protect them players, but you have to come out fighting for yourself because those players will drag you down and it's going to be you who's going to lose your job over it."

Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:56:36 GMT

From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.

They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.

When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.

What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.

"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.

Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.

The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.

The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.

Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.

The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.

The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.

Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.

We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.

"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."

Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.

"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."

Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.

Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."

As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.

There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.

That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.

"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.

"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."

A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.

Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.

The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.

"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."

They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.

"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."

She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.

Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.

As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.

So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

TV star's brother 'never recovered' from her death

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:32:27 GMT

The brother of TV presenter Caroline Flack took his own life having "never recovered" after his sister's death, an inquest heard.

Paul Flack, 55, was found unresponsive at his home in Sandringham Road, Norwich, on 21 June, and died later in hospital.

His partner told Norfolk Coroner's Court how he had struggled with his father developing dementia and his younger sister's death in 2020.

Area Coroner Johanna Thompson gave a narrative conclusion, stating Paul Flack died while under the influence of alcohol and that his "intent in doing so is unknown".

He was described as "everyone's favourite person" by his partner Joanna Millington, but she said this "took its toll".

His sister, the ex-Love Island and X Factor host, was found dead at her home in Stoke Newington, east London, on 15 February 2020.

"We then went into lockdown for Covid," said Millington, who provided a written statement to the court.

"I do not think Paul ever recovered from this."

An inquest later established Caroline Flack took her own life, aged 40, having feared press intrusion ahead of her trial accused of assaulting her boyfriend.

Earlier, the inquest heard Paul Flack sought help for low mood from his GP in August 2020, but he did not attend follow-up appointments or counselling.

The self-employed graphic designer also struggled to find work as the "industry had begun to decline", which "contributed to his sadness", his partner of 32 years said.

His father Ian developed dementia in his early 70s in recent years, and died at the beginning of this year.

Millington added: "[Paul] was a lovely person, he took a lot on from everyone.

"There was no suggestion he would ever harm himself, he said he never would."

On the day of Paul Flack's death - which was Father's Day - the inquest heard he and Millington enjoyed some time together as a family.

At 18:30 BST, his daughter offered him a cup of tea and a slice of cake she had made.

He declined and instead went to the shop and bought four beers and spent the rest of the evening in the garden listening to music while his partner and daughter watched a film inside.

Before going to bed at about 22:20, his daughter found he was no longer in the hammock outside.

She screamed when she then found him unresponsive.

A neighbour attempted CPR and another neighbour called an ambulance.

The coroner heard Millington told a neighbour he had been in a "bad mood all day" and that it may be because they were celebrating Father's Day so soon after his dad's death.

He was pronounced dead at Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital at 23:45.

A toxicology report found he had a blood alcohol level four times over the legal alcohol limit to drive.

Paul Flack was born in Enfield in north London, but his family later moved to Norwich, where he lived much of his life. He had two children.

No family members were present at the inquest

Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:31:04 GMT

A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction.

The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than £6,000.

His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56m.

The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.

"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.

"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.

"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.

"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."

Pokémon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.

The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.

One set which cost him £300 at the time went for £75,000 at Wednesday's auction.

The cards, all filed into bespoke Pokémon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the franchise.

Ewbank's said "jaws hit the floor" when the man presented his 42 sets of cards to them.

"When we saw what he had – all in mint condition – we couldn't believe it," said James Spooner, its head of trading cards.

The auction house added the sale had been their most successful in more than 30 years in business.

Its top lot was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, including a Charizard card in near-mint condition. It had been pitched at £15,000-£20,000 but bagged £100,000.

Andrew Ewbank, who runs Ewbank's and conducted the sale from the rostrum himself, told bidders he was "going for a lie down" afterwards.

"The build-up to this... has been phenomenal, and on the day it did not disappoint," he added later.

"We had bidders from all over the world.

"The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for."

"It was a hell of a ride," he told the BBC.

Ewbank added that Pokemon was "booming" at the moment.

He said people who were young when the franchise first came out were now in their 30s and 40s and had a "bit of disposable income".

"Nostalgia is a big of part of it," he added.

"It's about bringing back those memories of childhood."

Ewbank urged anyone who thought they had something valuable in the attic to "get it down and looked at".

"If you buy something for your son, as happened in this case, and they don't want it, well, maybe pop it away because you never know what value it might have in the future," he said.

The record sum for the Pokemon collection beat the previous best, set only on 9 October in London, when a sale at Stanley Gibbons declared a sale total of £872,000, according to Ewbank's.

Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo target UK

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 10:34:17 GMT

The Met Office have named a new storm, Boelo, which is set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.

Storm Boelo will be hot on the heels of Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season.

Storm Austen is expected to bring strong winds to south-west England during Friday morning.

The Met Office has issued an amber wind warning for Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly, Plymouth and parts of Devon valid between 1am and 10am on Friday.

Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen, the Government of Jersey has said.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

Wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Austen's arrival on Friday

Storm Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.

The strongest winds will move into Scotland on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight.

The Met Office have also issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday.

Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.

There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time.

Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding.

Yellow wind warnings have been issued ahead of Storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend

It's not unusual to get storms so close together, in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.

A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.

These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.

Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know

The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.

The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.

This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.

In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read anymore'

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 06:41:29 GMT

Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench says her eye condition has left her unable to perform on stage or read, more than a decade after she was diagnosed.

Dench was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012, a condition that affects her vision and has made it incredibly difficult to even recognise faces.

Speaking to Emma Barnett on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she said: "I can't be on stage. I can't do a play anymore. I can't do a film anymore. I can't read anymore."

She also revealed how her condition can lead to awkward encounters, saying she sometimes approaches the wrong people "and give them an almost hug" before realising her mistake.

When asked about ageing, Dench, who's 91, replied: "There's nothing to say for it at all. [I] don't think about it too much."

Dench has enjoyed a career spanning more than seven decades and is one of Britain's most celebrated actors, with a body of work across theatre, television and film.

She won an Academy Award for best supporting actress for playing Queen Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love in 1999, and became internationally recognised for her portrayal of "M", James Bond's boss. She made her debut as the character in GoldenEye in 1995, becoming the first woman to play the role.

But her sight loss has increasingly affected her ability to work, with the actress previously speaking about struggling to see on film sets and having difficulty learning scripts.

Despite her condition, she has continued to make public appearances and speak openly about adapting to life with deteriorating vision, stating that "the radio has always been important to me".

During the interview, Dench recalled being invited to lunch by former MI6 chief Sir David Spedding, describing the experience as "very exciting". When she asked where her driver should drop her off, she was told: "No, no, we'll send a car to you, we'll come and pick you up."

However, she arrived about 20 minutes late after the driver struggled to find her house. "I said, 'I'm sorry for being so late because your driver couldn't find my house.' I loved it."

Asked if she had any views on who should play the next Bond, she simply replied "no".

Dench also discussed meeting American actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.

She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door.

Dench said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling."

Asked what she had said to him, Dench replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall."

The conversation then turned to Dench's love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine and said the moment sparked her passion for the playwright.

"He walked on and he said 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?"

She also admitted to being " besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them."

"It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added, "it's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."
