How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election

BBC News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 05:30:22 GMT

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.

I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.

These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.

"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Meanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition.

It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.

A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime.

In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for.

Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.

In Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November.

No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction.

"It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.

The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness."

"As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."

This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.

The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.

With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.

The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

People are vibe coding copyrighted apps with AI – will tech firms sue?

New Scientist October 21, 2026

I am waging a silent rebellion against Amazon. The internet giant owns Goodreads, the leading service for tracking and cataloguing books, but is generally considered to be a poor steward of the platform, which is built on ageing technology. Frustrated with the user experience, I have used AI to vibe code my own Goodreads app, relegating the official one to mere plumbing in my private fiefdom. Take that, Amazon, for I have breached your terms of service!

I am not alone in my AI-enabled rebellion. It feels like I come across daily examples of people using AI to unofficially remix and remake software, whether that is creating a free copycat version of Adobe Photoshop, stripping the ads from their smart TV, mashing up video games or getting printers working on unsupported devices. It is all happening so quickly that lawyers don’t seem to have sprung into action to prevent it, though in some of the more egregious copyright-infringing cases, I would expect them to eventually.

Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality

For my Goodreads app, Amazon probably doesn’t know, or even care, about what I am doing. I won’t bore you with the full technical details, but I have built the app in such a way that it avoids mass “scraping” Goodreads – systematically harvesting data from its website – which would be easy to detect and block. By treading lightly, my app aims to resemble a human user and fly under the radar.

Advertisement

This connects to another ongoing battle over the interaction between AI-enabled individuals and companies: AI agents. The promise of an AI agent is that it can go out on to the internet and do things for you, like shopping or booking appointments. A flurry of examples has launched recently, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, and companies have begun fighting back, with the likes of Amazon and JPMorgan Chase blocking Muse in high-profile pushbacks. Ironically, Meta sits on both sides of this battle: its automated tools blocked a protest account on Instagram after detecting activity from a Claude AI tool that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems”.

All of this comes down to a much older conundrum: where do your rights end and others’ begin? We have seen this play out every time a major new technology has hit the internet, and the results of a few historical examples might inform what happens next with AI. The first is a technology you probably don’t even think about anymore: your web browser.

In the late 1990s, the two main browsers were Microsoft’s Internet Explorer and Netscape’s Navigator. They worked slightly differently, and websites often instructed users to choose one over the other. As more browsers flourished, Microsoft pushed back, most notably in 2003 by blocking a competitor browser called Opera from accessing its MSN website, a popular destination at the time. In the end, browsers began misidentifying themselves to websites as other browsers in an effort to avoid this. Today, the right to use any browser you like has essentially won out against the right of websites to restrict them, although the rise of dedicated smartphone apps has put some of the power back in companies’ hands.

Nested within this battle was another: ad blockers. Once your browser has fetched the HTML code for a website, should you be obligated to display it all on your screen? As websites began displaying adverts to make money, people began downloading ad blocker add-ons to take back control of their browser. In response, companies developed new techniques for displaying ads, and ad blockers adjusted to remove them. Today there is a stalemate, with around 30 per cent of internet users blocking ads.

Finally, there is the grandfather of all internet copyright battles: Napster, a peer-to-peer file-sharing service that people used to illegally share music files. The companies mostly won this battle thanks to the rise of Spotify and other similar music streaming services – with an easy legal option, piracy faded away, the side effect being that most people generally don’t own the music they listen to anymore.

Internet users largely prevailed after the browser wars, ad blocking is at an impasse and streaming music seems to have benefitted the big corporations. What does all of this mean for AI?

The difference here is decentralisation: just as I have used AI to create my own Goodreads app, so could anyone else, each of them slightly different. Fully blocking them all without restricting normal human access would be a monumental task. There is a slight caveat here – most AI use is centralised through the big providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, and Amazon could theoretically ask them to build in a block against creating such software (or sue them), but I think that is unlikely. In any case, the availability of open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run on their own hardware makes that a losing battle.

I think it is most likely that we will be heading for a mix of all three. When it comes to remixing software, anything you do in the privacy of your own computer is going to be very hard to stop. Once you release it online, however, expect the lawyers to hunt you down. What we might see is the sharing of prompts that will get an AI to do the work for you in private – writing “recreate Photoshop, make no mistakes” isn’t something that any lawyer can stop – and there already exists a slightly more complicated version of this in the form of an instruction set for AI called Reverse Engineer Anything. As with browsers, individual choice will win, but this time the choices will be even more granular.

Hannah Fry: ‘AI can do some superhuman things – but so can forklifts’

For software that goes out into the wider internet, including AI agents, there will be two tiers. I expect Meta and Amazon will eventually come to some kind of agreement that allows Muse to shop for you. We are already seeing this with the development of a “personal agent protocol” that Meta is developing with businesses, including payment-processing services like Shopify and Stripe. For anyone using a commercial AI agent, what you can and can’t do will be decided by the companies, just as music streaming services dictate how you listen.

But why should you use a commercial AI agent? People like me with a little technical know-how and even less coding ability are already using AI to create their own independent agents. As AI gets better at writing software, the barrier to entry will get lower and lower. I think companies will just have to come to accept this, as they have done with ad blockers. In future, a decent percentage of users that look like humans will actually be custom-made bots in disguise, doing things solely for the benefit of their creator. These bots will be ungovernable, for good and for ill.

Cholesterol may disrupt the brain’s cleaning system in Alzheimer’s disease

New Scientist October 21, 2026

The flow of fluid through the brain was drastically reduced in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease, and cholesterol may be responsible. Disruption to the glymphatic system, the brain’s waste-clearance network, contributes to the build-up of harmful proteins associated with the condition. Now, cholesterol has been linked to a reduction of this circulation, perhaps by blocking crucial passages within the brain.

However, this is far from established and many questions remain. “I would regard this more as a hypothesis-generating piece,” says Roslyn Bill at Aston University in Birmingham, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia, which affects around 50 million people worldwide. People with Alzheimer’s accumulate two types of harmful protein in their brain: beta-amyloid, which aggregates into plaques, and tau, which forms tangles.

Advertisement

Many studies suggest that one contributing factor in Alzheimer’s is a failure to clear waste chemicals from the brain. The brains of people without Alzheimer’s flush out harmful waste through the glymphatic system: a network of narrow channels running along the outer walls of blood vessels in the brain. Glymphatic flow is reduced in mouse models of the condition, but evidence is mounting that this could be restored via drugs, light and sound exposure or even inhaling a high dose of carbon dioxide.

To better understand this disruption, Do-Geun Kim and his colleagues at the Korea Brain Research Institute in Daegu, South Korea, studied two groups of mice. Some had been genetically engineered to express five mutations associated with Alzheimer’s in people, while the rest were healthy.

The team injected a dye into the cisterna magna, a chamber at the back of the brain that is full of cerebrospinal fluid. Different mice were then euthanised 5 minutes, 15 minutes, 30 minutes, 60 minutes or 120 minutes after the injection.

Free newsletter

In the healthy mice, the dye spread along the outside of arteries running along the underside of the brain, and then into brain tissue, over the first 30 minutes. By 120 minutes, the dye was almost entirely gone, suggesting it had been cleared by the glymphatic system.

However, in the genetically modified mice, the dye accumulated around the outsides of the arteries, with little of it reaching brain tissue. “The passage is somewhat blocked,” says Kim.

Normal glymphatic flow occurs just outside blood vessels. Brain cells called astrocytes wrap their foot-like extensions around these vessels, creating narrow channels – called perivascular spaces – through which liquid can flow. The researchers found that these spaces were significantly narrower in the mice modelling Alzheimer’s disease than in the healthy ones.

A duo of drugs that boosts our glymphatic system, which clears waste from our brain, also improves the removal of proteins associated with the onset of Alzheimer’s disease

Furthermore, they found that what little dye made it into the modified mice’s brains mostly ended up in their amyloid plaques. The researchers suggest the plaques acted like a sponge, soaking up fluid that would normally circulate through the brain.

Finally, the team looked into the potential role of cholesterol in glymphatic dysfunction. One of the most important risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease is mutations in a protein called apolipoprotein E, and one of its main functions is to produce cholesterol in the brain.

The researchers stained mice brains with a fluorescent marker that binds to cholesterol. In the healthy mice, they saw lots of fluorescence in the brain after 5 minutes, with levels then declining. Although unclear, this may be due to cholesterol being released into the brain in response to the dye and then being cleared. However, in the modified mice, the cholesterol signal increased up to 120 minutes.

Boosting the brain’s waste-disposal system is increasingly showing promise for Alzheimer’s disease, with a study now suggesting that a novel approach eases brain deficits and symptoms associated with the condition

Cholesterol has an array of roles in healthy brains, including regulating signalling between neurons. It is possible cholesterol also transports chemicals from perivascular spaces to neurons, says Kim, who says there may be something about Alzheimer’s disease that changes cholesterol so it blocks that flow.

“The perivascular spaces are the highway for fast fluid inflow,” says Maiken Nedergaard at the University of Rochester in New York, one of the discoverers of the glymphatic system. “If that is compromised, it’s really hard to get something into the brain.”

However, she says the study doesn’t clearly show what role cholesterol may have in glymphatic function or why it behaved differently in the modified mice. “Why is the cholesterol mobilised?” she asks. Bill wants to see the experiments repeated with live mice, so the flow of cerebrospinal fluid can be tracked in real time, rather than in microscope slides from dead mice.

Digital scents could add a new dimension to virtual worlds

New Scientist October 21, 2026

Imagine if, in addition to sharing photos of those muffins you just baked, you could share their delicious aroma, too. That’s the promise of an AI-assisted device that can transmit smells over the internet. So far, it works on only a small number of scents, including orange, beer and cake, but its creators hope the system will ultimately recreate more smells. The scent of a pine forest or the aroma of coffee, for example, could then add a new dimension to virtual worlds and long-distance communication.

Although it is now routine to communicate sight, sound and even touch sensations electronically, smell is “still a very undeveloped sense”, says Chunyu Yang at the Ohio State University. That’s partly because odours involve complex chemistry. Whereas vision, for example, can be broken down into combinations of red, green and blue pixels, says Yang, there’s no simple building block underlying smell. Any attempt to convert aromas into electronic signals has to recognise combinations of very different molecules.

Smell-seeking drone uses moth antenna to follow a scent

To solve the problem, Yang and her colleagues built an electronic nose, or “e-nose”, as well as a smell generator, then used machine learning to connect the two. The e-nose consists of arrays of sensors made of metal oxide. When different gaseous components of smells, such as ethanol (from alcoholic drinks) or limonene (found in citrus fruits), bind to the sensors’ surface, this changes their resistance, creating different electrical signals.

Advertisement

The researchers then trained an AI algorithm to recognise the distinctive signals created by smells from five different foods or beverages: orange, cake, coffee, beer and red wine. Teaching the AI to correctly recognise the smells was “the most challenging part” of the entire study, says Yang, because to generate enough data to train the system, she had to expose the sensors to the various smells hundreds of times.

This information was then sent over the internet to a smell generation device that the researchers are calling “Scentronic”. This part of the system involves miniature containers holding liquids laced with each of the five smells. Above each container is an atomiser that vibrates in response to electric signals, forcing the liquid in the container through a cotton filter and releasing fine droplets into the air, creating the appropriate smell, or combination of smells.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Yang built several different designs including stringing the atomisers onto a necklace and a wristband, and mounting them on a handheld device. When she tested the handheld device on 14 volunteers, they correctly identified the smells being transmitted to them 73 per cent of the time, on average.

She also built a prototype that reproduces taste, involving a cup of water with electromagnetic pumps containing flavoured liquid fixed around its edge. “When it receives information from the internet, the corresponding liquid will be dropped into the cup.”

Alternative methods to generate smells remotely have been suggested, including heating wax to release particular scents, and even stimulating neurons directly to create the experience of smell. But Yang argues her method is both fast and practical. She now hopes to expand the repertoire of the system, to create more complex aromas.

A declining ability to detect scents is linked to conditions including Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. But restoring our most neglected sense might not only reduce cognitive decline – studies also show it could even reverse it

She suggests the entertainment industry could be first to develop the technology, to create more immersive virtual worlds. But there could also be health applications. For instance, the smell of food transforms the eating experience, so the technology could be adapted to make soldiers’ or astronauts’ rations more palatable. The Scentronic system could also enable doctors to assess distortions in patients’ sense of smell, for example, in post-viral illness or neurodegenerative disease.

The Scentronic system is “a great idea” and a step in the right direction, says Marianna Obrist at University College London, although she points out that recognising a smell and then releasing a matching one from a limited library is very different from the ease with which we can transmit sound and vision. “There’s still a long way to go before we can truly record and replay smell experiences.”

Falling sea levels due to El Niño will hit mangroves and corals

New Scientist October 21, 2026

Higher sea levels in the eastern Pacific due to the monster El Niño are expected to cause record coastal flooding and erosion in the coming months. But on the other side of the Pacific, falling sea levels around Australia and the Coral Triangle – an area to the north of the continent – pose another threat that is only just starting to be recognised: mass die-offs of mangrove forests, with corals and seagrass meadows also impacted.

During the super El Niños in 1982/83 and 2015/16, there were mass diebacks of mangrove forests in northern Australia, says Norman Duke at James Cook University in Australia. In the 2015 event, around 76 square kilometres of mangroves on a 2000-kilometre-long stretch of shoreline in the Gulf of Carpentaria died.

This was due to a prolonged 40 to 50 centimetre drop in sea level for at least six months. Whether there is a similar or worse event during this El Niño will depend in part on how much rainfall there is.

Advertisement

El Niño has killed hundreds of children in Sudan

“Both [previous] events coincided with periods of low to no rainfall,” says Duke. “Mangroves, lacking inundation or other sources of moisture, died of thirst.”

During neutral and La Niña years, trade winds blowing west across the equatorial Pacific pile up warm water around Australia’s northeastern coast. When these winds weaken or reverse during El Niños, those waters spill across the Pacific. The result is a kind of see-saw effect, with sea levels falling in the west and rising in the east.

Because the current El Niño is so strong, it is producing a greater swing in sea levels than usual, with sea levels already up to 40 cm higher than typical in parts of the eastern Pacific near the equator but lower in a large swathe of the western Pacific, including around northern Australia and the Coral Triangle.

Free newsletter

Long-term tidal cycles can amplify or counteract the effects of falling sea levels, says Neil Saintilan at Macquarie University in Australia. Mangroves grow in the upper part of the tidal range, so if the tidal range decreases at the same time sea level falls, they are left high and dry, he says. “This happened in the Gulf of Carpentaria in 2015/16.”

During the ongoing El Niño, the tidal range in the Gulf of Carpentaria should be higher than normal, reducing the risk of dieback – though sea levels may fall further than in 2015.

However, along the coastline west of the gulf, the tidal range will be smaller than usual, says Saintilan. “We are anticipating extensive mangrove dieback there.”

This El Niño will bring predictable disasters, so why aren’t we ready?

The full scale of these sea-level effects on tidal ecosystems around the Pacific is only just becoming apparent. A 2025 satellite study concluded that in 2015/16, 34 per cent of the anomalies in mangrove leaf area index – a measure of canopy health – globally were due to sea-level changes.

Changes in sea level also affect corals and seagrass, Duke suspects. Shallow reefs and seagrass meadows are exposed during low tide and can dry out if falling sea levels leave them exposed too long. Even if they remain submerged, the temperature will be higher if the water is shallower, on top of the temperature rises caused by global warming and El Niño.

Though the El Niño is still months from its peak, it is already breaking many records. Two main factors are behind how it became so powerful

“Samoan colleagues refer to El Niño events as ‘Taimasa’ – periods marked by the smell of dead fish and coral, as they die on exposed coral reefs,” says Duke.

“It is quite possible that the sea-level drop contributes to the depth of reef dieback, though this would be dominated by the marine heatwaves themselves,” says Saintilan.

However, it appears that no studies have attempted to quantify the relative contributions of sea-level fall and marine heatwaves to the coral bleaching events and die-offs in the western Pacific during recent El Niños. “Despite several attempts, I have been unable to convince research colleagues working on corals and seagrasses that these events also contribute to those habitats as well,” says Duke.

Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery

New Scientist October 22, 2026

With powerful lasers and a tiny piece of plastic, researchers have for the first time emulated a violent process that may take place on the sun. The experiment could help shed light on why the outermost layer of the sun’s atmosphere is so mysteriously hot.

For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why the sun’s outer atmospheric layers – a region called the corona – are thousands of times hotter than the sun’s surface, reaching several millions of degrees. “It is as if the air grew hotter as you walked away from a campfire,” says Wei Sun at the China Institute of Atomic Energy.

Now, Sun and his colleagues have emulated some of the conditions on the sun in the lab and, for the first time, observed how tiny bursts of electromagnetic radiation, or solar nanoflares, could power the corona’s puzzling heat.

Advertisement

Sunquakes may be caused by weird beams of electrons from solar flares

Nanoflares are known to occur when magnetic fields within the corona abruptly rearrange themselves and emit energy in the process. But for this rearrangement to happen, the exact conditions, such as the shape of the magnetic fields, must be just right, says Sun. He and his colleagues investigated how these conditions could arise and ultimately lead to nanoflares. They fired four very powerful lasers onto a tiny plastic target, which produced a patch of plasma – a hot mixture of charged particles – about 2 millimetres across. This plasma was not an exact recreation of plasma in the sun’s corona but behaved analogously.

The team created plasmas in two different scenarios, once using a flat target and once using one with a wavy surface. In the second case, the plasma became unstable and the magnetic fields it contained rearranged themselves and ultimately produced a nanoflare.

This nanoflare made a big difference to the temperature of the plasma. It reached temperatures of 799,726°C, which was nearly double the temperature achieved in the flat target version of the experiment where no nanoflares occurred.

A similar process – instability leading to nanoflares leading to plasma heating – could feasibly happen on the sun, says Sun. In fact, the parameters that determined their tiny plasma’s behaviour matched those observed in regions of the sun where blobs of colder plasma “rain” down through the corona. He and his colleagues also completed a computer simulation that corroborated this.

Coronal holes allow more charged particles to escape the sun as solar winds, and on 29 January, NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory spacecraft spotted a vast new one

Rony Keppens at KU Leuven in Belgium says that these simulations support the team’s interpretation of the experiment and make for an interesting entry on to the list of effects that may be contributing to coronal heating. Coronal rain blobs really could lead to the kinds of instabilities that the researchers now spotted in the lab, he says. Yet, in Keppens’s view, the new experiment does not definitively resolve the coronal heating puzzle, as other plasma behaviours, such as certain types of waves in it, could also contribute to it.

Going forward, Sun and his colleagues want to upgrade their experiment to create more three-dimensional plasmas and use more precise techniques for diagnosing its behaviour. And they want to make their laboratory measurements more directly comparable to reality – for example, by using data about the sun collected through telescopes, says Sun. “It is important to check that the laboratory is reproducing what the sun does,” he says.

Earth entered its ‘bad decades’ after dinosaur-ending asteroid strike

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Decades of chaos and destruction, filled with devastating earthquakes and tsunamis, followed the asteroid strike 66 million years ago that wiped out all dinosaurs apart from birds.

The long-term global chaos inflicted by the Chicxulub asteroid, which was up to 15 kilometres in diameter and struck what is now the Gulf of Mexico, has been revealed through analysis of sediments preserved on the New Jersey coast, thousands of kilometres away from the impact crater.

It has become increasingly apparent in recent years that the asteroid’s effects weren’t confined to a single, disastrously bad day, but instead lasted a lot longer. For instance, the deformation of the crust to a depth of 35 kilometres left the impact site hot for millions of years.

Advertisement

We could protect Earth from dangerous asteroids using a huge magnet

It is also now thought that in the shorter term, a catastrophic maelstrom of fire engulfed much of the planet as debris that was hurled into space rained back down on Earth, burning up as it re-entered the atmosphere.

“Earth’s ‘bad day’ is when the Chicxulub impact occurred,” says Kenneth Miller at Rutgers University in New Jersey. “However, that was just the beginning of the story.”

The asteroid strike unleashed an earthquake felt around the world that was between magnitude 10 and 11, creating tsunamis that may have been a kilometre high close to the impact zone.

“Chicxulub rung the bell of the planet, and then it continued to ring for decades,” says Miller.

Free newsletter

“These deposits in New Jersey change our view about how long organisms were exposed to extremely detrimental environmental degradation,” he says. “That’s a fancy professor way of saying shit was really bad for 20 years.”

The researchers took rock cores from multiple sites on the New Jersey coastal plain, more than 2500 kilometres from the impact crater, to study the geology in the area in the years following the disaster.

These cores show that sediment layers deposited after the fallout from the asteroid were mixed and remobilised multiple times.

Such reworking of deposits is only possible through large, ongoing earthquakes and tsunamis, says Miller. Possibly more than a dozen aftershocks, which may have been in the order of magnitude 7 and 8, were felt on the New Jersey coast alone.

Earliest alligator flourished in the wake of the dinosaur extinction

Miller and his colleagues say the cores recovered from New Jersey record the transition from the catastrophic moments following the Chicxulub impact right through to a longer-term disruption, a period they have now named Earth’s “bad decades”.

Another intriguing finding from the New Jersey cores is the presence of large quantities of kaolinite, which normally forms over centuries from weathering in tropical regions, but may have formed in just years at the team’s study sites.

This could have been due to the presence of vast amounts of fungi, which can accelerate the formation of kaolinite, says Miller. The team speculates this is possible evidence that, during the nuclear winter-like conditions thought to have followed the impact, much of the planet’s vegetation died, providing a veritable feast for microorganisms.

Top predators still prowled the seas after the biggest mass extinction

The team has developed a new timeline for the first 20 years post-asteroid, beginning with the extraordinary and dramatic events of the first day.

This was followed by dust settling back to Earth from the atmosphere, leading to near-complete darkness for up to three years, followed by nuclear winter-like conditions for up to 20 years and fungal proliferation. All the while, the planet was beset by aftershocks and tsunamis.

“New Jersey preserves one of the highest-resolution records yet recovered of the first decades after Chicxulub, allowing researchers to resolve environmental and geological processes year-by-year to decade-by-decade, rather than viewing the aftermath as a single catastrophic instant,” says Miller.

Craig O’Neill at Queensland University of Technology, Australia, says the team has presented a record that “lets us really unpick what was going on immediately after the impact”.

“This builds on a long compendium of work globally suggesting that the environmental and biological impacts of ‘mega-events’ like Chicxulub go far beyond the impact blast itself,” he says.

The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago filled the sky with fine silicate dust, which blocked out sunlight and lingered for 15 years

Chris Kirkland at Curtin University, Australia, says the site records processes that operated over years to decades after the impact, rather than simply its immediate aftermath.

“The really interesting aspect of the study is the potential to resolve not just the immediate consequences of the impact, including ejecta fallout, sediment reworking and tsunami-related processes, but the longer-lasting environmental disturbance,” he says.

Annemarie Pickersgill at the University of Glasgow, UK, says the New Jersey findings provide further evidence for long-term seismicity also recorded in other regions of Earth.

“These [New Jersey] sites preserve a detailed record of the geological and environmental conditions in the decades following the Chicxulub impact, providing new insights into the aftereffects of a very large impact event,” she says.

All tropical coral reefs could collapse within 50 years

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Imagine a world without tropical coral reefs, a world nearly devoid of iconic species like elkhorn and pillar corals and sea creatures like the clownfish from Finding Nemo. That world could come to pass within 50 years due to humanity’s continuing fossil fuel emissions.

At least 96 per cent of shallow-water coral reef ecosystems are at extremely high risk of collapsing by 2075, according to an assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the leading authority on endangered species. The remaining ecosystems weren’t evaluated due to lack of data, but are probably just as vulnerable, according to Marcos Valderrábano at the IUCN.

“All coral reef ecosystems that we assess, they are all critically endangered, and that’s really surprising,” he says. “In some regions of the world, there is a lot of bleaching, but some other regions of the world are not doing that bad. But what the projections are telling us is that this is going to be affecting all coral ecosystems in the planet in the next 50 years.”

Fishers detonate a bomb every hour on one Indonesian coral reef

The IUCN assessment was presented at the biannual UN biodiversity summit now taking place in Armenia. It shows countries where they need to protect reefs by reducing fishing quotas and pollution, according to Valderrábano.

Scientists have previously cautioned that warm-water coral reefs are probably crossing a tipping point beyond which they couldn’t recover, but the IUCN warning demonstrates how quickly and massively reef die-offs could unfold.

The shallow reefs in tropical and subtropical waters undergird ecosystems that can include thousands of species of corals, molluscs, fish and larger vertebrates like sea turtles and sharks. They cover only 1 per cent of the ocean, but support 25 per cent of marine species. Up to 1 billion people rely on coral reefs for fishing, as well as for tourism income and for protection from erosion and storms.

Free newsletter

While small pockets of coral could live on after the collapse of larger ecosystems like the Great Barrier Reef, they could become too dispersed for the eggs and sperm they release into the water to cross-fertilise.

“If the population size gets so small that you don’t have another coral to mate with nearby, then reproductive failure will happen,” says James Guest at Newcastle University, UK. “That species is in what’s called an extinction vortex.”

Coral reefs also exist in deeper, colder waters, including around the UK coast, but they are much less biodiverse and corals there don’t form symbiotic relationships with algae.

Coral reefs on a remote archipelago shrugged off a massive heatwave

So far, only one shallow-water coral reef ecosystem has collapsed. The reefs of the western Galapagos Islands lost 95 per cent of their coral – the IUCN’s threshold for ecosystem collapse – after the 1982/83 super El Niño climate phase unleashed a marine heatwave, turning golden brush corals into white skeletons overgrown by string algae.

But since then, four mass bleaching events have devastated many other corals. These animals form a symbiotic relationship with algae, which live inside the coral’s tissue and provide it with sugar from photosynthesis. However, algae stressed by warming or polluted waters can give off damaging reactive compounds like free radicals. It is thought that corals temporarily eject the colourful algae in self-defence, leaving the coral a ghostly white. If the warming lasts long enough, the corals essentially starve to death.

All these mass bleaching events came after strong El Niños, and experts fear the current record El Niño will usher in another one. Regardless, individual reefs are now bleaching nearly every year due to global warming, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Yet another mass-bleaching event could speed up coral collapse, since reef ecosystems don’t have time to recover if they are hit by more than three bleaching events within five years, says Valderrábano. “It would definitely reinforce that perverse loop,” he says.

Bleaching has devastated reefs around the world, raising fears of an irreversible shift. Yet new interventions have revealed that corals can be remarkably resilient if we can give them enough help to recover

The IUCN projection is based on a “middle-of-the-road” scenario with moderate emissions reductions. But such a future isn’t necessarily a death sentence for all shallow-water reefs because scientists don’t know exactly how fast corals worldwide can adapt to warming, says Guest. His research in the Pacific archipelago of Palau suggests corals there have been developing 0.1°C of additional heat tolerance per decade.

“But if we get a really severe heatwave, it’s quite likely that the increase in heat tolerance isn’t going to be enough to protect those reefs,” he says.

Some scientists have called for interventions like spreading sunshades over reefs or geoengineering clouds over the ocean to protect species like coral from the record current El Niño. But the best defence for corals is reducing emissions, says Valderrábano.

“The more we can do to reduce pressure on them, the better chance they have of using their natural capacity to adapt and recover,” says Guest.

Adults may be more creative than children – but less confident about it

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Adults are often thought to be less creative than children, as we swap painting for presentations and sandpits for spreadsheets. But in a new study, children actually performed worse on creativity tests than adults – yet made up for it in confidence.

“We found that adults are actually more creative thinkers,” says Mathias Benedek at the University of Graz in Austria. “But children enjoy creativity more and are much less worried about what others think about their ideas.”

How to extend and improve your life by getting more creative

There is a popular belief that children are more creative than adults, he says, which may come from children having more time and opportunities to engage in creative activities. Yet prior research suggests that creativity actually increases with age.

Advertisement

These studies were often based on a single task, like imagining alternative uses for everyday objects, says Benedek. Taking a broader approach, he and his colleagues recruited 92 children (aged between 4 and 7) and 70 adults (aged 25, on average) to carry out three creative tasks.

First, they had to come up with as many alternative uses for a tin can as possible within 3 minutes. Then, they drew freely for 8 minutes, and in the final task, they had 8 minutes to draw an animal that doesn’t exist.

Five people who weren’t involved in the research were then trained to objectively judge creativity based on originality and whether the final result fulfilled the brief of the task.

In the first task, the adults scored 3.9 points, on average, out of 5, while the children scored 2.9 points. One of the adults imagined a tin can could be used as a “Halloween candy box when on (a) diet”, whereas some children imagined it as a rattle.

Free newsletter

In the second and third tasks, the adults scored 0.6 and 1.9 points higher, respectively, than the children.

The findings underscore how creativity draws on combining ideas from prior experience, says Wendy Ross at King’s College London. For instance, adults are probably aware of more animals than children, so have a greater variety of creatures to draw from when producing a fantasy animal.

After completing the tasks, the participants were asked questions like “How well do you think you performed the task?”, “How much were you worried/anxious to not perform well on the task?” and “How much fun was the task?”.

The researchers found that the children were substantially more confident in what they produced, scoring their performances 4.8 and 4.6 points for the free drawing and animal tasks, respectively, compared with the adults’ 2.8 and 3.3 scoring.

An experiment showed AI users had the most creative ideas when they used it in moderation – not too much and not too little. Columnist David Robson puts the finding to the test, and explores what we lose when we over-rely on AI

The children also reported lower anxiety compared with the adults. “If the purpose of creativity is to have enjoyment in it, to play and to be unfettered humans, then children are doing better at that,” says Ross.

But the two groups got a similar level of pleasure from the animal-drawing task. Adults may have liked that task’s specific instruction, which may have meant they worried less about being judged for their idea, says Benedek.

Regardless of the quality of the end result, people should try to be more creative for their wellbeing, says Ross. Engaging with the arts has been linked to reduced mental health problems and greater social skills. “Creativity, especially when done with other people, is really beneficial to your mental wellbeing – and you don’t have to score 5 out of 5 on a ranking scale,” she says.

PLOS One DOI: 10.1371/journal. pone.0346553

Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Cybersecurity experts around the globe are racing to update systems and prevent the most disruptive AI-enabled hack yet discovered. A flaw uncovered in widely used code has made 70 per cent of websites worldwide vulnerable to data theft and defacement.

Government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands were taken offline as a precaution when the news emerged.

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

PHP is a computer language commonly used to power interactive websites, such as the content management system WordPress, which runs news sites and blogs; social networks like Facebook; and key reference tools like Wikipedia. The hack therefore affects websites, rather than individuals’ personal computers.

Advertisement

The issue actually involves two flaws, both found by cloud security company Wiz. They relate to how PHP handles errors involving memory: in certain circumstances, data can be left behind after an error, which can then be accessed by a malicious actor. That data can include private information, but it can also allow an attacker to run malicious code.

Every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, but the PHP Foundation, which oversees development, has already issued an update to overcome this.

The foundation didn’t respond to a request for interview, but said in a blog post that signs of the vulnerability emerged in 2024. Yet nothing was done. This is because there was no immediately obvious practical way for hackers to exploit it at the time, and because there was debate about which of several fixes was most appropriate.

Free newsletter

“We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources,” the PHP Foundation said.

In 2024, the flaw was thought to be impractical to take advantage of, but Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK, says AI has moved the goalposts of what is possible since then.

“It’s actually very, very difficult to exploit it. It requires millisecond timing,” says Woodward. “The reason it was thought to be too complicated was it would have taken a team of people yonks to actually work out the right timings. But what AI does, it doesn’t go for tea breaks, it doesn’t go home at 6 o’clock: you can just set loads of them running and eventually they’ll come up with the right answer of how to exploit it.”

Wiz said in a blog post announcing the discovery that there are probably further bugs along similar lines in the PHP code base, which developers will also need to identify and rectify. Wiz didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Every time a new technology hits the internet, there is a battle between the rights of users and major companies. To see how this will play out with AI, columnist Jacob Aron looks to examples from the past

Independent cybersecurity expert Junade Ali told the Science Media Centre that two thirds of websites use PHP and may be vulnerable to this latest technique.

“The key long-term risk with these new vulnerabilities is that organisations fail to implement protections and update software, particularly in legacy systems,” said Ali. “The security posture of websites using PHP has dramatically improved over the past decade, but this highlights that this is an ever-present problem – particularly when AI agents are capable of remorselessly pursuing the goal of finding new vulnerabilities.”

Woodward thinks that while most large websites will have already patched their systems, smaller sites with less expertise and resources could still be vulnerable months or years from now. “There will be this long tail and you’ll find some surprising sites have not been patched,” he says.

AI has grown extremely capable in the field of cybersecurity over recent months, which includes working out how to hack computers and how to defend them from hackers, creating a destabilising effect that is yet to reach an equilibrium.

There is a growing backlash against the way AI companies have gone about tackling mathematical problems – and now some mathematicians are opting to avoid AI altogether

In April, news broke of an unreleased AI model created by Anthropic called Mythos, which the company had kept under wraps because it had been found to be extremely good at hacking. The news sparked panic among cybersecurity experts. NHS England pulled its open-source projects, for instance, over fears Mythos may scour code for flaws and exploit its systems.

Three months later, OpenAI admitted one of its prototype models had escaped a testing environment and hacked another company, Hugging Face. Not to be outdone, Anthropic announced within days that its Claude model had gone rogue and broken into machines at other companies on three occasions.

We even learned from the National Cyber Security Centre, the UK government department tasked with securing the nation’s IT infrastructure, that the country’s four main cyber adversaries – Russia, China, North Korea and Iran – are using AI to boost their ability to perform “relentless” attacks on the UK.

Labour's Kerrin Leoni has resigned as a candidate, following video emerging of her campaigning with gang members.

In a statement, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said:

"Kerrin Leoni has resigned as a Labour candidate. I have made it very clear that campaigning alongside gangs is unacceptable.

"The footage that has emerged is inconsistent with the standards I expect of Labour candidates.

"I understand that families are complex. You can't choose your family, and I firmly believe people should be supported to leave gangs and turn their lives around.

"But candidates are responsible for their own choices, and when they fall short of the standard I expect, I will hold them to account.

"Because nominations have closed, Kerrin's name will still appear on the ballot. However, she is no longer a Labour candidate and does not represent the party."

One of the most consequential figures in this year's election will not be on the ballot next month. She may not even be in the country, having instead begun measuring the drapes at her new mansion in Sydney.

More than three years after she called time on her premiership, the ghost of Dame Jacinda Ardern still hangs in the political air like a different kind of power.

"Everything I've ever thought about doing has been, in some sense, about helping people," Ardern used to say, but right now some of her old foes – and perhaps more than a few old friends as well – might be happier she concentrated more on her Australian digs.

In New Zealand, opinion surveys have her beating out most others in the preferred Prime Minister stakes, while her international profile remains impressively intact – certainly here in the British capital where these words are being tapped out. Even Waterstones has her memoir prominently displayed in the section the bookstore chain usually sets aside for rock star biographies.

And why not? The emotionally nimble premier remains the New Zealand political figure who Brits are most likely to think they know and, in many cases, sincerely admire, an affection dating back to the earliest days of her premiership.

An Olympic gold medal won by a New Zealand rowing legend has been replaced after it was stolen during a burglary at his Christchurch home.

Leslie “Les” O’Connell, 67, said at the time of the February theft that he and his wife had been in Napier for a wedding when the break-in occurred, leaving their home unattended.

O’Connell said he was “gutted” at the time and appealed directly to those responsible not to destroy the medal.

However, since the theft of his original medal earlier this year, the New Zealand Olympic Committee (NZOC) has worked with the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to secure an official replacement.

O’Connell said the support he received since the theft meant a great deal to him and his family.

“Since the medal was stolen, I’ve been humbled by the level of support and goodwill to find a solution,” O’Connell said.

“I’m incredibly grateful to the NZOC and the IOC for making this possible.”

Email us

O’Connell said the medal meant a “great deal” for his family’s second and third generations.

“Particularly around Olympic time, the medal normally goes on school trips; it’s really valuable to show kids what you can achieve, and the medal is a symbol of that,” he said.

“The kids love handling it, they love touching it, they love putting it around their neck. If that inspires someone to do something, that’s good.”

Despite having a replacement medal, O’Connell still hoped the original would resurface, as “it’s of no value to anyone else”.

“If there’s someone out there who has the medal or knows something, please do the right thing and return it,” he said.

New Zealand Olympic Committee chief executive Nicki Nicol said she was pleased to source a replacement for O’Connell and his family.

“Winning an Olympic gold medal is something many athletes aspire to, but few have the honour of achieving,” she said.

“We’re grateful to the IOC for helping replace this special taonga for Les.

“These athletes helped shape New Zealand’s sporting legacy and their achievements continue to inspire generations of New Zealanders.”

O’Connell had won the medal as part of New Zealand’s men’s coxless four at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympic Games after consecutive world championship titles.

“As we head back to Los Angeles in 2028, we do so with pride, following in the footsteps of what Les and his crew achieved there in 1984,” Nicol said.

It’s not the first time a member of the winning coxless four team has had their gold medal stolen.

In 2006, thieves broke into Shane O’Brien’s Sandringham home and took his gold medal, as well as the bronze and silver medals from the 1986 Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh, among other items.

National has said it’s an “appalling look” that a Labour Party candidate was seen mingling with gang members while wearing a party-branded jacket.

It was revealed yesterday that Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni spent time with gang members while “visiting whānau”.

She initially denied it before footage began circulating showing Leoni at the event amongst Mongrel Mob members, while wearing a Labour Party jacket.

The topic has become controversial, with The Post reporting the event being advertised online as a “fundraiser for the Mongrel Mob’s Rogue Chapter”.

National MP Paul Goldsmith this morning told Ryan Bridge TODAY with Nadine Higgins that it was an “appalling” look.

“We’re not sure whether it was the Labour Party fundraising for the Mongrel Mob or the Mongrel Mob fundraising for the Labour Party,” he said.

“Whichever way it was, it’s an appalling look.”

Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan maintained Leoni’s take.

“Look, we don’t have all the details; we’ve just got what’s reported in the news, we’ve got what Kerrin has said and I’m going with that.

“She was at a whānau event.”

When asked by Higgins whether people should distance themselves from family who are gang members, Goldsmith said they could make other decisions.

“You do get to choose whether you go in your Labour Party jacket to a fundraiser; that’s a separate issue,” he said.

“It just goes to show it’s very murky and unclear the mixed messages the previous Labour Party sent to the gangs; ‘we don’t like you some days and we’ll fundraise you others’.”

He said the Labour Party was “all over the place” when it came to gangs.

“Chris Hipkins was trying to put distance between himself, the Green Party and the Māori Party on their close relationship with the Mongrel Mob,” Goldsmith said.

“But the reality is the Labour Party has been in lockstep with those two parties opposing everything we’ve done on law and order in the past three years...”

Chris Hipkins yesterday said he was accepting Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni’s word that she didn’t visit a gang pad as part of election campaigning.

The Labour leader is expected to address the situation at the A&P show in Hawke’s Bay this morning.

Radhakrishnan also questioned Goldsmith on National “not delivering its 500 police officers”.

“Which means that we have more gangs than police and meth has tripled, that’s the real story.”

Labour has not yet released its law-and-order election policy.

Speaking with Mike Hosking Breakfast on Newstalk ZB this morning, Act leader David Seymour said he saw the video of Leoni’s event “flash up on his screen” last night.

“Look, I think what is happening and why it’s been in the news for two weeks and why everyone’s talking about it, is because it reveals what’s at stake this election.

“Labour and their allies let gangs and violent crime get out of control because their basic attitude is, ‘what happens in life is somebody else’s fault’, including crime.”

A young man from Vanuatu was mistakenly diagnosed with syphilis from a sore on his foot but actually had a rare disease that is still lingering in the Pacific Islands.

Tauranga-based sexual health medicine specialist Dr Massimo Giola said the man had yaws, a tropical skin infection that causes lesions or ulcers, but can be treated with penicillin.

Giola said there was no cause for alarm among the New Zealand public, as the disease does not spread easily, but he wanted other clinicians to be aware that they might come across yaws in their practice.

“There’s no reason to panic or for Kiwis to think this is a new epidemic, absolutely not, it’s been around for a millennia probably, and it doesn’t spread easily at all,” he said.

The case was highlighted in a report in the NZ Medical Journal published today.

The young man was first referred to Giola as a case of syphilis, presenting to him with a coin-sized ulcer on his right foot that was reddish in colour and inflamed.

Giola has worked in sexual health services in the Bay of Plenty and the Rotorua Lakes district for about 10 years and after talking with the man, immediately suspected he did not have syphilis, but yaws.

Yaws can be mistaken for syphilis as it is caused by a very close relative to the syphilis pathogen, with the difference between the two diseases only being a few nucleotides across a whole DNA genome.

“Yaws used to be very endemic in the Pacific, so it was all over the place basically, but the World Health Organisation [WHO] started an eradication campaign that was successful, however there are still a few remaining pockets,” Giola said.

“It’s still present in places like Vanuatu, Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea.”

The disease usually presented in childhood with a sore appearing on the lower legs or feet, and typically healed without treatment but sometimes complications could emerge from infection, he said.

About 75-80% of people affected by yaws were children under 15 years of age, according to WHO.

University of Otago deputy vice-chancellor, Pacific, Professor Dianne Sika-Paotonu, said if left untreated, yaws could result in disfigurement and debilitating complications.

Permanent scarring with skin and bone deformities could occur with chronic lesions that could also lead to restricted movement in the affected joints, she said.

The young man Giola saw came to New Zealand on a seasonal visa and was likely infected later in life.

In order to contract yaws a person would need “very intimate and prolonged skin to skin contact” with an active case, Giola said.

It was not possible to get the disease from using shared public spaces such as a public toilet or an airplane.

“There’s absolutely no reason to discriminate against people from the Pacific Islands because of this,” he said.

It was important New Zealand clinicians were aware that yaws was still out there when screening patients, and to prescribe the correct treatment, which was typically a shot of penicillin, he said.

The disease was rarely seen in developed countries.

Yaws is categorised as a neglected tropical disease by WHO, forming part of a group of diseases that affect mostly tropical or subtropical communities but receive very little global health funding.

Giola said there was some patchy knowledge about the potential for complications with yaws because there had not been enough investment in research about the disease.

“Part of that is because yaws mostly only affect poor countries and these are diseases of poverty, and there’s just not much money being invested in research,” he said.

Sika-Paotonu said inequities and disparities in health and health outcomes have persisted over time for Pacific and Māori communities in Aotearoa New Zealand and in the Pacific region.

She said ongoing shortages of healthcare professionals, inadequate resourcing of providers and difficulties in accessing primary care services all remained significant challenges.

“Addressing gaps and inequities for different communities requires properly resourced and targeted approaches that are appropriate and that recognise the specific needs of different groups that may be present,” she said.

“When people cannot easily access a health professional or face delays in follow-up care, diagnoses are more likely to occur later, and treatment may therefore be less effective.

“Ensuring timely and accessible healthcare is essential so people can receive care when they need it most.”

The recent HIV crisis in Fiji highlighted the ongoing health needs in the Pacific.

In September, Fiji’s Government declared an HIV national emergency after figures showed one in 60 adults was living with the virus.

The alarming emergence of such high rates of HIV in the population was linked to a growing methamphetamine crisis in the country and the sharing of needles from drug use.

The Herald earlier spoke to Sir Collin Tukuitonga, a prominent Pasifika doctor, about a trend of “bluetoothing” that was contributing to the surge in HIV cases.

It involved drug users taking blood from themselves and injecting it into a friend to share the supply of a drug, enabling another person to get high off the drug because they couldn’t afford to purchase it.

Sika-Paotonu said without improvements in equity and accessibility to timely healthcare, the existing pressures would likely further widen existing disparities in the Pacific region, and for Pacific and Māori communities.

Giola said after the young man received treatment, his lesion had fully healed and he had recovered.

Trains in Auckland have been cancelled or delayed this morning after the City Rail Link tunnel was temporarily closed.

The closure early this morning meant trains were not stopping at some stations, including Karanga-a-Hape and Te Waihorotiu.

Auckland Transport (AT) says the “infrastructure issues” affecting the network have since been resolved and all train lines are returning to their normal route.

“Expect some delays and cancellations while trains return to schedule,” AT’s website says.

Passengers are still being advised to check the live departures board or digital screens at stations before boarding.

Buses are also accepting train tickets, AT said.

The East West, South City and Onehunga West lines were all affected by the closure.

Everyone is making ’90s alt-rock again. Why?

Sydney Morning Herald October 23, 2026

A new generation, including chart-topper Olivia Rodrigo, is tapping into the sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music.

It’s happened often lately. I’m listening to the week’s buzzy new albums, and all of a sudden – amid chiming guitars, singsong harmonies and crunchy distortion – I’m transported back to my teenage bedroom, listening to Siamese Dream and watching Daria in the orange after-school glow.

The sound and spirit of ’90s guitar music – from the melodic jangle of R. E. M. and Sugar, to the lush distortion of Sonic Youth and My Bloody Valentine – is suddenly everywhere. Earlier this year, Olivia Rodrigo – a noted ’90s lover who took The Breeders on tour and recently revived Lilith Fair for a new generation – even sent the sound to the top of the pop charts with her album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, and its jangly highlight, U + Me = <3.

Emily Massey, lead singer of US indie darlings Slow Pulp – whose new album Melodie builds inventively on their signature alt-’90s foundations – says the era holds an untarnished mystique for Millennials and Zoomers raised in its wake. “We were little kids in the ’90s, so there’s a sense of longing for a time you have some sense of but don’t have fully formed memories of,” she says.

Slow Pulp formed in Madison, Wisconsin, the city where Butch Vig famously produced the likes of Nirvana and The Smashing Pumpkins at his Smart Studios. “Growing up, there was something in the air, this feeling of, oh, that’s what’s cool,” says Henry Stoehr, the band’s songwriter and guitarist.

Over a decade removed from the last dregs of blokey landfill-indie, and with pop’s top stars offering diminished returns, rock music and fuzzy guitars – so central to youth culture in the ’90s – are cool again.

Charli XCX, a couple of years removed from “Brat Summer”, this year declared “the dance floor is dead” and pivoted to rock music on her new album. Alt-rockers like Phoebe Bridgers and Cameron Winter (along with his band Geese) have become surprise chart phenomenons, and bands like Turnstile, Fontaines D. C., Wednesday and This Is Lorelei are critical darlings and festival favourites.

Stoehr understands why the ’90s and its sonics has captivated a generation who came of age amid COVID lockdowns. “I feel like post-2020, there was this pent-up feeling of wanting to get out and enjoy yourself and just ‘vibe’, that psychologically lent itself towards club culture and party culture, just because people were deprived of that for longer than was ideal.

“We loved that stuff, too!” he adds. “But you reach a point where it’s like, ‘I’m kind of done partying and I want something that is packed with meaning, something that’s gonna hit me in the gut.’ And I feel like that’s the purpose that rock music has always served, and people are craving that.”

Swapmeet, a buzzy Adelaide band whose members are all 23, bonded over a shared love of ’90s acts like Sonic Youth and Pavement. Their new album Mount Zero touches on Swirlies-style noise and Flying Nun-inflected jangle-pop, while their last EP featured the reverb-drenched atmospherics of Mazzy Star.

Guitarist Maxwell Elphick says he got into grunge via Guitar Hero and the CDs his uncle gave him as a teen. The ’90s era’s scrappy DIY looseness immediately appealed to him.

“It feels like weird music became cool and popular then, like you didn’t have to be a great vocalist to be in a good band. It was very much just if you could write songs, you could do it, which was really cool. That’s why I gravitated towards it,” he says.

“We’d be making this kind of music anyway, but it’s great that people think rock music is cool again. Because I feel like everyone thought it was a little cringe for a bit.”

Of course, amid a critical discourse that favours innovation and “forward-thinking music” over repeating the sounds of yore, looking back can mean being overlooked.

“There’s not much originality left in music in terms of what hasn’t been done, and that’s not what we’re trying to do anyway, and I’m sure a lot of music heads would have something to say about that,” says Nina Pitchkites, vocalist/guitarist of US band Wishy, with an era-appropriate eye roll.

Kevin Krauter, the band’s guitarist, says while the new wave of ’90s revivalists aren’t reinventing the wheel, they’re tapping into the way music has functioned since the dawn of time. “Think about blues music,” he says, “they’re all just playing these standards, but what makes someone stand out and special is the unique style and personality they bring to it.”

For Wishy, whose fantastic new album Nature’s Pill revives ’90s power-pop and twee – a particular strain of sweet, fuzzy, melodic alt-rock laden with boy-girl harmonies and inspired by cult ’90s indie-rockers like Velocity Girl and Tiger Trap – the current era’s cultural conditions have set an intriguing proposition.

In the ’90s in the US, twee and riot grrrl – mostly on Pacific Northwest record labels like K Records and Kill Rock Stars – were driven by feminist politics and anti-macho sensibilities. So, has the age of Donald Trump and the manosphere set the stage for a ’90s-twee revival?

On a couch in his parents’ home in Carmel, Indiana, Krauter ponders the question. “You saw the same thing in the Bush-era of the early 2000s, and we got a lot of effeminate emo music coming out of that, guys wearing really skinny jeans and guyliner, sort of throwing a big middle finger to the macho stereotype that was the dominant structure of the state and culture at the time,” he says.

When chauvinism and toxic masculinity is the prevailing culture, it seems natural that artists would want to subvert it. Suddenly, it’s more transgressive to be gentle and sincere – or, as three-inch badges in the ’90s put it, “twee as f—.” There’s already evidence in the burgeoning nu-twee movement featuring (admittedly less guitar-centric) cult bands like ear and Worldpeace DMT and The Femcels.

“You think about the Obama-era when we had Burger Records and garage rock, that whole scene was so macho,” Krauter adds as a contrast, citing the hipster hub of trash-rock bands like Black Lips. Burger Records folded in 2020 amid sexual assault accusations over its roster.

“I remember being in high school and going to DIY shows and the whole attitude of that scene was very ‘whatever, f— it’. But then, around 2016 when Trump was elected, you started to see more of this ‘softboi’ vibe enter the culture. And so it makes sense that people would rediscover twee attitudes and aesthetics right now”.

Although they’re an indie act, signed to the label Winspear, the wild success of bands like Geese points to breakout potential they never imagined a couple of years ago when Wishy released their debut, Triple Seven.

“I mean, hopefully all this will result in some kind of favour for us, that’d be nice,” Krauter deadpans. “Like, suddenly rock music is super lucrative again? That would be convenient.”

His cynicism is noted, but it’s not out of the realm of possibility that Rodrigo – noted fan of lovelorn indie melodies and crunchy riffs, a true ’90s twee-girl at heart – could bring them on tour as an opener.

“That’d be crazy,” Krauter says. “Olivia, hit us up.”

Slow Pulp’s Melodie, Wishy’s Nature’s Pill and Swapmeet’s Mount Zero are out now.

The funeral where the worlds of power, politics and organised crime came together

Sydney Morning Herald October 23, 2026

The 2023 burial of the father of disgraced former building union chief John Setka revealed the deep interconnections of Victoria’s troubled construction industry.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
