On a cold, drizzly late-August day in 2023, John Setka prepared to bury his father, Bob. The service was at St Leopold’s in Sunshine, a modern church built by the local Croatian community in the 1980s, and whose stunning stained-glass windows helped brighten the interior in defiance of the chilly weather. Amid the pews stood an ornate statue of St Leopold himself, a Croatian Catholic priest famous for hearing confession for up to 15 hours a day.

Despite the grim event, Setka, the then-leader of the Construction, Forestry & Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU), felt at home. Those around him were his people, his backers from the trade union movement and his supporters from Melbourne’s tight-knit Croatian community. There were other attendees, too. Sitting among the pale-orange pews at St Leopold’s that day was Jacinta Allan, the state Labor minister responsible for Victoria’s enormous Big Build program.

Allan struck something of an incongruous figure amid the burly unionists and proud Croatian community members. But her attendance was as much about supporting Bob Setka’s son as it was about paying tribute to the deceased. John Setka’s union members were being paid handsomely on the Big Build while the fast-expanding city of Melbourne got the infrastructure it needed. Allan, from Labor’s socialist left faction, was also overseeing projects where the CFMEU had out-muscled the rival right-wing Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) run by her ex-husband, Ben Davis. The senior minister would likely need Setka’s support if she ever wanted to become the premier of Victoria, so it was time for a public show of support for the grieving CFMEU leader.

Setka senior was lucky to have lived so long. He should have died in 1970. On October 15 of that year, Bob, an ironworker and rigger, was smoking a cigarette while looking out over Port Melbourne from high up on the West Gate Bridge when he heard a terrific cracking sound. “The bridge go down and I go like this, higher,” Bob Setka recalled years later of being catapulted upwards. As he flew through the air, he thought of his young family, which included six-year-old John. The next thing he knew, he was lying in the mud of Stony Creek, far below the bridge. He looked around and thought, Oh, my god, I’m still alive.

As soon as Bob’s brother heard the news, he rushed to the scene, unsure whether Bob was alive or dead, and somehow he found him. Many of the other men lying in the muck amid a twisted mess of concrete and steel were not so lucky. The dead numbered 35, with Bob being one of only 18 survivors. He gave aid to the fallen and never forgot to pay his dues to the only buggers he believed cared about workers’ safety: the men of the union, the Builders Labourers Federation (BLF).

When Bob Setka was buried at St Leopold’s, it was not just a family and Croatian community affair. Underworld figure Mick Gatto had published a message in The Age offering his “deepest and sincerest condolences to John and all the Setka family”, while politician Luba Grigorovitch would later pay tribute to Bob in the Victorian Parliament.

The worlds of his famous son – of power, politics and organised crime – had come together for Bob Setka’s funeral.

Boze Setka was born in 1934 in the short-lived Kingdom of Yugoslavia, but when he arrived in Australia in the 1960s, he became known simply as Bob. Those who worked with Bob described a quiet, humble man. He was tall, with an enormous frame like his son, but he lacked John’s gregariousness and had none of his son’s mercurial ability to combine menace with charm and humour.

But there were shared threads in their respective lives, whether it was unionism or pride in their background. For John Setka, the story of his father’s survival was a pivotal moment, a touchstone he returned to over the decades to explain his choice of career: that of a union man. “That’s why my lucky number’s 18,” he would say, referencing the West Gate disaster. “There was 18 survivors that day.”

Years later, John Setka remembered going to school in Melbourne’s west with children whose dads did not survive the fall. On Father’s Day at school, they would make gifts for their fathers and those children would be haunted by their loss. Setka the son never forgot. In one CFMEU video clip, he can be seen choking back tears as he hugs his own son while Bob speaks about surviving the West Gate calamity.

Like so many other Croatian migrants to Melbourne in the 1960s and 1970s, Setka senior gravitated to the growing diaspora communities in the city’s industrial west and Geelong. Work was plentiful in the factories and building sites of the burgeoning city, and there were opportunities for men like Bob Setka to make a new life for their families.

The Setka family lived in working-class Footscray, and by John Setka’s own telling, he was a tearaway and often in trouble. When police arrived at the front door of the family home looking for him, Setka’s mum, Mila, never doubted her son. “Johnny’s a good boy,” she’d say on repeat. Decades later, Setka would laugh at his mother’s unwavering devotion, no matter what wrong he’d done.

By the time he was 19, John Setka was following his father’s footsteps into the construction industry as a labourer and part of what was then the Maoist-led Builders Labourers Federation (BLF), the union Bob had long been a proud member of. John Setka’s union mentor was the much-feared and admired BLF leader John Cummins, a man who was twice jailed for contempt of court after ignoring orders not to visit building sites. A photo from that time shows Setka listening intently to Cummins, the giant younger man stooping to not miss a word from his much shorter boss.

It was an enduring relationship. Even 20 years after Cummins’ death, Setka ensured he remained the patron saint of the CFMEU, with his image and that of the Eureka flag plastered on cranes. The precise political learnings Setka took from Cummins remain in dispute today, but one lesson was unmistakable: project power and take no prisoners.

The BLF was renowned for its unforgiving approach to industrial relations and politics. They wanted it all and nothing was too good for building-industry workers. Then-prime minister Bob Hawke described the union as run by the principle, “If you get in their road, you get bashed in the head with an iron bar.”

Setka was often that iron bar. As a young union agitator, he was convicted of dozens of trespass-related offences – and some for assault – for entering building sites once the BLF had been deregistered by Hawke amid revelations that one of its leaders, Norm Gallagher, had taken kickbacks from construction company bosses.

One witness described Setka in the 1980s taking on eight police officers, with three on each arm and another two lifting his legs as they removed him from a picket line – literally the giant Setka against the world or, in this case, eight cops. It was one of numerous such incidents throughout the 1980s and into the 1990s. When one unionist was dragged offsite by police, the 19-year-old Setka said, “I’m going to stick to the bitter end.” And he did.

After it was outlawed, the BLF began running as a rebel union, its membership shrinking to several hundred by 1990 after the federal parliament voted to extend its deregistration. By that stage the union could only employ three people: Cummins, leader Gallagher and Setka. Two years later, the fight was all but over as the BLF ran out of members and money.

The branch executive moved on Gallagher, claiming he’d misappropriated funds, and later removed him as leader. Gallagher in turn called the police on his comrades and testified against Setka, with Cummins calling the former leader the “police pimp”. The BLF, having shrunk to next to nothing, went out in a bitter whimper, not glory.

That same year, 1992, a successor union was on the scene. The construction branch of the CFMEU was emerging out of the ashes of another, less-militant building union: the Building Workers’ Industrial Union. Setka, by then 28, was now a young father, with his son, born in 1990 to his first wife. He faced an uncertain future, with attempts made to block him from joining the CFMEU due to his infamous reputation. But after tense and extensive negotiations in 1993, Setka and Cummins moved over to the new union.

Setka and his erstwhile mentor helped shape the nascent union in Victoria, bringing over some of the rebel culture of the BLF. By 1996, Cummins was president of the Victorian branch, a position he held until his death in 2006 at just 58. Setka became a prominent organiser, rising through the ranks to look after the crucial CBD building sites where many of the union’s members worked. It brought inevitable conflict – old habits die hard. In 2003, Setka, by then 38, was arrested after he threatened a building company manager, telling him, “You just f---ing watch, I’ll get you. I’ve got a 12-year-old son and I swear on his f---ing life, I swear on my son’s life, you watch, I’ll fix you up.”

It did nothing to stop his ascent. Outside the Magistrates’ Court, about 50 unionists held a noisy rally in support of Setka while the union’s then secretary, Martin Kingham, defended his organiser, who was found guilty and fined. Promotions followed: Setka was elected to the position of union assistant secretary, and then, in 2012, its boss. But the lessons he’d learnt at the family dinner table about community, politics, militant unionism and power, he never forgot.

Similar to the experiences of so many migrant families of the time, Setka had grown up in a community with one foot in the new country and one still in the old. The politics of many in the overwhelmingly working-class Croatian diaspora weren’t particularly left-wing. Instead, many were fiercely anti-communist and celebrated Croatia’s fascist past, which included the mass murder of Serbs, Jews and Romani.

One of the founders of local Croatian soccer club the Melbourne Knights, Srecko Rover, had been an intelligence officer for the ultranationalist organisation Ustaše. Setka later became a director of the Knights and had a Croatian coat of arms tattooed on his chest.

Setka would regularly lunch at Footscray’s Croatian Club, known for its generous serves of seafood and cevapcici, a Croatian delicacy of spicy pork or beef sausage. A stone bust of wartime Ustaše leader Ante Pavelic has pride of place in the club’s foyer. Pavelic was leader of a pro-German government in Croatia from 1941 to 1945 and the club was once named after the fascist Pavelic, but that was changed amid complaints by the local Jewish community. That said, rooms at the venue are still named after other Croatian war criminals.

Like his dad, John Setka hated to be called “comrade”, a greeting still commonly used among the left of the union movement. He preferred the term compare, which translates loosely into “brother”.

Setka looked after his Croatian compares. Some, like his old mate John “Perky” Perkovic, were given well-paid jobs as union shop stewards for large building firms, before being elevated to roles as senior union organisers. Others, like businessman Jadran Delic, had their building companies introduced onto sites by the CFMEU with a nod and a wink that their engagement would signal the end of union trouble. It didn’t seem to matter that Delic’s business partners included some of Australia’s most notorious drug traffickers, or that he’d once declared, in a court case brought by one of his injured workers, that he structured his companies to make it harder for his union-member employees to sue him.

When policeman and Croatian Club identity Tony Juric was charged and jailed for corruption, the CFMEU was waiting for him with a cushy role upon his release. Tony Crnac, a Croatian drug trafficker who served time for a massive cannabis importation, was elected to the CFMEU’s governing body, its branch committee of management.

When a former Melbourne Knights football club chairman, Matt Tomas, started his first crane company, TJF (it was whispered in the industry its initials stood for “The Job’s F---ed”), the CFMEU made sure it flourished. Tomas was something of an entrepreneur. He started a waste-disposal firm with a Hells Angels bikie boss and one of Setka’s ex-girlfriends.

But Tomas’s most enduring business relationship was with another of Setka’s closest friends. When TJF collapsed, owing both the Tax Office and workers, Tomas launched Elite Cranes, which quickly became another favoured CFMEU firm. His partner in the business was Mick Gatto.

Setka’s detractors in the trade union movement constantly whispered about the unsavoury culture he appeared to be championing within the CFMEU, but no one could argue that his wasn’t an extraordinary ascent to power. It was a rise his father could never have dreamed of: from being muscle on building sites to running one of the country’s most important unions.

If anyone doubted John Setka’s influence, they needed only to watch Jacinta Allan moving among the mourners at Bob’s funeral. As the stained glass split the winter sunlight into colourful shafts, it was clear what had drawn the politician to St Leopold’s – even if she regarded Setka warily. Her husband, Yorick Piper, was a former CFMEU official, albeit from the union’s timber workers division, who was suspicious of Setka and his shady friends.

All the same, Setka had emerged as a key figure in a nascent but powerful Labor Party faction known as the industrial left. Its fundraising muscle and control of a bloc of votes within the Australian Labor Party (ALP) could influence political careers. Allan was not immune to the industrial left’s power.

Nor was Setka impervious to Allan’s power, being the politician overseeing the Big Build. The CFMEU’s ability to wield its industrial strength on major rail and road projects would undoubtedly be aided by a good relationship with the infrastructure minister. For instance, if Allan didn’t resist the CFMEU push to replace the rival AWU on the Big Build, Setka’s power and resources would grow even more.

If Boze Setka’s funeral was all about the most powerful unionist in the land burying his much-loved father, Allan’s presence was also a nod to the realpolitik of the ALP. And even though none of the mourners knew it, Allan’s kindly disposition towards the CFMEU was about to pay even greater dividends. In just under a month’s time, the premier of Victoria, Dan Andrews, would resign. In his place, he would install Jacinta Allan, the minister for the Big Build and friend of the CFMEU.

This is an edited extract from Building Bad: The explosive inside story of the CFMEU by Nick McKenzie and Ben Schneiders (Hachette), out October 27.

Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 20:12:24 GMT

Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children

A teacher wounded in last week’s shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.

Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.

Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him before a parent fatally shot the teen gunman.

Drury, who is still hospitalized, released a statement on Wednesday.

“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.

Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”

Drury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.

She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said “my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”

Public schools in the central Oregon city began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.

The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.

UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 20:00:49 GMT

Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years

The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing.

The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks.

The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs.

This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures that came into force in the mid-2010s, in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash.

The senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, it was later expanded to cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds.

It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helped lift the cap on banker bonuses, which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary.

The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls.

Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers.

The regulators said removing these “unnecessary burdens” would save businesses about £2bn over 10 years while cutting the Bank of England’s and FCA’s costs by £11.5m and £229m each year, respectively.

The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. They said in a joint statement that the “high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers”.

‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian tradition

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 19:18:11 GMT

In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming

Wendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina.

“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.

Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.

Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.

There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.

The Jewish Agricultural Society, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than 100,000 Jews earned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.

Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.

Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.

Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.

Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection of pe’ah, a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.

“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”

But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept of bal tashchit focuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.

“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”

A number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. The Sacred Slaughter Institute trains students to become a shochets, ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessen tza’ar ba’alei chayim, or animal suffering. Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profit Adamah Farm in Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.

Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigorating Judaism and the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.

Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acre Ma’alot Farms in Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.

Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”

At Ekar Farm, located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”

Non-profit farms exemplify the idea of tzedakah, or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.

Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat from Robariah Farms in South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certified shochet, he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.

The laws of kashrut, or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”

Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acre Migrash Farm in Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to be yoshon, or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eating chadash, or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.

Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”

Flo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songs

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 19:00:47 GMT

Shepherd’s Bush Empire, LondonRichly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat

The last time Flo & Joan played Shepherd’s Bush Empire, they found a setlist on stage left by beloved indie-rock band the Feeling on the previous night. It made the sisters contemplate their own relationship to the music industry. Are Flo & Joan a proper band or doomed for ever to remain “musical comedy”? The problem with which, they deadpan here, is that “no one takes it seriously”. Cue this new show, its structure inspired by that chance discovery. Tonight, the duo play a suite of new songs that, title by title, matches the setlist of the band who preceded them four years ago.

And so goes the first half of With Feeling, which by turns delivers on and subverts that challenge – and proves handsomely entertaining either way. In the sisters’ hands, Fill My Little World becomes a neurotic number about the surfeit of stuff (cheap food, fast fashion, AI slop). Never Be Lonely returns to a favoured topic, Flo & Joan’s toxic co-dependency – with an added sight gag involving Joan (AKA Rosie Dempsey)’s questionable trumpet skills. Further numbers address the risks of poor punctuation and the need, in a society giddy on unfiltered self-expression, to “bring back shame”.

Elsewhere, those secondhand titles inspire bits of business or bad puns rather than whole new songs. That’s just as much fun: Flo & Joan are more expansive on stage than they used to be, amusing one another very infectiously as they navigate – via a wide array of musical styles, sibling backchat and surprise interventions – to the end of their setlist stunt.

Then comes act two, in which they unleash their rock band fantasies (leathers, bandanas, drumkit) on some well-loved numbers from their back catalogue: the one about social gaffes and the eternal cringe they engender (The Rest of My Life); the nonsense spoof folk song Lady In the Woods. As ever with Flo & Joan, you get richly wrought lyrical wit, sumptuous harmonies and musical surprises – this time with a droll top layer of bathetic rock posturing. A proper band, they may never be – for which, when improper is this much fun, we should all be grateful.

Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festival

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:52:18 GMT

Shrine Auditorium, Los AngelesWith performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities

At Chappell Roan’s Super Graphic Spectacular, the sincerely camp pop star imagines a world where the most vulnerable among us aren’t wielded as scapegoats, and where life can be good, so long as we are good to one another.

That better world takes the form of a two-night extravaganza at Los Angeles’s Shrine Auditorium, part kiki ball, part fabulous revue, celebrating the first anniversary of the Midwest Princess Project, the non-profit Roan founded in 2025 to support transgender youth and LGBTQ+ communities.

Named after her breakout album, The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess, the non-profit has raised more than $800,000 and supported more than 60 organizations in its first year. Its work extends the promise at the heart of Roan’s music: that queer people, particularly those who grew up feeling estranged from their surroundings, can find somewhere to belong. For an artist whose rise has been inseparable from the extravagant performance of identity, the event offers a way to translate that feeling of collective recognition into practical support.

The Shrine Auditorium, with a capacity of about 6,300, is at least 10 times smaller than the crowds Roan usually plays to. The bill, however, is hardly modest. Pop stars Lola Young and Tinashe share the stage with drag acts and burlesque performers whose influence on Roan’s gleefully excessive presentation is unmistakable. Hosting the festivities is Caleb Hearon, everyone’s favorite algorithm-touted gay guy. “Why’s a man here? It feels like Chappell doing Make-A-Wish,” he jokes at the beginning of the night.

On the first of the two nights, straight men are in the minority. They dangle from the arms of their fabulous girlfriends, who wear sequins and cowboy hats, like accessories themselves, dressed in black bandanas and Spider-Man tees. Both groups queue for the same bathroom. “Restrooms are non-binary tonight,” a security attendant announces. Roan has not skimped on a single detail.

She has transformed the Shrine into a rococo burlesque ballroom, its gilded scrollwork set against great, swooping red velvet curtains. Blaine Petrovia, the night’s opening act, slides down a tall pole at the center of the stage, executing extravagant, sensual flourishes in a slutty circus routine.

There is hardly a pause between the night’s five acts as Hearon ushers performers on and offstage, vamping about straight men (why are they all fake photographers?) and straight women (ditto, but witches?).

Lola Young, the first of the night’s two guest singers, takes the stage in what might be called normal-people drag, looking a little out of place. She performs just three songs, closing with her hit Messy. An extraordinary vocalist still early in her career, Young has yet to master stage presence or crowd management, though her awkwardness remains charming, much as it did when PinkPantheress used to sheepishly carry a bag on stage.

The house band remains the same throughout, presumably to lend the night some cohesion, but Roan’s two guest singers struggle to distinguish themselves from it. The coherence of Roan’s universe is also its limitation: the show is so thoroughly organized around her sensibility that its glammed-up, exaggerated arrangements don’t quite work for everyone. Tinashe, the night’s second guest singer, is a case in point.

Tinashe’s latest album, for my money one of the best of the year, is supremely chic. Here, the band distorts its sleekness into chintz. It’s a testament to Tinashe’s deftness as a performer that she rises to the occasion, delivering Roan-filtered versions of her songs with ease, but the crowd doesn’t quite respond in kind. When she sings Nobody Wanna Dance Anymore, the audience largely proves her right. Devastatingly, that is one of the only two (two!) songs Tinashe is allotted.

The space made for Roan proves worthwhile when the headliner launches into an extraordinary hour-and-a-half set. It confirms her status as one of the greatest performers in pop, and possibly in any genre, working today. She emerges relatively understated, by her standards, in a gray gown, with a long red fishtail woven into her hair.

Roan’s world is one of ballroom, drag, glam rock, girlhood splendor and sex. She hiccups her way through Midwest Princess hits – Femininomenon, Casual and Super Graphic Ultra Modern Girl – without a hair out of place.

By now, Roan’s production is so perfected that the cracks that peek through tonight feel graciously illuminating. Several songs into her set, she begins to look noticeably nervous, taking swigs from her lilac Stanley cup, forgetting lyrics and smiling diffidently. “I have a surprise,” she announces, telling the crowd that she is about to bring out a guest who has “paved the way”. Cyndi Lauper? I think. Madonna, if we’re being incredibly ambitious.

Then Christina Aguilera appears in black lingerie, and Roan, who has spent the evening functioning with the precision of the well-oiled Femininomenon she is, suddenly becomes a giggling fan. Aguilera sings Beautiful, accompanied by piano, while Roan watches from the bench in disbelief.

There is something especially moving about hearing a song you have taken for granted, through sheer ubiquity, suddenly acquire a new resonance. As Aguilera sings Beautiful to a predominantly queer audience, the familiar becomes elemental again. “Words won’t bring you down.”

Roan appears charmingly nervous as the two duet her indie-folk ballad Coffee, forgetting her words again and regaining her composure only after Aguilera leaves the stage. Then she becomes the slick, precise performer again, leading the crowd into the YMCA’s sexier, uncloseted cousin, Hot to Go!

She closes with the song that traces her escape from her conservative Missouri upbringing into a world of her own making. In Los Angeles, surrounded by fabulous gays, Pink Pony Club needs little explanation. Pink confetti bursts overhead, and the fantasy she once sang about is no longer somewhere else. It is here.

Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:10:11 GMT

Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state

Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.

The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.

Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.

“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.

“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.

“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”

People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.

The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.

Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.

Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.

There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.

The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.

Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.

People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.

The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.

Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.

European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.

Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.

A musical based on Amy Winehouse is in development for London’s West End.

The project is still in early stages with Catherine Schreiber, a Tony award-winning producer (Cabaret, Rent), attached to the project, according to Variety. Casting is reported to currently be under way.

Mitch Winehouse, the late musician’s father, is also said to be involved with the show, indicating that it will probably feature her most loved songs.

The Guardian has approached Amy Winehouse’s record label for comment.

This week, the 20th anniversary of her landmark album Back to Black was celebrated with a tribute concert at London’s Roundhouse featuring performances by Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae.

“Back to Black remains a miraculous set of modern love songs in vintage clothing,” wrote the Guardian’s Dorian Lynskey, adding that “re-enactments can be limiting”.

On 23 October, an expanded reissue of Back to Black will be released, including four unreleased demos, B-sides and a live album recording at Amsterdam’s Paradiso in 2007.

Mitch Winehouse has hinted at the possibility of a musical based on the singer over the years.

“A musical celebrating her life and music is being talked about for the near future,” he said in a 2017 interview. “It is something I’d really like to happen, and I’ve said I’m happy for it to go ahead.

“It would be for the West End. We want to do something that remembers Amy for what she was; there’s so much more to her than just the drugs and the alcohol.”

That is now set to come to fruition, joining the multiple posthumous music releases, films and TV specials that have been released since Winehouse’s death in 2011, aged 27.

In 2011, the rarities collection Lioness was received as a “flawed memorial for a flawed star”, while Sam Taylor-Johnson’s 2024 biopic of the musician was slammed as a “grotesque insult” by the Guardian’s Laura Snapes.

Meanwhile, Asif Kapadia’s 2015 documentary about the singer won the best documentary Oscar, and was praised by the Guardian as “an intimate and passionate tribute, tracing the awful trajectory of her celebrity destiny”.

A current London exhibition by the artist Alex Margo Arden assembles ephemera from Winehouse’s life in a Chelsea apartment, with items including ballet flats laid in tribute to the singer and a birthday card from Ronson and Adele that she never had the chance to open.

Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:58:51 GMT

People near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the water

Oily slicks of kerosene still appeared to be leaking into the River Taff this week, several days after a breach of thousands of litres was spotted by members of the public.

The breach into the Welsh river was identified last Friday, after people reported strong chemical odours emanating from it. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) officers arrived on site soon afterwards to identify the source of the pollution and were assisted by the south Wales fire and rescue service, which placed absorbent mats and booms to contain as much kerosene as possible.

Residents along the Taff were advised to keep windows and doors closed last week, after it emerged that thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cynon Taf had entered the river. Four kilometres (2.5 miles) of waterway were affected, according to NRW.

GE Aerospace is a US multinational company that designs and builds military and commercial aircraft systems and engines. Its site in south Wales is among the world’s largest maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for commercial aircraft engines, employing more than 1,350 people. In 2017 GE Aerospace was the recipient of £5m in funding from the Welsh government, intended to support innovation and sustainability in the aerospace sector.

Despite early estimates of a volume of about 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled, NRW was unable to confirm what quantity entered the river, and could not comment on possible enforcement action while its investigation was under way and it gathered information.

Public Health Wales advised that the community should avoid all contact with contaminated areas along the busy stretch of river, which runs parallel to many popular trails on both banks, including the Taff trail. People near the river had been complaining of sinus problems and headaches.

“Kerosene vapours may be mildly irritating to the respiratory system. Our current assessment is that people who can smell kerosene may experience temporary irritation, particularly if they are exposed for prolonged periods,” said the health body.

Sarah Llywelyn, who lives in a riverside home in Glan Y Llyn downstream from the GE Aerospace facility, was among those who reported the leak to NRW.

“The smell was absolutely unbelievable. My eyes burned as soon as I opened our door into the garden. I knew it must have been huge because of the smell, and it’s a fast-flowing river – it was essentially unsafe from the point of contamination to Cardiff Bay. We moved here because of the river. What I want more than anything is for lessons to be learned. This should never happen again.”

A visit by the Guardian to the site found oily slicks still leaking into the Taff five days after the incident began. NRW believes that the pollution has now been stopped from entering the river.

An NRW spokesperson said: “Fuel that entered the drainage system before the leak was stopped by the operator could remain within parts of that network and whilst containment measures help reduce and capture pollution, they are not always able to separate all fuel from flowing water. Our work to investigate this incident and assess environmental impacts is ongoing.”

Prof Steve Ormerod, from Cardiff University’s Water Research Institute, confirmed that the photos of the leaks appeared to show the kerosene still entering the waterway through the bunding (a secondary storage system, usually to catch overflows). “The Taff has been recovering from its grossly polluted past,” he said. “So this incident is a potential setback to clean water species such as salmon, dippers and kingfishers that have been recolonising the river.

“Kerosene is a mixture of paraffins, naphthenes and benzene-like chemicals that risk direct toxicity to aquatic organisms, reductions in oxygen transfer across the water surface, and suffocation through impaired gill function in fishes or insects. Effects on feather waterproofing are also likely in the birds that have no choice but to enter the water to feed. Overnight rain was insufficient to raise river levels and flush the Taff, so kerosene will still be lurking in backwaters and eddies along the river.”

Gerwyn and Jordan Lewis from Ynysgau farm, directly opposite the site of the main spill into the river, said they were advised by NRW that the river was unsafe for animals to drink from due to kerosene pollution, meaning that areas of the farm with access to the river could not be safely grazed.

“We simply cannot take the chance of our animals becoming seriously ill or dying. Our winter feed stocks could now be depleted at an alarming rate, leaving us facing the possibility of having to purchase substantial additional feed at considerable expense.

“We also operate a tourism business comprising campsite pitches and glamping accommodation, a sauna and cold plunge facilities, all beside the affected river.”

A GE Aerospace spokesperson said: “The safety of our employees, neighbours and environment remains our top priority. We are continuing to work closely with Natural Resources Wales to address a fuel spill that occurred during repair work at our site on Friday 16 October. The source was identified and isolated on Friday, and containment and clean up are ongoing, with specialist teams working both on and off site.”

A survey conducted by the players’ union Fifpro in 2023, after the most recent Women’s World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, found 80% of players’ return flight had been in business class. Ninety-four per cent flew in business class on their outbound flights.

The total prize fund for the tournament is yet to be decided. Fifa has named the United States as the host of the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028. The Guardian revealed this month the US was lined up to stage the event, with Los Angeles and San Diego among the favoured host cities.

The competition will feature 19 teams, with seven already qualified: Arsenal, Club América Femenil, Barcelona, Gotham FC, Naegohyang from North Korea, Corinthians and Wuhan Jiangda. Six European teams will take part, with the AFC, CAF, Concacaf and Conmebol being represented by three clubs each, plus one team from Oceania.

Fifa’s chief women’s football officer, Sarai Bareman, said: “We undertook a detailed assessment to identify the most suitable host for the inaugural edition of the Women’s Club World Cup. Ultimately, the United States’ recent excellence in staging top Fifa tournaments, combined with the significant interest in women’s football there plus its elite sporting infrastructure, made the country the standout option.

The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:30:45 GMT

The current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevail

Organisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.

What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.

Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.

As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.

Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.

Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.

But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk.

The Guardian view on England’s north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:25:45 GMT

The prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. His government must redistribute wealth to close deadly inequalities

Andy Burnham’s call to abandon “40 years of neoliberalism” rests partly on the damage that he says it has done to northern England. A new study – published in the Lancet this week – adds weight to his argument. It found that for adults aged 25 to 49, death rates in the north were 13% higher than in the south in 1981. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival?

The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on. Deindustrialisation stripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales. Austerity then weakened support systems. These reasons also underscore Mr Burnham’s analysis that Britain’s economic model and concentration of power in London have failed its regions.

The question for the budget is what will it do about these inequalities. The north has substantial levels of deprivation, lower rates of pay and fewer healthy years of life for its people. Among people under 75, the Lancet study found that mortality in northern England was 26% higher than in the south. To close these gaps means helping poorer households with the rising cost of essentials and sending more resources to deprived areas. Investment in, say, early years education and council budgets would help to deal with the social conditions underlying ill health.

Reducing regional inequalities requires redistribution – not just devolution alone. Giving a poorer area more control over an inadequate budget does not increase the cash it can spend. Mr Burnham’s idea to let mayors retain locally raised taxes may help. But without a way to ensure each region gets enough resources to meet their needs, such a policy might simply preserve existing disparities. Researchers at Manchester and Liverpool universities and Health Equity North divided England into two roughly equal populations along a line from the Wash to the Severn Estuary. Closing the north’s health gap, they claim, could add £18bn a year to its economy.

Regional policy plays a complementary role to redistribution by aiming to change where wealth is produced. However, in a recent paper, Steve Fothergill of the Industrial Communities Alliance warned that “the UK has moved away from a long‑established framework that explicitly sought to promote jobs and growth in its less prosperous places … the UK now deploys a weaker set of tools for regional economic development than at any point since the mid-twentieth century”. Mr Burnham needs to reverse this trend.

The chancellor, John Healey, says that he wants a budget for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs”. But a richer northern England would not necessarily be a healthy or more equal one. During the 19th century, when Manchester became known as “Cottonopolis”, Friedrich Engels – bemoaning the city’s “disgraceful unhealthy slums” – was shocked to be told by a local businessman: “And yet there is a great deal of money to be made here.” Bringing investment and good jobs to economically weaker regions matters. But whether the resulting prosperity translates into secure incomes, decent homes, good public services and longer lives is just as important. Mr Burnham’s ambition needs to meet twin challenges: where wealth is created and what life it lets people enjoy.

Tommy Robinson tells court he had photos taken of journalists’ homes to pressure them

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:23:55 GMT

Far-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate them

The far-right activist Tommy Robinson has told his harassment trial that he used private investigators to track down journalists who had written about his alleged role in the 2024 riots, and had photographs taken of their homes “to put pressure” on them.

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denied in court that his actions, which included sharing photos of the wife and daughter of one of the journalists, were designed to intimidate and bully.

“I’m not coming to beat [them] up … they know that,” he said, referring to messages and telephone calls, including a voicemail message left for the editor of the Daily Mail after Robinson had paid to get his personal number.

Robinson is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, in 2024. He denies the charges.

Robinson, 43, gave evidence and was cross-examined on Thursday, when he claimed he “felt it was totally reasonable” to publish a photo of Dirnhuber at his home because he was “in a race against time” to get the Mail to remove a photo of his ex-wife, which the Mail published in a story about him being in Cyprus, with the headline: “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.

However, he conceded that when he sent messages to the journalists, spoke to one on the phone, and left a message on the voicemail of the Mail’s editor-in-chief, Ted Verity, he had not asked for the Mail to remove the image.

Robinson said he believed he was “restrained” in the voicemail he left for Verity, in which he said he would make him and his family famous, and went on to say he told the journalists involved that he would get their addresses because he was “using it as a play card”.

The prosecutor Ben Holt asked him about Dirnhuber and his partner having to leave their home as a result of threatening emails he allegedly received, and about Young’s family having also considered leaving their home.

“The entire situation, I wish didn’t happen, I wish that none of that had happened,” said Robinson. “I was unfortunately in a situation where I was panicked.”

Referring to the journalists and how they felt about messages he sent to them, he told Southwark crown court: “They know I’m not going to come and beat them up. They know that.”

Holt continued: “They are scared of you, Mr Lennon,” to which came the reply: “They are not scared of physical violence from me.”

Robinson was also asked about messages and online posts directed at the journalists by others after he had started using his own X account to tweet about them, including one post from an X user who told Dirnhuber they would beat the “fuck” out of him.

Asked by Holt if he appreciated that messages such as this had been “generated” by his own output, Robinson said: “I don’t agree with any of these messages … I don’t know who sent these messages. I don’t know, I don’t know, I don’t know.”

Robinson had been in Cyprus in early August 2024. At the time, violence was breaking out across England in the wake of the murder of three girls in Southport. He told the jury he was with “my ex-wife, my three children and three other families and their children”.

In the witness stand, Robinson claimed he had not “stoked” the riots, but tried to calm things.

The first day of the trial was told on Monday that journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after Robinson deployed “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics”.

The trial continues.

US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:18:12 GMT

Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition

Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together comments made by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.

Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.

“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom.

The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.

“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”

The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.

Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”

After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned to the BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition, after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.

While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.

Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.

“The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said.

In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January.

During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president.

Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.”

Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.”

In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.

“I think it is intertwined with his profession and therefore any harm that may be alleged under his professional trade and occupation would be reflected with how he conducts business with Mar-a-Lago, at least for discovery purposes,” she added.

We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:00:45 GMT

Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future

Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval

On Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments.

At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project.

There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering. The simple truth is that even as we pursue our ambitious target of net zero by 2050, we will need oil and gas for years to come as a bridge to that clean-energy future. And imported gas has a higher carbon footprint than gas produced at home. The transition to net zero is a process, not a moment. I want Britain to make that transition on our terms: reducing our dependence on foreign fossil fuels, supporting good jobs and growing our economy so we can help people with the cost of living.

I know this news will be warmly welcomed in Aberdeen and by oil and gas workers across Scotland. Their jobs support families, businesses and entire communities. Yet, like many others, their industry has suffered from deindustrialisation, with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives. Our oil and gas workers have powered our nation for decades, and they will continue to play a key role for decades to come. Last week, I promised the Scottish people that we would reindustrialise their nation. I believe the transition to clean energy represents the best chance we will ever get of making that happen. I am determined to ensure that the next generation of energy jobs is created across Scotland and all nations of the UK.

That is why, alongside the decision on Jackdaw, we are establishing an energy wealth fund – something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago. It will begin with an initial £2bn and allow us to convert future North Sea oil and gas tax revenues into clean-energy programmes across the country. This investment in renewable energy will enable us to substantially delink gas and electricity prices by the end of this parliament and bring down bills in the long term.

This government is taking a pragmatic approach that supports our oil and gas industry today, while driving the growth of the clean-energy industries of tomorrow. We are also making a sustained effort to bring energy costs down over the next decade and in line with those of our European neighbours. I know, however, that people need breathing space right now. I will do everything I can to ease the pressure on household budgets in the short term. One of my first acts as prime minister was to remove VAT from electricity bills, and households have seen that reduction in their bills this month. I have now asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to look at removing standing charges from gas bills at the earliest opportunity.

after newsletter promotion

I will ensure the government continues to take action to reduce both gas bills and electricity bills as part of our fundamental changes to the energy system.

The manifesto on which Labour was elected committed us to issuing no new oil or gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea and to reaching net zero by 2050. I stand by both promises. Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires. More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.

There are two ways we can transition to clean energy. One way, the traditional Whitehall way, is to make people carry the burden of change while others take the rewards. The other is to make the transition work for people by creating good jobs, backing British industry, keeping bills as low as possible, strengthening our energy security and giving communities a greater say over their future. This government chooses the second path.

I want Britain to believe in itself again. We can have secure energy, strong industries and a cleaner future. And we can make net zero mean jobs, opportunity and prosperity. That is how we bring back hope.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:59:54 GMT

Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory

For the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war.

But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK.

Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks.

Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract.

Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months.

Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.”

The factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles).

The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to the brutal new reality of drone warfare. But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower.

“In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening.

He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad.

The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds. These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028.

The factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda.

Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said.

after newsletter promotion

The Telford investment followed an agreement in 2024 between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely.

Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the “reindustrialisation” of Britain desired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems.

Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine. US intelligence services in 2024 reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate Papperger in apparent retaliation against the company’s production of weapons for Kyiv.

The German company’s market value has risen from about €4.2bn (£3.5bn) in the days before Russia’s invasion to €47bn on Wednesday, though it has dropped back from a peak of nearly double that last year. Rheinmetall and other European defence companies, including BAE Systems and the British jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, have benefited particularly from European governments eager to reduce reliance on the US arms industry at a time when the White House has shown itself willing to divert supplies to its own militaries ahead of allies.

Papperger said more governments were saying they wanted control over their weapons production. That could help to mollify Donald Trump, the US president, who has shown himself willing to undermine previously firm alliances.

“To be a strong partner, you need strong armies,” said Papperger. “But on the other side, you need a strong industry. And this is what we do at the moment. We build up the industry.”
