Reform snowflake Zia Yusuf demands safe space from ITV’s racism hunters

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:56:57 GMT

How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?

The world has gone mad. What has happened to the country when you can’t even have a bit of racist and sexist banter with your mates at work? Time was when up to 20 million viewers would settle down to watch Till Death Us Do Part, for 30 minutes of laughter with Alf Garnett moaning about black people while calling his wife “a silly old moo”. That was a Britain that was worth living in. These days the thought police are everywhere. The wokerati from London, Oxford and Cambridge who are out to ruin everyone’s lives. What’s wrong with letting sleeping racists lie?

Well, Zia Yusuf has had enough and he’s not going to take it any more. After the ITV exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party, he has posted a six-and-a-half-minute video on social media promising extreme retribution against the undercover journalists who posed as Reform-friendly.

You have to love the irony. Because for the past six months, Zia has been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary. Now he may be equally as half-witted as Chris Philp, but the last time I checked, they weren’t the same person. Maybe Zia has a crush on the Philpster. Longs for the gym bod and absence of brain. Zia isn’t even an MP. When the Gorton and Denton Reform association prefer the dislikable Matt Goodwin, you know how loathed you are.

Hoping to add some gravitas by sitting in front of a union jack in a wood-panelled room, Zia prepares to address the nation. And it turns out that he’s not the slightest bit bothered that some Reform members are racists and misogynists – it was probably as much of a surprise to him as it was to the rest of us. What really seems to bother him is that ITV didn’t ask permission to film colleagues being racist. Which is a bit like being annoyed that Pete Hegseth wanted to broadcast a live execution because it was being streamed on pay per view.

Zia has clearly never heard of undercover public interest journalism. And he’s crushingly disappointed by the deception. He had imagined that ITV would have taken the trouble to personally write to him, asking permission to film people being racist. And he would have happily let them do so. Because then everyone would have known exactly what was going on. I mean, think of the possible consequences of not doing it this way. It might turn out that there were dozens of other undercover journalists in Reform. All just hoping to catch each other out. No one at Reform HQ might be who they say they are.

There was no knowing where any of this could end. It was quite possible even that Robert Jenrick was a plant. That his defection from the Tory party had been a plot dreamed up by Kemi Badenoch. A long game to place one of the least trusted and least talented Conservative politicians at the heart of Reform.

And it had worked brilliantly. Nigel Farage had taken the bait and had appointed Honest Bob as his so-called “shadow chancellor”, making Reform look more and more like a care home for unsuccessful Tories. Job done with Nige tanking in the polls. Some day in the future, Kemi would reward Jenrick with a peerage. The Conservative establishment looking after one another as usual. How things ought to be.

First, though, Zia was promising retribution. He wasn’t just alleging that crimes had been committed by ITV. He was stating it as a fact. Which might get a little awkward for him. The most detailed crime was that ITV had directly affected the outcome of a council election in which Reform had lost one ward by 24 votes. The facts were this, apparently. ITV had paid their journalists to put a curse on the 200 leaflets they had been asked to distribute by Reform so that the people reading them voted for Labour and the Conservatives.

Sometimes you wonder if a man can actually be this dim. At which point you have to consider if the whole video is a double bluff and that Zia is also a Tory stooge who has managed to embed himself at the heart of Reform. That his desire to deport women and children is just a front. Because first, the journalists weren’t being paid by ITV to canvass for Reform. They were being paid to be undercover journalists.

And second, the idea that 200 leaflets could swing 24 voters is clearly absurd. Of the 200 leaflets it is likely that all 200 of them would have been put straight in the recycling. A leaflet changes the mind of about one person in 10,000. Leafleting is something parties do for their own benefit. To make them feel like they are doing something useful.

Having got all this off his chest, Zia wanted to express his hurt. His disappointment. The psychological damage that had been done to Reform activists and workers in HQ. Men and women who had been entitled to believe they had been in a safe space, where racist outbursts would be well received and applauded. Only now they had been forced to consider the possibility that some people might find them offensive. How could that possibly be right?

The violation had been so severe that Zia had been forced to issue a Reform Victim Support card for those most badly affected by the ITV investigation. Much like the yellow card that people with cancer get given. Find yourself on a crowded train full of foreigners and you just brandish the card and all black and brown people are obliged to leave the carriage and give you a seat. And if the police come across a dishevelled-looking man wearing a teal tie and babbling about how foreigners have ruined the country, they can call the hotline number on the back of the card and a Reform outreach worker will come and pick them up and take them to a refuge.

Who would have guessed that the snowflake slayer in chief would turn out to be the biggest snowflake of all? Hiding in plain sight. “We will never give up,” Zia concluded. On day one of a Reform government, perhaps Nige would create safe spaces where people could be as abusive to foreigners and women as they liked. This was a Britain of which we could all be proud.

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:52:27 GMT

Parents, colleagues and others encouraged her to go to police but she feared she would not be believed

A woman told her mother that Russell Brand had raped her and “didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain”, a court has heard.

The woman also told a colleague she was “bleeding everywhere” and that Brand had shouted at her, saying, “Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets”, Southwark crown court heard on Thursday.

The woman told her parents, friends, boyfriend and a sexual health nurse about the alleged attack and several encouraged her to go to the police but she feared she would not be believed, the court was told.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. The 51-year-old denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

The court heard on Thursday from 24 witnesses connected to the woman, who alleges Brand anally raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. She alleges they had consensual vaginal sex before the comedian “flipped” her over and raped her.

Giving evidence over video link, a friend who had accompanied the woman to the gig said the comedian had signed off the show by saying: “If you see me out in the foyer and you think ‘I really fancy him and would like to have sex with him, but I can’t because it is Russell Brand’, you probably can … my age range is from 16 to death.”

The woman’s parents said their daughter had confided in them shortly after the alleged attack and feared she had contracted HIV. In a witness statement read by the junior prosecution counsel, Suki Dhadda, the woman’s mother said: “She said he forced anal sex on her and didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain and asked him to stop.”

Her father said his daughter told him: “They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted. I turned to her in the car and asked her if she asked him to stop, and she said ‘yes’ several times. It was then I said to her: ‘You have been raped, that’s rape.’”

The woman’s colleague told the court the alleged victim was “ashen, greyish, and looked ill” when describing shortly after the alleged attack how Brand had “really fucking hurt” her.

The colleague told the court: “She described that he got aggressive and pushed her down on the bed and she couldn’t breathe and she was trying to say stop because it was hurting her. I said: ‘Did you stay stop?’ and she said: ‘Yes, multiple times.’”

Recalling the woman’s account, the colleague added: “She was bleeding everywhere, from her anus, and he shouted at her, Mr Brand, he said: ‘Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets’ or something like that, and she was very embarrassed.”

The witness said she told the woman she had been raped and encouraged her to go to the police but the woman replied: “They won’t believe me. I went to his house.”

A friend of the woman also told the court that she had encouraged her to go to the police, but the alleged victim “felt it wasn’t worth it”.

“She didn’t think she would be believed,” the witness said. A couple of days after the alleged attack the woman told her Brand had treated her “like an animal”. “She was in a lot of pain and asked him to stop anally raping her and he wouldn’t,” her friend said.

Another friend recalled how the woman had told her that Brand called her “dirty” after the alleged rape and how “he had gone from being charming to violent and cold-hearted”.

The friend added the woman’s “face was as white as a sheet” when she bumped into Brand at the Edinburgh festival in the summer after the alleged attack.

In her witness statement read to the court, the friend said she was at the festival when Brand was “pinging off” the woman’s phone with messages and calls.

“She was concerned that he had tracked her down because he was still pursuing her in the lead-up to that. He was becoming increasingly frustrated that she wasn’t responding to him. I could see he really want to see her and have sex with her from the using crude sexual language in the messages,” the friend said.

In 2024, the woman confided in another friend about the festival encounter and said she had replied to one of Brand’s messages saying: “I wouldn’t treat a dog the way you treated me.”

Another friend spoke of the toll the alleged rape had had on the woman, saying she had been a “bright, confident and bubbly girl” but the encounter with Brand had “changed her”. “It’s like she lost respect for herself after that day. She blamed herself for what happened,” the friend said in a witness statement.

The woman’s former boyfriend told the court that she had not wanted to have anal sex but had “surrendered”. In cross-examination by Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC the man was asked about a witness statement he had given in June 2025 in which he said the woman had “come round” to having anal sex.

The trial continues.

Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:42:54 GMT

Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault

Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw?

What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?

Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.

The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.

In the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked.

The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included the Internet Archive, Wikipedia and 4Chan.

The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties.

Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug.

However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”

The flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.

In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.

Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.

CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.

after newsletter promotion

The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.

Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.

It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.

Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” it said in a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” the NSA said. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”

The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem.

China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.

Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:39:49 GMT

Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage

Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.

Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.

He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.

The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.

Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.

It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.

Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.

The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.

The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.

The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.

AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.

The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.

The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.

Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”

He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.

The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.

Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.

The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.

According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.

In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.

Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.

Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.

In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.

It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.

In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.

At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

Sri Lanka stun England with second-highest ODI chase despite Brook’s 202

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:37:40 GMT

Liyanage hits six for win with one ball to spare

England captain’s record innings not enough

Harry Brook pulverised his way to the fastest double hundred in ODI history and still ended up on the losing side. This was an absurd contest, with Sri Lanka hauling down a target of 430 in Rawalpindi, the second-highest successful chase in the history of the format. Only that magical 438 game, 20 years ago, trumps it.

Pavan Rathnayake, Dasun Shanaka and Avishka Fernando were the headliners, turning it around for Sri Lanka after they were reduced to 24 for two. Rathnayake top-scored with 130, Fernando struck 97, and Shanaka, with 97 of his own, was the most brutal of the lot. After being taken apart with the ball, his revenge act included eight sixes.

None of the trio were there at the close as England suddenly found themselves back in it, eight needed by Sri Lanka off the final over. Josh Tongue rattled the stumps of Dunith Wellalage and Eshan Malinga with consecutive deliveries, but Janith Liyanage walloped a six down the ground to close the night, finishing his stay on 61 with a ball to spare.

So a sublime piece of work, even by Brook’s high standards, came in vain. His footwork was the standout during his 202, tap-dancing across the crease as he ramped, scooped and sliced the ball behind both sides of the wicket with remarkable ­consistency. It took him 114 balls to reach 200, beating Shubman Gill’s 117-ball effort for India against West Indies three weeks ago.

“It was a nice innings; unfortunately it doesn’t mean anything now,” he said. “Being on the losing side, it has no value whatsoever in my eyes.”

England’s captain will also have to reflect on the makeup of his side for the next two games of this tri-series after back-to-back defeats. A ­notable selection call could so easily have been forgotten in victory. Adil Rashid, expensive against Pakistan on Tuesday, was left out for Liam Dawson as England opted for the skiddier left-arm option.

Tom Banton punched his way to 50 for the fourth game in a row, but the first major act was the third-wicket stand between Joe Root and Brook. The pair hopped into the DeLorean and went back to January in Colombo, when they put on 191 in a series decider against Sri Lanka. Brook began slowly, just 13 off his first 24 deliveries, but took advantage of the part-timers, thumping Kamindu Mendis and Liyanage to reach his half-century off 42 balls.

Harry Brook’s 202 was England’s highest ever one-day international score, beating Ben Stokes’ 182 against New Zealand in 2023.

• It was the highest ever score and first double century by a batter in an ODI defeat, the previous record being Charles Coventry’s 194 not out for Zimbabwe against Bangladesh in 2009.

• 429 for four was England’s fourth-highest ODI total, the record being 498 for four against the Netherlands in 2022. It was their highest outside England against a Test-playing nation.

• The 859 runs scored in total was the second highest ODI aggregate and the highest in a game involving England, beating the 807 in a February 2019 win over the West Indies.

• Brook’s 144 runs in boundaries – 21 fours and 10 sixes – surpassed Jos Buttler’s England record of 124 in that game. The two teams combined for 93 fours and 552 runs in boundaries in Rawalpindi, both records for a one-day international match.

• Sam Curran broke his own England record for the most runs conceded in an ODI innings. Curran's two for 103 from nine overs exceeded the 98 runs he gave up in a 2023 loss to the Windies.

• There were an ODI record-equalling four century partnerships – Brook with both Joe Root and Will Jacks for England, and Sri Lanka’s Pavan Rathnayake with both Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka. It was the fifth ODI with four such stands, the most recent coming in July as England beat India at Lord’s. PA

Highest successful run chases in men's ODIs

Sri Lanka's astonishing effort on Thursday slots in as the second-highest successful chase in men's one-day international history …

438-9 South Africa v Australia, Johannesburg 2006

430-8 Sri Lanka vs England, Rawalpindi 2026

406-2 India v West Indies, Guwahati 2026

374-6 Netherlands v Scotland, Dundee 2025

372-6 South Africa v Australia, Durban 2016

364-4 England v West Indies, Bridgetown 2019

Milestones follow Root every time he bats nowadays and this time it was the mark of 8,000 ODI runs. He quietly accumulated as Brook began to torment Sri Lanka’s frontliners as well. While Root miscued on 69, Brook reached his hundred from 75 balls.

As Will Jacks joined in and bashed a few himself, it became clear that an enormous total was on, as was the double for Brook. He moved from a ton to 150 in 22 balls; he took 17 more to reach 200. A cute ramp off Liyanage was a fitting stroke to get there. The only thing missing was a red-inker, with Brook perishing off the final ball of the innings.

Lost within Brook’s genius was Jacks’s power, his unbeaten 66 ­taking 30 balls. Wellalage was the only bowler to escape Brook’s wrath, not conceding a boundary off the 27-year-old. Two for 56 has never looked so good.

Sri Lanka lost two wickets quickly. Tongue bowled Kamindu with a corker and Kusal was gone before facing, run out by Gus Atkinson’s fingertips at the non-striker’s end. But Rathnayake and Avishka refused to collapse.

Harry Brook is far from the first player to score more than 200 runs in an international innings and end up on the losing side – it happened to West Indies legend Brian Lara on three occasions. Azhar Ali and Len Hutton shared the feeling of scoring a double ton and ending up losing a Test by an innings.

The Englishman is, however, the first to endure the feeling in a one-day international.

At 250 for three, with 16 overs left, Sri Lanka were far better placed than England had been at the same stage, but it still felt so very far away. Rathnayake reached his century off 87 balls, thriving with that low-hands setup at the crease, and England failed to find a quiet over or two.

Shanaka blitzed Sam Curran’s moon ball as he passed 50 and with 109 needed off 60 Sri Lanka finally looked the more likely victors. Downing Street rejects Witkoff’s description of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’

Downing Street has rejected the description of Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” made by Donald Trump’s chief negotiator on the Ukraine war.

Steve Witkoff met the Russian president in St Petersburg on Wednesday as he sought to make a new push to end the invasion of Ukraine, with the US putting pressure on Kyiv to agree to a settlement.

In a Russian state media video clip posted on X, Witkoff told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”

When asked about Witkoff’s description of Putin, a Downing Street spokesperson said: “We certainly do not recognise that characterisation, and President Putin has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own Russian people, who he has sent to their deaths on the frontline.

“He is starving children and the elderly of the heat and warmth, and systematically targeting critical national infrastructure. Ukraine’s foreign minister summed it up well this morning when he said: ‘This night, the residents of Kyiv heard what Russian humanitarianism really sounds like.’”

Asked if the government would make this argument directly to the US administration, the spokesperson said: “We engage regularly at a range of levels with a range of partners on Ukraine, and I’m sure we will continue to do so.”

Downing Street’s remarks came after the Scottish secretary, Douglas Alexander, told LBC that Britain viewed Putin as “somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil”.

Alexander added: “We simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.”

After Witkoff met Putin, Russia agreed to resume peace talks with Ukraine and the US in principle. Trump has suggested Russia and Ukraine are “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war.

Despite this, Russia has continued to launch missile attacks at Ukraine, including a drone strike on Kharkiv as Putin and Witkoff spoke.

Last week, Andy Burnham welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Downing Street and backed the Ukrainian president amid Trump’s attacks.

Trump had suggested Zelenskyy should be replaced and declined to say whether Russia was responsible for the war.

How to face the end of the world – according to Plato and the Stoics

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:00:43 GMT

Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse

Do your feelings of existential dread extend beyond your own personal mortality? Do they include fears about the survival of our culture and institutions, our species, nonhuman life and the Earth itself? Do you feel like there’s nothing that can help to wrap your head around the biggest problem we face: the end of the world as we know it?

Apocalyptic expectations are on the rise. According to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey, 39% of Americans believe that we are living in the end times.

Yet the feeling that the world is coming to an end is nothing new. Anticipating and preparing for the end of the world is an ancient practice. In fact, many of the ways in which we envision future catastrophes can be traced back to the ancient Mediterranean world.

Greek and Roman authors set up their accounts of the end of the world as the product of reason rather than divine revelation – the product of the rational study of the laws of nature that govern the universe. They saw the end of the world as an inevitability and typically saw the aftermath, if there was one, as a repeat of the cycle of human development. The main piece of wisdom they seek to provide is how to face catastrophe without fear.

This is particularly true of the Epicureans and Stoics. Their goal is to meet all events up to and including the end of the world with equanimity. The Roman poet Horace offers a summation of this ideal in his Odes: the “righteous and resolute man” will remain “undaunted even if the sky should fall and the ruins strike his head”.

These ancient texts do not explicitly offer solutions or means of avoidance, and as Horace makes clear, they can envision the end of the world as the ultimate test of masculine endurance. Yet they also provide an understanding of the long perspective of human history, and how humanity relates to cosmological and geological history. Unlike our doomsday prepperism, their form of preparation did not require any building projects or financial expenditures; rather, they encouraged preparation that was psychological, epistemological and ecological. This required one to study nature in order to understand its workings and the place of humanity within it.

My new book, How to Face the End of the World, offers several passages from ancient Greek and Roman authors about the end of the world in the original Greek and Latin, along with my translation and introduction. The collection begins with a passage from the archaic Greek poet Hesiod’s Works and Days. The other texts are by ancient philosophers: Plato, Lucretius and Seneca. Each developed different scenarios for how the world could end, but all posited that the end would come from the forces of nature, rather than the wrath of the gods.

Ancient Greek and Roman accounts of world destruction, as well as Jewish and Christian apocalypses, tap into what is likely an underlying psychological truth about these types of stories. They are a means to understand the future, and to realize the hidden natural and divine forces at work in the cosmos. Their power to reveal ultimate truths and to prepare us to face the future may explain why stories about the end of the world are found across cultures and why they have persisted from the ancient world to today.

Hesiod (ca 700BC) is the classical world’s intellectual forefather for envisioning the end of humanity. One of Hesiod’s most famous stories is the myth of the metallic races. It traces the succession of humanity from the ideal time of the primordial “golden race” to the present “iron race”.

Hesiod predicts that at some point in the future, Zeus will destroy the current iron race. He enigmatically makes no mention of what will happen after this destruction. His silence served as an impetus for later authors to imagine different scenarios, ranging from a continuation of the cycle and a return to the Golden Age, to the end of humanity and the world itself.

Also contained in Hesiod’s account is the suggestion that humans can avoid Zeus’s wrath by honoring the gods and living a just and simple life. The prophecy of doom is not a fixed certainty, but rather a warning of what could happen.

Plato (420sBC–347BC) is perhaps most famous today for the portrayal of his hero, Socrates, and for the political philosophy of the Republic. Less well known is that he invented the story of Atlantis, which serves as part of his theory of cyclical global catastrophes.

In his dialogues Timaeus and the Laws, Plato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes. In short, the world does not end, but advanced societies do.

With his stories, Plato appears to be testing the imagination of his audience. In the Laws, it seems clear that he is engaging in a thought experiment about how human society might rebuild after a global catastrophe. Unlike the violent post-apocalyptic narratives of today, Plato imagines that the survivors would live in peace and work together.

Epicurus (341BC–270BC) believed that the goal of life is pleasure and freedom from disturbance. For Epicurus and his followers, there was a strong connection between ethics and physics. In other words, understanding the nature of the universe was linked to living a good life.

Epicurus theorized that the cosmos consisted of atoms and void, as opposed to the other elements of earth, air, fire and water; that the gods existed, but did not care for humans. As a result, death was nothing to us – simply the dissolution of atoms back into the void. There was no punishment or reward to expect in the afterlife.

Very little of Epicurus’s work survives from the reported 300 volumes he composed, but a brief account of how worlds end is preserved in one of his letters: “A world is an encasement of a heaven, which contains stars and an earth and all phenomena and is separated from the infinite; it ends with a boundary that is either thin or thick and when this boundary breaks apart everything within it will be ruined.”

Epicurus’s most famous disciple was the Roman poet Titus Lucretius Carus (ca 98BC–ca 55BC). One key way in which Lucretius departs from and develops Epicurus’s teachings can be seen in his accounts of the end of the world. Lucretius offers two scenarios: slow, gradual decay, or one sudden day of destruction.

When we come to Stoic cosmology, we seem to leave the realm of plausibility and have to abandon our deep-seated notions of time’s arrow moving in one direction. But if you prefer to think of time as moving in great cycles of creation and destruction, or ever had the feeling of deja vu, the Stoics are for you.

Founded by Zeno of Citium (ca 334BC–ca 262BC) in Athens during the late fourth century BC, the Stoics argued that “creative fire” was the primal building block of the cosmos. Eventually this fire would consume everything and then the cosmos would be reborn, events known as the ekpyrosis (conflagration) and apokatastasis (restoration).

Only brief fragments and reports, some of them hostile, remain of the early Stoics on this theory. Some Stoics even rejected the idea of cyclical conflagrations. There are no detailed accounts of how the conflagration would unfold or how humans should prepare for it in the fragments that survive of the early Stoics. Most likely, it was believed to lie in the distant future.

The Stoic perspective on the end of the world changed during the Roman period. For example, as part of his daily practice of ethical philosophy, the emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a brief reminder to himself in his Meditations that the end will come very quickly.

The most detailed Stoic accounts of the end of the world survive in the works of Seneca the Younger (ca 4BC–AD65). Among Greek and Roman authors, Seneca had the greatest interest in the end of the world. He wrote about it throughout his career, exploring different apocalyptic scenarios in several of his philosophical works, as well as one of his plays, the Thyestes.

Although Seneca’s descriptions of destruction go into great detail, he is not solely focused on the catastrophe itself. Rather, exploring the end of the world serves a deeper philosophical and therapeutic purpose. Like the Epicureans, the Stoics closely connected the study of ethics and physics. Understanding nature’s cycles could help one to live a better life by understanding that death is a part of nature, both for the individual and for our world.

In his Natural Questions, Seneca also considers how people would react when experiencing a global catastrophe. Seneca states that the destruction is close at hand, so perhaps his interest in human reactions to catastrophe was part of his own psychological preparation for the event.

What is the wisdom provided by these Greek and Roman authors? How might their visions of the end of the world help us today, if at all? On one level, we can see the origins of several narratives and ideas that are still very much alive today: the myth of decline from the Golden Age, Plato’s story of Atlantis, the Epicurean theory of total planetary destruction, as well as the Stoic theory of eternal return. Overall, however, it may simply seem depressing to read account after account of the end of the world.

Nevertheless, there may be value in envisioning the various forms that future global catastrophes could take. In 2020, a group of scholars published a piece arguing that morbid curiosity and exposure to apocalyptic and similarly frightening narratives can provide psychological tools and resilience when real catastrophes hit.

One of the members of the team, the literary scholar Mathias Clasen, wrote that mental time travel, the ability to imagine possible futures, has been important for human development. Apocalyptic narratives serve a key purpose in that they allow humans to imagine and plan for the “worst-case scenario”.

Other scholars, such as philosopher Hans Jonas, have urged us to accept that the odds are high that catastrophe awaits us in the future. We should not only envision the future as catastrophe but wager that the future will be bad rather than good. Yet this is not simply a prediction of doom and despair. As the contemporary philosopher and cultural critic Slavoj Žižek noted in Too Late to Awaken: What Lies Ahead When There Is No Future?, perhaps envisioning the future catastrophe as inevitable is paradoxically the way to avoid it.

Ancient philosophers might be best known for writing lengthy tomes. They did not compose works summarizing their theories of the end of the world but rather included them within larger philosophical arguments on nature, ethics and politics. But there also was the tradition of distilling ideas into a short work, or enchiridion, that one could keep close to hand – the literal meaning of the word. We can perhaps let the ancient Greek and Roman apocalypses discussed here and collected in my book serve as a low-stakes method of doomsday prepping.

Excerpted from How to Face the End of the World: An Ancient Guide for Apocalyptic Times (2026), published by Princeton University Press and reprinted here by permission

Christopher Star is professor of classics and director of the Axinn Center for the Humanities at Middlebury College. His books include Apocalypse and Golden Age: The End of the World in Greek and Roman Thought

South Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against Australia

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:53:38 GMT

Rabada and Mulder lead hosts to victory in second Test

Boland bats for more than three hours as nightwatchman

It took time, it gently frayed nerves, but South Africa sealed the second Test in Gqeberha deep into the final day, clear by an innings and 31 runs, levelling the series with one to play. Although Australia made 295 and got within 28 overs of safety, they did not deserve to save this game, even if Scott Boland and Travis Head did.

Letting South Africa escape from 40 for four to pass 400 was the first offence, then came Australia’s capitulation for 99 to be forced to follow on. The salvage operation was in waters too deep.

Australia got an early boost from a washed-out morning session that cut the day’s ration from 98 overs to 82. The next boost came from Boland: having done it all with the ball while nobody else could match him, he then led with the bat. He had the nightwatch job in the first innings, batting briefly on the fourth morning, then had to do it a second time that evening, taking Australia to stumps at 156 for four.

On day five, though, his stay was anything but brief. With his team four wickets down and 170 runs behind, Boland settled in for the most substantial innings of his Test career, a personal best of 166 balls, while his 40 runs nearly doubled his previous best. He outlasted century-maker Head, outlasted Steve Smith and passed the tea break after an extended session.

There was the odd dabble at the wrong ball, the odd bit of luck with an edge, but the rest was an exercise in careful defence on the front foot, evasion on the back, batting out maidens with relative ease and taking rare chances for a stylish cut.

At the other end, Head did not tarry in the 90s with a few carved boundaries through the off side, then settled right down after raising his first official hundred in an away Test – his World Test Championship final ton against India at the Oval in 2023 being defined as neutral in venue. By his standards it was a sedate 121 from 190 balls and while it continued the spectre of the draw became a little more material, even though change hovered one wicket away.

It was fitting that the day was defined by Wiaan Mulder, the shortest, least rapid and least celebrated member of South Africa’s fast-bowling stocks. Humility is at Mulder’s core, the man who declined a shot at breaking the world record score, the man who does whatever job his team asks of him: new ball in Durban with two spinners, old ball when Kagiso Rabada returns, stepping up for more overs when Anrich Nortje is injured, bowling into a serious wind, batting three when nobody else wants it, batting seven when they do, attempting to bat time when Australia were bowling for victory, stopping them from batting time when the tables had turned.

Here, his approach was simple and skilful: hit the seam, wait for jag. Head got plenty, shorter and faster than expected, making him jump, forced to glove down on to his stumps. Boland got a better one, fuller and decking into the gap for the right-hander, even his set defence no chance of keeping it out.

after newsletter promotion

An over later, Mulder repeated the dose to Pat Cummins, the ball moving a little less this time to make him play inside the line. Mulder’s three for 64 will not be written on any walls, but it won the match.

That left the score 262 for eight, with Smith already gone, and while reputation would suggest that he was the most important wicket, that belies his long record of having no effect on fifth days. Showing no sign of the stiff neck that had hampered him the previous day, Smith nonetheless torpedoed his brief innings with an atrocious shot, trying to pound a pull shot off Rabada from outside off stump, hitting a catch up in the air.

With nothing needed but to bat time, it was a decision as poor as Marnus Labuschagne’s attempted six off Simon Harmer’s spin the previous day. The comparison of either to Boland’s determination is catastrophically unflattering. While the lower order is not primarily to blame, you could equally ask why Mitchell Starc tried swinging Rabada over the leg side, instead finding fresh air and losing leg stump. Or why Josh Hazlewood tried a booming drive through cover to nick to slip, stranding Alex Carey on 37 not out. Marco Jansen got that last wicket, Rabada finished with four.

With so few overs to go, and with heavy cloud starting to roll in, this was a match that could have been saved with more application from one or two players. It concluded an Australia performance riven with fundamental failures of decision-making, from players whose celebrated wealth of experience gives them no excuse for that shortfall.

For South Africa, it is a dramatic comeback from their own heavy loss at Durban and a reminder that all revelry and disappointment is temporary. There will be another portion of each, however, to be doled out next week in Cape Town. The decider beckons.

What would make neonatal units safer for babies?

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:27:59 GMT

Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson, Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her baby

I support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS (17 October). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.

There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with the Accident Compensation Act. This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, the Cartwright inquiry ushered in the creation of the independent Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.

All complaints – from patients, public and staff – about any health facility, organisation or practitioner go first to the office of the HDC for investigation. If the HDC deems it necessary, it goes to the various professional disciplinary bodies or to the Medical Council of New Zealand. HDC reports on complaints are publicly available.

In 2005, the government passed its “no fault, no blame” legislation. This brought in a duty to report “any risk of harm to the public from authorities responsible for patient safety”. This freed clinicians to engage with any compensation cases with openness. The system has its critics, but overall works well. Dr Pamela S Melding St Helens, Merseyside

Mark McDonald’s column is a breath of common sense. The Criminal Cases Review Commission is still considering Lucy Letby’s convictions, yet Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall has constructed a programme of reform on the assumption that the central conclusion of the case is beyond question. Meanwhile, barely enough time has passed for reflection on what would actually make neonatal units safer.

Thirlwall’s answer appears to be surveillance, suspicion and blame: cameras in cots, encouragement to report colleagues and an explicit retreat from the “no blame” culture developed precisely to make organisations safer.

But what makes a hospital safe? Is it a nurse wondering whether a colleague is about to report them, or a nurse confident enough to admit that they have made a mistake? Is it a doctor practising defensively, or one willing to report a near-miss before it becomes a tragedy?

Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety. A frightened workforce will hide mistakes, keep quiet about doubts and practise defensively. Patients will pay. Mark Hanson Hitchin, Hertfordshire

In March this year my daughter was born and died in the neonatal intensive care unit seven days later. I believe her death was preventable and one key mistake was made that resulted in her death. But I don’t blame the consultant who made (what I consider to be) the error. She was doing the best she could in a difficult situation.

What I find concerning is the follow-up from the trust’s management. They have bent over backwards to try to hide their tracks rather than discussing it openly and using it as an opportunity to learn and ensure other babies don’t suffer a similar fate. The response has been so heavy-handed that it’s an insight into the fear and blame culture doctors face, which I find so concerning. Mistakes are an opportunity to learn. Name and address supplied

Mark McDonald makes many good points. But sadly he overlooks the role that patients and families play in their healthcare and safety. The NHS needs staff who can speak up without fear. But it also needs patients who are listened to, informed, supported and involved. Some of the most important safety signals come not from systems, but from the people experiencing care. If there is one lesson from the Lucy Letby case, it is that patients and families must be recognised as partners in identifying risk, seeking answers and driving improvement. Paul Whiteing CEO, Action Against Medical Accidents

Carers can’t live on 51p an hour

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:26:59 GMT

Emma Sainsbury questions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a home

For 13 years, I have cared for my lovely 101-year-old adoptive mum who requires round-the-clock care. I feel blessed to care for her and have no regrets. But love does not pay the bills.

Carer’s allowance is £86.45 a week for 2026-27. Spread across 168 hours, that is roughly 51p an hour. As a sole carer, I have no downtime. I still work part-time as a self-employed therapist when Mum’s health allows, but when she is poorly, my work stops while the bills continue.

I do not claim carer’s allowance as the frequent paperwork required to report changes in my self-employed earnings is difficult to manage alongside my caring responsibilities.

Last winter, our electricity bill exceeded £400 a month because Mum needs heating round the clock. This is the reality of caring in a cost of living crisis. I worked hard to buy and pay off my own home. But it had no downstairs bedroom or bathroom, and was unsuitable for Mum. I had to rent it out, hoping one day to live there. Eventually, caring and the costs of maintaining the property forced me to sell, and I faced a capital gains tax bill.

I do not blame HMRC for applying the rules. I question whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities force them to make difficult decisions about their homes. Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security. We need more than praise: we need practical support and a system that recognises the real cost of caring. Loving someone should not mean years of essential care leave you financially vulnerable. Emma Sainsbury Author, Love, Laughter and the Hidden World of Unpaid Carers

Do Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties?

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:25:52 GMT

Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill

Your editorial on the dysfunction in Northern Ireland politics (15 October) does not mention the main cause: the denial of basic democratic rights to the people by the Labour party.

The party national executive committee refuses to run Labour candidates in any Northern Ireland election, whether to district councils, the Stormont assembly or the Westminster parliament.

This means people here, including affiliated trade unionists, are denied the basic democratic right to vote for our Labour government, which is setting our taxes and winding us up for war.

This undemocratic stance by Labour is not an act without consequences. By suppressing cross-community Labour party electoral politics, it forces the electorate into their ethnonational blocs and incentivises the sort of communal sectarian politics and stalemate that we are well used to. Boyd Black Secretary, the Labour party in Northern Ireland

It is undoubtedly true, as your editorial says that “Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve”. However, there are problems with your assertion that the current model of power-sharing “designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable”. In fact, it plays a part in maintaining the current “cycle of dysfunction”.

I have family in Northern Ireland who would prefer to vote for parties that do not fit into this category, but doing so under the current rules would be pointless. They are part of a growing number of voters who do not primarily identify as being part of either “community”.

However, even if parties such as the Alliance, the Greens, People Before Profit were to win a majority at Stormont, they would under the current rules not be allowed to form an administration. In fact the current system reinforces sectarian division by stipulating that only those parties self-identifying as nationalist or unionist can “power-share”. Ireland needs real change. The current system cannot deliver it. Declan O’Neill Oldham, Greater Manchester

Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:10:18 GMT

Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker

This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I? Review: Ali G: Who Iz I?

The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sue Sacha Baron Cohen over footage of the local politician used in new satirical comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?

In the film, Michael Aboud is shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. He also schools them in how to fire bullets from the middle of these buttocks by the repeated up and down manipulation of a rubber penis.

Aboud and a fellow student, former preacher and aspirant actor Joshua Loudermilk, are then recruited by Morad to help in a mission to prevent the birth in the US of the baby of a (fictional) South American drugs kingpin.

This involves Aboud and Loudermilk abducting his heavily-pregnant girlfriend and driving her in a phoney ambulance to a remote unstaffed medical facility, where she gives birth (to a lifelike prosthetic).

They then abandon her, Morad having placed her live baby in a zipped bag, and drive with it towards Mexico. Loudermilk is later seen attempting to discharge fire from his fake buttocks, while Aboud takes the decision to drop the baby – at that point being dangled from a drone at a substantial height – to the ground to prevent it touching US soil. The actions could not be anything other than extremely serious for a real infant.

Until the Guardian contacted Aboud on Tuesday, the businessman was unaware of his participation in anything other than what he believed to be a nonfiction film. In a statement, Aboud called Baron Cohen “and his entire film crew … a bunch of liars [who] deceive people to benefit themselves. They claimed that this would be a documentary about the illegals crossing the border. Then they said they were adding in this self-defence guy from Israel.”

He added: “It is my opinion that Sasha Cohen [sic] is a pervert. Plus he talked about how Muslims are all gay because they follow the sex practices of Mohamid [sic]. No one should spend one penny watching anything he produces or appears in. I plan to sue him.”

Pressed further on whether he stands by his actions in the film, Aboud declined to comment.

The film repeatedly stresses that neither Aboud nor Loudermilk are “in on it”. Loudermilk has not responded to requests for comment, but his social media feed suggests a level of understanding about the project not shared by most of his fellow participants.

Earlier this week, Loudermilk posted on Facebook that “I got to spend 12 hours one on one with Sasha [sic] and he taught me soooo much about the fun of making others laugh” as well as a link to a video promo for the film, saying, “I am in the trailer.” On 10 January, he also posted a headshot of himself, saying: “Howdy. Done with Sasha Cohen movie and ready for more.”

Representatives for the film have told the Guardian that Loudermilk was unaware of the true nature of the film.

Aboud’s shock at his involvement is particularly surprising given that he, along with Loudermilk, features in the second trailer for the film, which was released a fortnight ago.

That clip alone contains considerable clues to those involved that all is not what it seems. In his address to the recruits, Morad, who was a fixture of Baron Cohen’s 2018 show Who is America?, advises the group that they should not be fooled, for the immigrants they are set against “are not coming here to mow your lawn, trim your trees, rake your leaves, clean your house, care for your babies, bus your tables, wash your cars, paint your houses, build your fences, install your roofs, drywall, plumbing or electric. They are coming to kill you.”

Another section of the film involves Ali G hosting a “free speech” web show in which he is given a questionable script to read by South African producer Dirk Visser, who could not be contacted for comment.

The character also presides over a gameshow of Visser’s invention in which contestants, against the clock, must stuff mannequins depicting “undesirables” including rappers, gay people, Muslims and Mexican babies into pretend shower cubicles, before pressing a button to seemingly activate the release of the poisonous gas Zyklon B. The segment ends with a mass Nazi salute.

One of those who takes part is the disgraced former Republican congressman George Santos, who tells the camera his takeaway from playing the game is that next time he would try to grab more babies, as they’re easier to fit in the shower. In correspondence with the Guardian, Santos also suggested he was unaware of the true nature of the film, “as me and my team had no involvement”, and declined to justify his behaviour.

Ali G: Who Iz I? opens in the UK, US and Australia on Friday

Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:00:29 GMT

Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation

Exclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’

If you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.

Unlike the first film, Ali G in Da House from 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared in Baron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting.

The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.

The high concept is that Ali is now washed up, short of money and unpopular, and old-school media figure that he is, he disapproves of a plan by his heavily pregnant partner Julie (Morgana Robinson) to launch an OnlyFans account. But on trying to sell his fax machine in a Staines high street pawn shop, an old fax chunters out of it with an offer from HBO for a new show. Overexcited, Ali and Julie head off to the US to sucker some people in the traditional style; the smallscreen setup blown up to high-def cinematic proportions. His fictional woke tormentor decides to take him down and, by employing the Israeli hardman, tries to convince credulous and aggressive Republicans that Ali is a Mexican terrorist whose baby must be prevented at all costs from being born on US soil. The movie does make a few people look silly, yes, although Baron Cohen doesn’t land a huge punch on a big name the way he did in the Borat sequel.

So who iz Ali G and what iz the point of trundling him out again? The first film implied he was once a Robert Smith-type goth, but that is now forgotten about. Interestingly, one person who this film doesn’t allude to is Tim Westwood, the BBC Radio 1 hip-hop DJ and son of the Bishop of Peterborough whose speech mannerisms were held to be one influence on Baron Cohen’s great creation, and proof positive that white people did indeed patronisingly ape a street way of speaking. Westwood’s subsequent all-too-unfunny history, perhaps, doesn’t mesh with trying to revive Ali G now as comedy IP. The movie outings of Ricky Gervais’s David Brent and Steve Coogan’s Alan Partridge worked better because they could more plausibly represent the melancholy of getting older and irrelevant. Ali G feels older in the wrong way, and the On-the-Buses humour with Julie is tired. The best bits will be available on TikTok and Instagram reels soon enough.

Ali G: Who Iz I? is out on 22 October in Australia and 23 October in the UK and US

Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:53:35 GMT

A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief

The synth-heavy production on 1988’s I’m Your Man has always been divisive – even Leonard Cohen’s longtime collaborator Anjani Thomas subsequently expressed misgivings – but on its opening track, it really works. The Pet Shop Boys-ish arrangement chafes against Cohen’s growling vocal, amplifying First We Take Manhattan’s shiver-inducing sense of brooding menace.

Seven years – and a personal financial crisis – after 2004’s half-hearted Dear Heather, Cohen returned to the studio with his powers freshly marshalled. As if to underline the point, Old Ideas opened with the sharply witty Going Home, on which Cohen’s muse addresses the listener directly, disparaging the artist himself as “a lazy bastard in a suit”.

Cohen famously called his 1977 LP Death of a Ladies’ Man “a catastrophe”, which perhaps reflected more on its drug- and booze-soaked recording with dangerously erratic producer Phil Spector than the finished album. It’s an outlier in Cohen’s catalogue, but one with much to commend it. Certainly, he maintained an understandable fondness for the rock’n’roll-influenced Memories, often performing it live.

Cohen’s renaissance continued apace on Popular Problems. Released the day before his 80th birthday, it sounded suspiciously like a masterpiece. Almost Like the Blues found him reflecting sorrowfully on man’s inhumanity to man – not merely torture, killing and war, but “all my bad reviews” – and staring down his own mortality, replete with a jab at Richard Dawkins.

Shruggingly titled, largely recorded in collaborator Sharon Robinson’s garage and packaged in a sleeve featuring a selfie, Ten New Songs was an understated return to recording after Cohen’s five years of Buddhist study. But beneath its unassuming veneer lurked beautiful songs: the chanson-like A Thousand Kisses Deep is an exquisite reflection on regret and time’s passing.

Nowhere else on this album does the cocktail of Cohen’s songwriting and Spector’s more-is-more approach to production gel so perfectly: the title track is a fantastic song. Moreover, the weight of Spector’s arrangement, the way it causes the tempo to drag, seems to complement rather than suffocate its mood.

Other artists have made albums that looked imminent death in the face – Warren Zevon’s The Wind, Queen’s Innuendo – but You Want It Darker, released less than three weeks before the end of Cohen’s life, may be the most poised and affecting. “I’m ready, my Lord,” he sang on its title track, a complex, thorny examination of faith.

In which a brief tryst with Janis Joplin – “We fell into each other’s arms through a process of elimination,” he later recalled – turns into a kind of eulogy, not just for the late singer, but for the era in which they met. It’s haunted by the sense of optimism extinguished.

Rock stars of a certain vintage were wont to write despairing state-of-the-world addresses in the late 80s – Lou Reed’s New York is full of them – but Everybody Knows is a cut above, its relentlessly bleak worldview leavened by black humour: “Everybody’s got this broken feeling, like their father or their dog just died.”

Against stiff competition, Songs of Love and Hate may be Cohen’s darkest album. Avalanche is its claustrophobic heart, a relentless, shimmering guitar figure, a confusing but compelling tumble of imagery, with his voice at its most poisonous. Nick Cave called it one of “the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world”.

Inspired by the story of the Lagerkapellen – concentration camp orchestras whose music accompanied forced labour and executions – there’s something eerie about Dance Me to the End of Love’s klezmer-inspired melody and lyrical pleas for lifelong fealty. The latter are filled with intimations of darkness; it’s never entirely clear that love will overcome them.

“I’ve seen the future, baby, and it’s murder”: Cohen’s apocalyptic response to the sociopolitical upheavals of the early 90s – most obviously the Los Angeles riots – depicted a world in which “attitudes are all extremist and they’re all defensive”. Thirty-four years on, it sounds grimly prophetic, its upbeat soft-rock backing only serving to amplify the unease.

Cohen found writing a trying experience – lurid stories abound of him beating his head against the floor while working on Hallelujah. He poured it all into the thrillingly vivid, mordantly funny Tower of Song, which has often struck a chord with other artists, covered by everyone from Phoebe Bridgers to Tom Jones to the Jesus and Mary Chain.

Anthem is home to perhaps Cohen’s most-quoted lyric: “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” But in truth, it’s just one among a plethora of memorable lines in the song’s gospel-infused paean to hope and human imperfection, a song he later suggested represented “everything my whole work and life had gathered around”.

Even by the standards of Cohen’s synth era, the backing of I’m Your Man is low-rent and cheesy, but it fits perfectly with a song about abasement. Its emotional tone shifts from lustful to desperate to hopeless: “A man never got a woman back, not by begging on his knees,” he notes in a moment of clarity, then carries on regardless.

Hallelujah’s progress from an album Cohen’s US record label refused to release to his most famous song – via, of all things, a cover by John Cale that appeared on the soundtrack of Shrek – is fascinating. Cohen later proposed a moratorium on its use in films, but, in truth, it has survived ubiquity with its power to move intact.

Cohen’s original intention was to try his luck as a Nashville songwriter. If you squint, you can just about make out the shape of a county song in So Long, Marianne’s beautiful admission of guilt, although it’s hard to imagine the Music Row treatment could improve on its wonderfully ramshackle string accompaniment.

Another Cohen classic with country music in its bones – Kris Kristofferson said he wanted the opening lines on his gravestone – Bird on the Wire was coaxed out of a depressed Cohen by his then girlfriend, Marianne Ihlen. It sounds utterly, authentically defeated, like one long sigh, destined to soundtrack moments of gloomy self-reflection for the rest of time.

There are infinitely worse ways to start your debut album than with a song so good, it immediately becomes a standard, covered by Nina Simone, Neil Diamond, Roberta Flack and Aretha Franklin. Some recompense, perhaps, for the titular lady’s refusal to let Cohen touch her perfect body with anything other than his mind.

Reducing Leonard Cohen’s oeuvre to 20 songs is a thankless task: the compiler is abundantly aware that umpteen deserving songs have been neglected. Similarly, there’s no head-and-shoulders “best” song, merely personal favouritism. Still, you listen to Famous Blue Raincoat’s disconsolate depiction of a love triangle – in the form of a letter to the other male party – and boggle at the idea Cohen was dissatisfied with such an impossibly beautiful song, which so perfectly conjures up an atmosphere of shadowy small-hours reflection, and which comes complete with one of his loveliest melodies (subsequently pinched on – crikey – Leo Sayer’s When I Need You).
