Surfing faces a cultural reckoning as women’s voices grow louder over sexual abuse allegations

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:00:35 GMT

A culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settings

When news broke last week that a surfer had been provisionally suspended from international competition, after what the International Surfing Association (ISA) described as “recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community,” the response online was unprecedented in the world of surfing.

While investigations into those allegations are ongoing, the story prompted a deluge of comments detailing other alleged experiences of sexual misconduct and assault in surf industry settings, ranging from corporate brand houses in Hawaii to organised surf trips. While horrifying, for women who have existed in this subculture across the decades, those broader stories are sadly no surprise.

In 2019, as I stood in a bar in New York City at the afterparty of a World Surf League (WSL) Longboard Tour contest, I took stock of my surroundings. It was after midnight and the bar was packed with competitors who had just wrapped an event on a windy North Atlantic Ocean earlier that day. From the women’s side of the tour, teenagers gathered; nearby, other competitors and event staff, many well into their 40s, were dotted across the room. Alcohol flowed freely; the event was private, so there was no one checking IDs. In fact, surfers themselves could be found behind the bar pouring drinks. I reflected on the moment: who was tasked with keeping these young women safe while in a setting like this? And if something were to happen, how would we report it, and to whom?

Over the years, the stories between women working and competing in the industry have accumulated in private. Ranging from sexual harassment to assault, none of these stories ever ended in accountability. When I raised this issue with Surfing NSW a few years ago, I was told the process for something that happened at a Surfing NSW event would be to make the complaint to the event director, and it would then be passed on to the state body’s CEO. At the time, Surfing NSW said they had never received any such complaint. It’s not difficult to understand why.

In the WSL context, while I have competed in sanctioned events for more than a decade, I have never received any information about how to report an incident of sexual abuse to the WSL, or how that report would be treated. And in a male-dominated industry that is tight-knit and insular, where the same people move from institution to institution, where work is often contract to contract, and sponsorship decisions and other opportunities are relationship-based, trying to act against these ranks in search of accountability carries potentially career-ending risk.

Without any clear independent reporting mechanism or track record of taking these reports seriously, these institutions create a culture of silence that protects the accused and buries the stories of women who may have faced sexual violence while competing or working at surfing events.

What was most surprising about the recent allegations that prompted a statement from the ISA was not that they are being made, but that there has actually been a response. A surfer has been suspended, pending investigation, in a culture that had previously glorified a lifestyle where women’s bodies were sacrificed in favour of surfing talent.

Australian surfer Nat Young, who was the 1966 world champion and is credited with being one of the pioneers of the shortboard revolution of the 1970s, described a disturbing scene in the opening chapter of his memoir Nat’s Nat and That’s That. Young writes in the book published in 1998 that a friend “had strategically positioned the girl so that she was lying on her back with her head facing away from the youthful group of lechers and so was able to give the nod over her shoulder”. He adds that when the friend “slipped out”, another “slipped in”, then a third person and Young “had our turn in the same manner”.

“The Grunter”, as Young describes the girl in the book, “was really into group sex and we all greeted her with open flies every time we saw her getting off her school bus”. “The scene was starting to get a bit out of hand, the line getting longer and longer as friends and acquaintances from other beaches joined in,” he writes.

Young’s account is not the only one of its kind that exists in the pages of surfing’s magazines and memoirs that have been published over the years, serving as a tool to not just validate and normalise such experiences but laud them, weaving them into the central fabric of the industry.

Now it appears that wind has started to blow under the cladding that has kept this conversation confined to the private spaces of women, spoken in secret for fear of professional or social reprisal. For the first time since I joined the surfing community, I have seen the rumours written down, albeit so far in comment sections and Instagram posts. But will this be a reckoning beyond a passing moment of outrage? Will it lead to actual reform of the structures that have maintained this culture?

Lucy Small is a professional surfer, journalist and film-maker from Sydney, with a special interest in women’s sport

Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:00:33 GMT

The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman

How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford? TopTramp That’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.

Your Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown. You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends. I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00s Zach Braff would make it in the present day the way you did? KamesJ Back then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.

And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.

Have you thought about Garden State 2? Haggisneepsnfatties We did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.

When you agreed to join the cast of BoJack Horseman, how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end? topfoot I love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.

How much fun was it playing a small role in Arrested Development – to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms? Manofthesouth It was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.

Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.

Who would you most like to cast in Dr Acula: The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs? PickleMan Michael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.

You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be? Turnipsnitzel Morgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”

When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.

If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s a doctor on board, would you put your hand up? MrSOBaldrick Absolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.

Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you? waydgroods I was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.

Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:00:32 GMT

Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club

For Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway. Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle.

Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours?

Sometimes, you simply have to take a deep breath and the plunge. Nobody wants to die wondering. Guimarães knew the Newcastle team was breaking up. Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali had gone to Barcelona and Tottenham. The manager, Eddie Howe, was at the end of the line and would also leave. Guimarães went through with the £75m transfer and nobody can say it has not worked out so far.

Arsenal felt he would provide a different element for them, different ways of unlocking defences, plus his trademark work rate and snarl. Guimarães has brought all of that. Already he has made a difference. He even gave a little back to Newcastle when he scored his first Arsenal goal at Sunderland in September, paving the way for a 2-0 victory. Two Premier League games later, he scored the winner at home against Leeds.

Guimarães almost got another vital goal on Wednesday in the Champions League tie at Bayern Munich only for Manuel Neuer to deny him with an outrageous save. That would have put Arsenal 2-1 up. The game finished 2-2, Arsenal fighting until the end and equalising through Declan Rice in the 82nd minute. Still, it has not been easy for Guimarães and he surely has Arsenal’s visit to Newcastle on 21 November circled in his diary. His greatest hope is that he can build the same relationships at his new club.

“It was not just hard to tell Eddie but to tell the owners and my teammates [about deciding to leave Newcastle],” Guimarães says. “But I think the club went to a new rotation; a lot of players left, as well. The gaffer left. It was tough because my connection with the club was unbelievable. I never felt so loved like the way I was at Newcastle. I hope I can have the same love here at Arsenal.

“It was hard for me to say bye. I remember when I said bye to the lads, I was crying. They were crying as well because we were a family there. I lost many, many nights of sleep because it was difficult for me, for my family. But sometimes in your life you have to make decisions and in my mind, I needed a new challenge. I wish Newcastle all the best because they were so nice to me. It is just time to move on and I’ve been enjoying my time here at Arsenal, as well.”

Guimarães is enjoying his burgeoning midfield partnership with Rice, not to mention Martin Ødegaard, who tends to be the most advanced of the trio. That said, there is plenty of fluidity between the positions. There is the sense that the manager, Mikel Arteta, is searching for the perfect balance.

“Declan can play – like me – as a No 6, No 8 or No 10,” Guimarães says. “The manager is still trying to get the best version of ourselves. Against Bayern, I played more as a No 6, Declan played more as a No 8. I enjoy playing with him a lot; with Martin, as well. We have been on a good run so far.”

Guimarães’ battles when he was at Newcastle against Rice have been well documented. He said Rice had messaged him as he prepared to sign for Arsenal, saying: “No more fights, now we’re friends.” Guimarães is the player you loathe when he is against you but love when he is in your ranks.

What was the worst thing Guimarães said to Rice when they were in opposition? “It is difficult to say,” he replies with a smile. “I am like this when I play against teams. When we were playing against each other, I was not nice to him, he was not nice to me! Now we try to help each other on the pitch.”

Guimarães cannot believe how Neuer kept out his close-range header; the 40-year-old goalkeeper clawed the ball up against the crossbar and away. “He pulled off a miracle,” Guimarães says. “I asked him after the game: ‘How did you manage to save that?’ He said: ‘I don’t know. I just saved it!’ He’s unbelievable, one of the best keepers in the world. No matter how old he is, he is top.”

What Guimarães has seen with clarity is the remorselessness of the collective attitude at Arsenal; the insatiable will to win, which comes from Arteta. Next up for them is Everton at home on Saturday. Guimarães knows he is in the right place.

“The mentality of the club has changed a lot and Arteta shows this perfectly,” Guimarães says. “We don’t accept a draw at Bayern. We always want to win. That is the mentality that we go to the training ground with every day. Arteta is always a little bit addicted to videos and the way that he can make us feel better on the pitch. The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it?

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:46:26 GMT

I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe

Parts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too.

This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile.

The websites were turned off because of two serious security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre advised organisations that were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline.

It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week.

I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, I wrote about Heartbleed, a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation.

Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on a dangerous flaw in Log4j, a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we had XZ Utils, a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster. Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure.

The PHP Foundation made that point itself this week. Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels.

This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too. Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, said his company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already.

Automated systems powered by AI can hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documented about 48,000 vulnerabilities across the internet in 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught.

Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025 review by the UK government found that about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April, ministers admitted they couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired.

So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it. But companies and the organisations protecting us also need adequate funding.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

There are some things to be optimistic about. The OpenSSL Foundation, the not-for-profit company that fell victim to the Heartbleed vulnerability in 2014, received more than €400,000 from Germany’s sovereign tech fund last year to bolster its resources. The PHP Foundation has hired more staff and is using AI to help triage what’s important and what’s not. And a number of organisations deployed fixes before the current issue went public.

But more is needed. The solution is the same one we keep talking about, but rarely actually do anything about: the big tech companies making billions from software they get for nothing (because of its open-source nature) should contribute properly to maintaining it. Governments ought to do the same, rather than hoping a handful of exhausted developers will keep things ticking over indefinitely.

I’m growing sick of reporting on, and explaining why, the internet repeatedly breaks. I’ve covered Heartbleed, Log4Shell and XZ Utils – and am now documenting the fallout from PHP. I don’t particularly want to keep doing it. Yet I fear unless we start properly valuing those who keep our internet safe, I will be.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

One of the world’s leading marathon runners, Ruti Aga, has been banned for six years after anti-doping investigators found she submitted a fake prescription to explain a failed drug test.

The Ethiopian athlete won the Tokyo marathon in 2019 and has reached the podium at the Berlin and New York marathons. She tested positive for the banned substance methylprednisolone after winning a half-marathon in China in March, the Athletics Integrity Unit said on Thursday.

Aga said she had been given the substance by a doctor in Ethiopia to treat knee pain, but the AIU said it found the clinic named on the document did not exist and the supposed prescription had been signed by a family member who was not a registered doctor.

After that, Aga failed to respond to charges for the use of methylprednisolone and “tampering” with the anti-doping process, the AIU added, meaning the six-year ban was issued without a hearing. The 32-year-old runner’s ban includes two years for the use of the substance and four more for tampering.

What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 12:05:51 GMT

Andy Burnham pledged a new lease of life for Britain’s high streets. We look at how he can achieve it

Save high street with higher online sales taxes, PM urged

Middleton’s revival could be blueprint for other towns

On the road to Downing Street, Andy Burnham promised a new dawn for Britain’s towns and high streets.

For too long places outside the big cities had been “forgotten or written off”, he argued after the Makerfield byelection. To help towns like those in his constituency, he said his government would make sure that the places Westminster had neglected would now get fairness.

Four times more people live in Britain’s towns than in cities. Since the turn of the millennium, big cities and more prosperous towns have grown significantly faster than weaker local economies. In Manchester, the population rose by almost a third, amid a renaissance in Cottonopolis that its former mayor capitalised on before entering No 10.

In sharp contrast, towns have been growing more slowly than cities on average, and are ageing faster as well. Some are in population decline, including Barrow-in-Furness in Cumbria (6%), Peterlee in County Durham (11%) and Rishton in Lancashire (13%).

To turn things around, experts say the prime minister will need to nurture the ingredients of local economic success. Here we chart five of the critical components.

Roughly every five years official estimates of local deprivation in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are made using a range of statistics for an index of multiple deprivation.

Each metric is critical for a town’s success: income, employment, education, health, crime, housing and the living environment.

Jaywick Sands, near Clacton-on-Sea in Essex, has led the rankings in England since 2010. The least deprived neighbourhood is in the town of Harpenden, near St Albans in Hertfordshire.

Most parts of the country have pockets of deprivation. But there are also clear patterns: towns, particularly in the north of England, the Midlands and in coastal areas, typically have the highest share of the most deprived neighbourhoods.

When it comes to the vitality of a town, income and employment levels are critical for supporting high streets. Boston in Lincolnshire has the lowest level of resident earnings in Great Britain, with people earnings about half as much as those in St Albans. Employment levels are lowest in Gravesham in Kent, followed by Blaenau Gwent in south Wales and Hyndburn in Lancashire.

After more than a decade of austerity, local authorities across the UK lack the financial firepower to meet rising demand for critical public services and to support economic activity.

The low point was reached in about 2019, when local spending power in England had been cut by about a quarter from 2010 levels. Analysis by the Institute for Government shows the most deprived local authorities ended up with significantly deeper cuts than affluent ones.

Funding levels have started to recover but will take until at least 2028-29 to return to 2010 levels after inflation is taken into account.

Transport and other physical infrastructure – including housing, superfast broadband, water and power – are central to the prosperity of a place. High standards of healthcare and education provision are also vital. Without these ingredients, households will struggle to reach their local high street or travel to work. Businesses will also lack access to a skilled, healthy workforce.

During the 2010s more than one in four bus services were cut in England. Rural communities and towns suffered most. Subsidies have been cut, and – as with trains – fares have risen. Burnham has made public control over buses and cheaper fares a priority. Official figures show Warrington, the prime minister’s home town, had the biggest fall in miles travelled by bus since 2010 of any English local authority.

Regions outside London and the south-east have also had significantly lower levels of investment.

Retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a 10th of employment. But its visible position on the high street gives it outsize influence on public perception about local economic performance.

Over the past two decades the internet has transformed the high street. Online spending has rocketed from less than 3% of total retail sales in Great Britain in 2006 to more than 25%. As a consequence, many mainstream shops have either closed or been replaced by vape shops, bookmakers and barbers. Official data shows high street retail employment has fallen most in the East Midlands.

Retailers have suffered from weaker levels of consumer demand amid the cost of living crisis – compounding the challenge in places where households are feeling the pinch most. Closures have been most pronounced in the north of England, the Midlands and deprived coastal towns.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows places where retailers pay higher rents (which it said could reflect resilient consumer demand) typically have the lowest vacancy rates. At one end of the scale is London, with high rents and 7% of shops with shutters drawn. At the other is Newport, where despite low costs, 19% of all units lie empty.

Social capital – the strength of communities, relationships and trust – is a key ingredient of economic success, not just a nice to have. However, Britain has suffered a hollowing out of the associations, clubs, organisations and infrastructure that were once the beating hearts of communities.

Local council spending on culture, sport and other related areas such as tourism and libraries has nosedived since 2010. Towns and rural areas have faced bigger cuts than big cities. Figures show councils spent a net £92.84 per person on culture in 2010-11 after adjusting for inflation. That has halved – last year a net £46.43 a head went on culture and sport.

Looking at total rather than net spending reveals the areas that have cut the most. Hart district council spent £82.36 a head in 2010-11 – that has since been cut to £8.75. Havant’s spending went from £40.04 a head in 2010-11 to £5.66 in 2025-26. While the vast majority of councils have cut arts spending, others have increased it. Mole Valley spent £109.02 last year on culture and related services, up from £58.16 in 2010-11.

Tour de France 2027 routes revealed with British stages, time trials and a volcano

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 11:11:47 GMT

‘Britain offers us a symbol that ties the races together’

Tour de France Femmes will conclude on Puy de Dôme

The most ambitious Grand Départ in the long history of the Tour de France was unveiled in Paris on Thursday as the race organisers fleshed out the details of next summer’s men’s and women’s race starts in Edinburgh and Yorkshire.

Over six days of racing, Scotland, England’s Lake District and Peak District, Lancashire and Yorkshire, Wales and central London will be taken over by the snaking race caravan on a route that is expected to lure millions to the roadside.

Christian Prudhomme, the men’s Tour director, said he expected “a warm and massive welcome for the champions”. “From the start at the foot of Edinburgh Castle – the northernmost in the history of the Tour – to a team time trial in London, Great Britain offers us a symbol that further ties the two races together,” he said.

The sports minister, Stephanie Peacock, confirmed that £65m has been allocated to fund the six stages and said the Tour’s visit would “shine a spotlight on women’s cycling like never before”.

The men’s race starts in Edinburgh on 2 July and finishes in Paris on 25 July, with a final stage that maintains the tradition of racing up and over the cobbled streets of Montmartre.

Paul Bush, the managing director of Grand Depart GB, has big ambitions of his own for the race. “One of my aspirations will be to turn the UK yellow next year, for two weeks, so everybody is in yellow,” he said. “Now that would be pretty special.

“Now that would beat 2014. Not that I’m looking to beat 2014, because it’s not a competition. But if we could encourage everybody, workplaces, communities, old age pensioners’ homes, schools, everything to become yellow, I think that would really embrace the thing.”

In fact, the men’s Tour will begin and end on cobblestones. From the Royal Mile to the Champs-Élysées, the peloton will cover 3,479km of racing and take in two individual time trials, three summit finishes and a potential decider in the climbs of the Pyrenees.

The first British stage, from Edinburgh to Carlisle, will head through Midlothian and the Borders, while stage two, from Keswick to Liverpool, will cover 223km and take in Lancashire’s Trough of Bowland before finishing on Liverpool’s waterfront.

The final British stage will include eight climbs on the winding road from Welshpool to Cardiff, and is likely to be one of the hardest stages of the race.

After the transfer across the Channel, the peloton races across central France, from Cherbourg to the Jura, for the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier, followed by mountain stages to Sallanches and Les Saisies.

From the Rhone Valley, where the furnace conditions that characterised this year’s race are likely to return, the convoy heads into the Cévennes and the Tarn for finishes in Mende and Albi.

The second time trial is centred on Toulouse and comes before two brutal Pyrenean stages, the first crossing the fearsome Col du Tourmalet before a finish on the Col du Portet, and the second, to Laruns, taking in four major ascents and 4,300m of climbing.

The Tour de France Femmes begins in Leeds on 30 July, 13 years after the men’s race staged its Grand Départ there, with an opening stage from the Headrow to a likely sprint finish on Deansgate in Manchester.

The next day’s challenge, from Manchester to Sheffield, includes both Winnats and Snake Pass on a route which features almost 3,000m of climbing and which the race director, Marion Rousse, called the cornerstone of “the hardest opening in the history of the women’s race”.

But the showpiece stage will be in central London, with an 18km team time trial, routed from Westminster to The Mall, taking in Tower Bridge, St Paul’s Cathedral, Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace.

London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said the Tour’s visit would “not only cement London’s status as the undisputed capital of women’s sport, but also inspire more people to take up cycling, as we build a better, greener London for everyone.”

After the transfer to northern France, the women’s peloton heads south, via Calais, Magnanville and Bourges, to a first mountain finish at La Loge des Gardes before a penultimate mountain stage through the Auvergne to Clermont-Ferrand. The nine-day race climaxes on the steep volcanic Puy de Dôme, after a stage that climbs almost 4,000m.

Both routes were unveiled at Porte Maillot even as curfews remained in place in some parts of central Paris, including Place de la République and Les Halles. The French media described the nation as sinking “deeper into crisis”, but in the aftermath of the Covid pandemic and the controversies of climate change, the Tour has become well-versed in puffing out its chest in the face of adversity and threats.

However, disruption, due to both civil unrest and extreme temperatures, remains possible. Race organisers ASO faced a similar situation in July 2023, when climate activists and rioting threatened the race. That year, Prudhomme said the Tour was “in constant liaison with the state” and would “adapt if needed”.

Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 11:00:41 GMT

Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump

Historical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalent public support for his treachery. Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.

US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked by record-low poll ratings, he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation. Recent steps – his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle. All that’s lacking is an umbrella.

Why does Trump act this way? Partly, it’s personal. He doesn’t like Zelenskyy and it’s obvious why. Ukraine’s leader is everything he is not: courageous, principled, morally unimpeachable, hard-working and politically savvy. Partly, it’s money and power. Trump has set his shrivelled, grasping heart on normalising relations with Putin’s repressive rogue regime, opening the way for lucrative deals on energy, raw materials, and control of the Arctic and outer space. He likes the idea of a world dominated by three all-powerful blocs and authoritarian leaders: himself, Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. And partly it’s the unexplained, sinister hold Putin appears to exercise over this former society playboy, New York real-estate developer and serial bankrupt.

Whatever Trump’s motivations, the short-term consequences of his betrayal are potentially fatal for Ukraine’s bid to repel the Russian invaders and survive as a sovereign democratic state. For much of this year, Ukraine has been winning, or at least holding its own, in the contested lands of the Donbas and along the Black Sea littoral. More than that, by using homemade missiles and drones, it has taken the fight to Russia’s industrial heartlands and oil refineries, significantly undermining Putin’s ability to fund his war. Zelenskyy has also been winning the battle for international opinion, particularly in Europe, which itself is under escalating Russian hybrid attack. Amid Trump’s egregious backsliding, European nations have taken the lead in supporting Kyiv militarily, financially and diplomatically.

It’s hard not to wonder whether there’s a connection between Trump’s sudden, divisive, decisive lurch towards unabashed support for Putin and the fact that Russia, suffering unsustainable battlefield casualties, severe economic damage and deepening international isolation, is at increased risk of regime-toppling humiliation. Whatever the truth, Trump’s Putin bailout – his duplicitous Russia rescue act – could turn the tide.

Trump’s perfidy is the shame of the world, and it is the world – and not only Ukraine – that will pay the price over the longer term. This calculated attempt to force Kyiv’s submission imperils everyone. Ukraine, if it is allowed to fall, will haunt Europe and the wider geopolitical biosphere for decades, as was the case with Czechoslovakia after 1938. Trump’s Molotov-Ribbentrop-style pact with a warmongering dictator, an indicted war criminal, a smirking, bigoted mass murderer, may fatally compromise the western alliance and spell the end of Nato as an effective defence against eastern totalitarianism. Who among the democratic governments of western Europe, in the Elysée, in the German and Polish chancelleries, in Brussels or in Downing Street, can now trust a word that comes out of Washington? Its bond is broken, its honour in shreds.

Trump’s betrayal follows a pattern of lesser treacheries: arbitrary tariff wars waged against trading partners, the traducing of loyal allies, threats against Canada and Greenland, abandonment of a two-state solution in Palestine and most recently, his disastrous war against Iran – the real reason why US midterm voters, facing inflated fuel prices, are turning against him and his Republicans. But his Russian folly may be the most egregious and consequential. As MI5 has warned, Britain and Europe are under daily attack from Russia, its spy networks, saboteurs, cyber warriors and paid agents. Reports this week suggest it is menacing western space satellites, too. Don’t look to turncoat Trump for help. He’s on the other side.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Trump’s Munich moment is a disaster in the making for Europe’s security and defence. A Putin victory, accepted and facilitated by the US, would fatefully damage respect for international law and sovereign borders. Untold numbers of war crimes and crimes against humanity would go uninvestigated and unpunished in a partitioned, fractured Ukraine. China and others might soon follow the precedent established by successful Russian aggression. For all these reasons, Britain and its European allies can no longer afford to hold back. Indignant speeches at the UN, off-the-record murmurings and carefully calibrated verbal slaps on the wrist will not suffice, if they ever did. Andy Burnham, France’s Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Canada’s Mark Carney must lead the way in confronting Trump head-on, even at the cost of a definitive break with Washington.

Tell Trump publicly to knock it off. Take concrete steps to punish him for rewarding Putin and prove that the democracies of the world will not be bullied and sold out. Tell him if he really wants to be remembered as the US president who shattered the western alliance and ensured the triumph of authoritarianism, then keep on licking Putin’s boots – but he will be on his own. The UK, EU and Nato member states, Japan, South Korea and other like-minded countries, are far from powerless, economically, militarily and in numerous other ways. And despite what polls may suggest, healthy majorities of their citizens reject the hateful far-right lies and sick populist myths on which Trump and his pitiful emulators feed.

The US ultimately leads the west by consent, not by right. Consent can be withdrawn. Burnham could start by ordering the closure of US military bases in Britain, offensive symbols of a hostile occupying power. At all costs, Trump’s treachery must not stand.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:00:58 GMT

Nathan Fielder’s conversation-igniting film on the Theranos founder finds its darkest moments in her deceptive, Charlie Kirk-loving fiance Billy Evans

Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year

‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes

It’s likely that most audiences going into the surprise documentary smash You Can See Everything are familiar with either its nominal subject (and literal poster gal with an intense stare) Elizabeth Holmes, the tech founder serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors; or the film’s on-camera co-director Nathan Fielder. Holmes, as the movie points out, was all over the media as her company Theranos was hyped to the moon and then spectacularly imploded; she was also played by Amanda Seyfried in the well-regarded Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Fielder, meanwhile, may not have graced as many magazine covers, but is similarly familiar to prestige-TV acolytes from his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and its successor, the more reality-bending series The Rehearsal. A third figure not included in the film’s ad campaign becomes a key part of the film in the second half, and will also be familiar to many viewers.

This should leave Billy Evans as the odd man out. Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner (she has said they’re not legally married, though they did get engaged in 2018, have two children and seem to treat each other as spouses), is a not-particularly-famous guy whose screen time competes with the other three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama. But while Evans isn’t boxed out in terms of screen time or memorability, he does remain the odd man out in the sense that in all the discussion You Can See Everything has prompted about manipulation, shifting sympathies and who can or cannot be trusted, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks.

Well, everyone except Holmes, who never indicates so much as a moment of doubt or hesitation toward her common-law husband, at least so far as Fielder or co-director Lance Oppenheim show us. But the movie does show Fielder appearing baffled by Holmes – her absurd claims to have never lied in her adult life; her tautological and nonsensical explanation of how her blood-testing device does actually work (which basically amounts to “if everything about it worked, it would work”); her inability to understand Abbott and Costello’s most famous comedy routine – to the point of having trouble discerning whether she’s consciously scamming him or just, let’s say, reality-divergent. By comparison, Evans comes across as more of a slightly puzzling but recognizable nuisance.

When he calls a meeting to demand a percentage of the film’s profits – the kind of arrangement that might be typically reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician, not a nonfiction film extensively interviewing a notorious subject – Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on the question of whether Holmes knew about this request and what became of it, but Evans is the one who violates documentary norms by asking for profit participation (and getting it, at least temporarily). Earlier on, he demands privacy when he grows visibly uncomfortable with questions asked of Holmes while also appearing fully, frontally nude in the film. In a small but underlined moment, he casually relieves Holmes of egg-scrambling duty because he believes she’s not stirring vigorously enough.

And those are just some of his antics before the film’s two-year time jump, after which Evans seems to exert even more control over his partner. Given Holmes’s reputation as a Silicon Valley scam artist, it would make sense enough to categorize Evans as a real-life version of Hollywood’s favorite go-to villain: the evil tech bro. The film even refers to Holmes’s turn in that particular hot seat as the subject of The Dropout, which is not a story of heroes and villains, exactly, but certainly exists adjacent to narratives about tech-forward monsters.

Evans has plenty of grimly hilarious signifiers, before and after his partner’s incarceration. Beforehand, he can be seen listening to podcasts at double speed like a true #content consumer/wannabe timemaxxer. Afterward, he shows repeated signs (uncommented upon by Oppenheim or Fielder) of posturing but increasingly intense post-“woke” radicalization: he spends time at a shooting range, claims to carry a gun everywhere, volunteers that he’s a fan of Charlie Kirk and brags about his own supposed vindictiveness. He uses his sketchy control of Holmes’s social media to engage in petty clapbacks that seem entirely out of character for her; he uses his sketchy control of her AI likeness to side-boast about how much healthier she looks as a prisoner than she did immediately postpartum.

With paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that don’t amount to anything and a seeming possessiveness of the woman in his life, Evans checks plenty of tech-bro boxes – only without even a modicum of demonstrated tech expertise, seemingly not even in his fevered imaginings. Yes, Elon Musk propped himself up as a genius on the basis of other people’s companies and his vast fortune; Mark Zuckerberg is a dead-eyed egomaniac whose famous invention is a Friendster clone that bought up a bunch of other already-successful websites and Sam Altman’s career is littered with failures that in no way qualify him to order us all to treat AI as the future. But even if you see these guys as scammers nearly on par with Holmes, they have the distinction of having successfully made money and, in the case of Musk and Zuckerberg, placing some of their might behind products that people do actually use (in some cases, whether they really want to or not). One reason they’re villainized in fictionalized true stories like those powering The Social Reckoning (with Jeremy Strong as Zuck) or the upcoming Artificial (with Andrew Garfield as Altman and Ike Barinholtz as Musk) is that they have actually accrued power in the first place. There are stakes to their existence.

Evans has no such claims to fame or even big-canvas notoriety that could inspire something like the four-hour Musk documentary by Alex Gibney, released concurrently with You Can See Everything. It seems notable, too, that the similarly lengthy You Can See Everything has seemingly stolen focus from the more traditionally rigorous piece on Musk, a far more influential individual compared to either Holmes or Evans. Holmes was certainly a destructive force for the cancer patients whose hopes she raised, and Evans comes across like a restless creep, but it feels telling, and a little discomfiting, that the gossipy nervous laughter provoked by You Can See Everything is proving a vastly more headline-grabbing draw than a movie laying out the case against a maniacal on-again, off-again trillionaire who has done genuine damage to the world, and is poised to do plenty more. Does someone need to be as petty, strange and blatantly unsuccessful as Evans to be truly finished off in public?

Then again, Evans does make a compelling villain for precisely that restless lack of achievement. He will never be as influential as someone like Musk or Zuckerberg, but apparently aspires to that kind of overlord-level bravado (why else would you use your wife’s social media to pick fights?). He’s a fake-it-til-you-make-it-and-then-keeping-faking-it type, more akin to erstwhile reality star turned pretend mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt or any number of filibustering podcasters. Instead of Facebook or Tesla or a portfolio of Donald Trump-style scams, he can simply puppeteer the damaged brand that is Elizabeth Holmes – near-literally, when he shows off his AI version. Holmes is clearly manipulative (and based on available information about Theranos, an unambiguous liar), yet Fielder does locate, or maybe even manufacture, some kind of humanity through her inscrutability. There’s something haunting about her, sometimes in spite of herself. Evans is the odd man out in You Can See Everything because he seems to lack that kind of turmoil. He’s hustle-and-grind culture in its final dehumanizing form. The world is just something for him to absorb and scan for advantages at 2x speed.

Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:00:09 GMT

The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness

Years ago, I was in Washington DC when Prince Harry blew through on an official engagement. He was 28, with a full head of hair, a slightly louche gait and a public image that, on a tour of the Senate led by a baffled-looking John McCain, caused people to lose their minds.

Senate staffers stood five deep to get a glimpse; women materialised from every corner, more glamorously dressed for the office than usual. The excitement was so great that there were actual screams from behind the security line. I remember noting the prince’s prominent ears, the high colour in his cheeks and his habit, when addressed, of bowing his head, as if humbled by what he was hearing. Aw, I thought. Bless him.

But that was a long time ago. This week, Harry, now 42, appeared on camera in an interview in New York with GQ, playing to a very different audience. He looked older and schlubbier – don’t we all – the diffidence of youth replaced by something more pompous and belligerent, undergirded by what, in recent years, has appeared to be his bottomless well of hurt feelings. Harry was promoting something – a masterclass on “grief science”, which he has undertaken with Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor. But the question of why on earth he would double down on previous US media appearances, none of them successful, sat alongside the bigger royal question of the season: namely, what are he and his wife, Meghan, going to do?

Since the pair arrived back in the UK this summer after a six-year absence, watching them try to settle on a role has been a veritable festival of awkwardness, not least because it’s not entirely obvious where they have left to go. In March, Netflix ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, less than a year after it replaced the pair’s $100m mega-contract with a first-look deal. These well-publicised failures were compounded by the previous death of Meghan’s podcast, the couple’s parting with Spotify and what might politely be called their low productivity metric when it comes to anything not immediately related to the royal family.

In this, the Sussexes are no different to any other creators endlessly raking over their own lives for content. The difference, of course, is that Harry, with a lofty mindset inculcated from birth and which is presumably incredibly hard to shake, presents his every gesture as automatically belonging to that higher calling, public service. “I don’t do it for myself,” he says in the interview in New York when explaining the venture with MasterClass. (Side note: the real masterclass here is in watching the GQ hack trying to use Harry’s grief project as a Trojan horse for questions about the royal family, among them: “Do you grieve that?” in relation to Harry’s fallout with King Charles, and a sleight of hand reference to “anticipatory grief” in a reach to get his father’s health on the table. Honestly, I tip my hat).

“Trying to make an impact in the world, that is genuinely what energises me,” says Harry, sinuously pivoting away from the awkward questions. And if he stuck to harmless banalities about grief and, oh God, what he calls his mission as a storyteller, one might be inclined to say good luck to him. Harder to stomach is what appears to be his and his wife’s need for the public to participate in their grandiose delusions.

Witness the Sussexes in Nottingham last week, going on a walkabout under the auspices of a charity event that, to me, looked more like an exercise in self-gratification. As the king had already sternly warned the pair: they’re private citizens, now, with no officially sanctioned public engagements, and yet here they were, working a crowd like any active-duty royals. While Meghan smiled excessively with her “hello, little people!” act, her husband alternated between mild engagement with the well-wishers and sending category-five death stares to the hacks, poor sods, who’d turned up to cover this non-event. It was embarrassing, and awkward, and as someone pointed out on the internet, like watching David Brent return to the office after being fired.

And so, while the top line from the interview in New York focused on Harry’s indirect call for reconciliation with his family, it was another takeaway that struck me more forcefully. More than once, the prince talked about the importance of knowing yourself, adding that he had “put in the work” and clearly positioning himself as more evolved than his father and brother. I would suggest Harry’s journey of self-awareness has a way to go yet.

Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 05:00:07 GMT

If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor

However grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?

There are – or were – signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested has increased, while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year is one-sixth of what it was when records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate has fallen by 71%. If Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is re-elected president on Sunday, the country could reach zero deforestation by 2030. The arc of the moral universe seems to have bent towards justice.

But what my faith in human nature failed to account for was a perverse delight in destruction among a small cohort of the economic elite. There are people who appear to hate life and love death. Donald Trump’s removal of protections on public lands, the small bite – doubtless the first of many – he wants to take out of Yosemite, his assaults on the US National Park Service and the US Forest Service, his trashing of the Endangered Species Act: all are partly a response to lobbying by ranchers, loggers, frackers and miners. But this, I think, is not the primary driver.

More important to him, I’ve come to believe, is a vengeful desire to hurt. I doubt Trump hates the monarch butterfly. I’d be surprised if he knows what it is. But he does appear to hate people who love the monarch butterfly. Destroying the habitats on which this and many other endangered species in the US depend seems to be part of the “retribution” he promised. The New York Times was unable to find evidence that Trump has ever visited a national park. He probably doesn’t hate them either. But seemingly anything valued by the enemy – greens, liberals, socialists, feminists, anti-racists, “bureaucrats” and “blockers” – should be attacked on principle.

Wiping ecosystems off the map is an obvious demonstration of power. Extinction leaves a permanent mark, which is every dictator’s dream. It’s also a highly effective means of hurting those who resist him: the Indigenous people and other people of colour so often on the receiving end of environmental destruction; the regulators; the scientists and the rest of the intelligentsia; above all, people who care.

Caring could be seen as the far right’s meta-target. The “suicidal empathy” theme now crops up repeatedly in videos, newspaper columns and speeches: a professed belief that those who care about other people or species should be destroyed by those who don’t. This belief, by definition, is psychopathic. What exhausts my optimism is that, conned by shallow promises such as the use of brutal methods to address crime, people keep electing those who subscribe to it.

Physically and politically, Flávio Bolsonaro is the spitting image of his father, the jailed coup-plotter, Jair. When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil, he appeared to see ecological destruction as a kind of a holy duty. The deforestation rate rose by 59% in his four years, and attacks on Indigenous people and other forest defenders, as well as invasions by illegal ranchers, loggers and goldminers rocketed. The crudest forms of extractivism – regardless of their costs, or how they might hold back all kinds of progress – were a matter of policy.

The ideology of the far right in Brazil has been described as “beef, Bible and bullets”: violence against those who resist the seizure of their resources, an ultra-conservative evangelism and the expansion of cattle ranching, which is both a potent symbol of far-right machismo and the primary driver of deforestation in the Amazon.

Jair Bolsonaro looked back with nostalgia to the military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985 – which was actively supported by the US government – during which local oligarchs could do as they pleased, and those who opposed them were tortured and disappeared. The warnings couldn’t be clearer, but Brazil seems determined to revisit its nightmares. Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October, and is likely to become president.

If he wins the second round this week, the gleeful rampage of his supporters, catalysed by government policy, threatens not only the Amazon but the Atlantic forest in the south, the Pantanal wetlands, the Pampa grasslands and the savannah habitats of the Cerrado. This is politics as an orgy of destruction. Let’s eradicate our life support systems – that’ll teach the liberals!

Trump has been using all possible means to help Bolsonaro win. He gives the impression of seeing Latin America as the conquistadores did – one big heap of treasure, ready for looting. The region’s far-right demagogues are only too happy to help. Mass deforestation and the sudden ecosystem collapse that is likely to result offers a finality to their politics: there’s no coming back from this. You Indigenous people, you greens, you carers: you’ll have nowhere left to hide. The world will be ours, even if it is a world of ashes.

What might Bolsonarismo teach us? First, it appears there is no limit to the perversity of the ruling class, which would rather there was nothing left to share than cede any fraction of the planet to the poor.

Second, that it possesses all the tools – social and traditional media, the pulpit and the gun – required to make its perversity look like common sense, or at least irresistible, as force is deployed. Third, that the only defence we have against suicidal gullibility is what the Brazilians call conscientizaçao: raising awareness about the relations between exploiters and exploited, and the violence that underpins them. Otherwise all that is good, trusting and hopeful in humanity can be harnessed for a war against everyone and everything.

As for the idea that nobody wants to live on a dead planet, Elon Musk, with his preposterous plans for living on Mars – “Fuck Earth! Who cares about Earth?” – has killed that too. Extending the frontier of destruction, even to the point of human extinction, comes across as a matter of pride. The four horsemen ride again, not in cloaks but in stetsons and denim shirts, driving their cattle before them.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

A violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paint

The Guardian Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:00:06 GMT

Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable

Last Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central France was set ablaze. By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, and other scenes of unrest across France, were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.

For some, the flames announced a pan-European youth revolt, proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but about migration and Islam, urged Europeans to “close the borders”. The mayor of Limoges saw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.

I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading across Europe, driven by the same grievances and violence.

None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.

What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France, the mobilisation began in schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances had widened to encompass the cost of living.

In Belgium, meanwhile, students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours. Greek students have mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, while German pupils have protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.

Look beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. In Albania, student unrest builds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. In Serbia, students have led nearly two years of largely peaceful protests following the Novi Sad railway station disaster. Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students are running in this weekend’s election on their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.

Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images, slogans and tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.

Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain. Eurostat reports that EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026 TUI Foundation Youth Study found that 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.

Youth unemployment in the euro area remains substantially higher than overall unemployment. One study of French firms found a sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. The European Central Bank cautions that the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.

Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.

France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.

What happened in Milan showed how the two can blur. A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform, was followed by looting carried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence and scrutiny of police conduct.

But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

The misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.

This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.

For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, from the Trump administration to Vladimir Putin.

President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.

Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.

Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.

Alberto Alemanno is the Jean Monnet professor of EU law at HEC Paris and the founder of The Good Lobby

Key Trump Health Adviser Resigns Ahead of Midterm Elections

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Calley Means, who helped unite Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump, pushed food reforms but grew frustrated with stalled progress on the MAHA agenda.

By Christina Jewett

Reporting from Washington

Calley Means, a leader of the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from the Trump administration on Thursday, signaling a further erosion of a coalition that helped propel President Trump to power a second time.

Mr. Means, a top adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services, was a key official behind policies around food quality, including an effort to increase disclosure of the chemicals in food, remove artificial food dyes and ban soda from the federal food assistance program known as SNAP.

He also worked on an executive order to support the development of psychedelic medications, which got a boost from the podcast host Joe Rogan.

“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and R. F. K. Jr. — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt D. C. bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Mr. Means said in a statement.

In recent months, though, he began to feel stymied in his attempts to deliver on promises to improve the food supply, such as by defining ultraprocessed foods, an initial step to regulating them, according to a person close to him.

Vani Hari, a MAHA leader and healthy eating influencer, said that a turning point for Mr. Means came when the White House roiled the MAHA movement with an executive order supporting the increased production of glyphosate, an herbicide that the movement is particularly focused on eliminating.

“It became very clear in the last few months that no progress was getting made,” she said. “And when you’re spinning around in circles, you can only take so much.”

Mr. Means’s profile rose before he joined the administration, during a podcast tour on which he decried the manipulative tactics of lobbyists from his experience with the beverage industry. He continued to view lobbyists as a corrupting force in Washington, said Ms. Hari.

“Calley was the architect of MAHA,” Ms. Hari said. “He was one of the most successful food policy advocates in history, in my opinion, at this point. And it’s a sad day for the U. S. government to lose him.”

Mr. Means, who was a campaign adviser to Mr. Kennedy and Mr. Trump, played a key role in brokering their agreement to join forces in the final months of the 2024 campaign.

After Mr. Trump was shot in the ear during a rally in Butler, Pa., in July 2024, Mr. Kennedy spoke about wanting to offer support, given his family’s history of tragic political violence. Mr. Means encouraged Mr. Kennedy to call the president, starting what would become a running dialogue.

Their alliance has been credited with helping Mr. Trump win the White House again, given the support of voters who embraced a message of pushback on corporations to protect children from a toxic food supply.

The administration quickly secured agreements from food companies that pledged to remove artificial dyes and seed oils from their products. Mr. Means also played a key role in MAHA reports outlining goals to reduce chronic disease in children. He worked on other initiatives to require nutrition education in medical school, and on a revised food pyramid.

Mr. Means has shown little interest in Mr. Kennedy’s work on vaccines, finding it to be a polarizing topic. He has preferred to see Mr. Kennedy focus more on the healthy eating part of his agenda.

Before his work on the presidential campaigns, Mr. Means cowrote a book with Casey Means, his sister. They argued that people could avoid chronic disease through careful attention to diet, exercise and some less conventional efforts, such as monitoring glucose levels.

Mr. Trump last year nominated Ms. Means to be the surgeon general, but withdrew her from consideration when it became clear that she did not have enough Senate votes for confirmation.

Mr. Means also held equity in Truemed, the company he co-founded, for most of his first year at the Department of Health and Human Services, advising on an array of health topics. The company offered a marketplace of items people could buy with health savings account funds, which were opened to additional people under a policy that Mr. Trump enacted in 2025.

In the administration, Mr. Means could be outspoken and direct, and was a pugnacious profile on social media, castigating critics. In recent days, his frustration became apparent in his posts on one of his signature issues — the health effects of ultraprocessed food consumption, which he said was “highly tied to our chronic disease crisis that is killing Americans and bankrupting our country.”

Still, he wrote in his resignation statement that “the past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and health care incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.
