Trump Is Still Chasing His Yalta. Here’s What He Doesn’t Get.

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Michael Kimmage

Mr. Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War, is an expert on U. S.-Russian relations.

In February 1945, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin met at the Crimean city of Yalta to lay out the shape of postwar Europe. Yalta is typically used as a metaphor for appeasement or cynical realpolitik, and it is both. But it is also a metaphor for consequential diplomacy. The agreements made presaged a Europe separated into different zones, a state of affairs that lasted until the Central and Eastern European revolutions of 1989.

President Trump has been searching for his Yalta in the war in Ukraine since the start of his second term. It’s easy to see why: It could be an appealingly simple, Trumpian transaction, in which the leaders of great powers sit down and determine a course, while minor powers must take what they are given. Like F. D. R., Mr. Trump is willing to compromise on behalf of others. F. D. R. did not insist on full autonomy for Poland and the Baltic republics in 1945, and Mr. Trump has made it clear that he would accept truncated Ukrainian autonomy.

Though at times Mr. Trump’s nonlinear foreign policy has favored Ukraine, when it comes to negotiating an end to the war, Mr. Trump has done almost nothing to empower or include Ukraine and its European partners. His efforts to lay out the shape of postwar Europe are always directed toward President Vladimir Putin of Russia, who, in Mr. Trump’s reading of the world, is understood as the leader of a country with the entitlements of a great power. After almost two years of this, Mr. Trump has succeeded not in resolving the conflict, but rather in making the United States a sideshow to the actual process of peace.

We are in the throes of another such attempt. Mr. Trump has called for a change of presidents in Ukraine. According to Kyiv, the White House has also curbed Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite internet and delayed the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles. U. S. officials deny any disruptions. Simultaneously, Mr. Trump has been upgrading relations with Russia, with a deal to purchase Russian diesel and exempting it from new sanctions. Reports of a great-power conference between the United States, Russia and China on the sidelines of a larger summit scheduled for next month conjure a 21st-century Yalta, with China substituted for Britain.

Any such framework for peace in Ukraine is destined for irrelevance. Russia is not basking in the kind of overwhelming victory that gave the Soviet Union its leverage in 1945; it has experienced something much closer to defeat in Ukraine. Mr. Putin is trying to transform an unwon war into diplomatic concessions that the United States has no authority to give — and no ability to deliver.

Eight decades ago, the United States commanded two assets in Europe. One was an immense military presence augmented by the fact that the United States was about to become the world’s sole nuclear power. Having helped to liberate most of Europe from fascism, the United States also enjoyed widespread trust and moral prestige. Mr. Trump has devastated America’s reputation in Europe. He has imposed aggressive tariffs and made territorial threats to Greenland and plans to significantly decrease the U. S. military presence. In Europe, the United States is a fading power, not an ascendant one.

Then there is America’s role in the war itself. Mr. Trump started withholding U. S. military aid to Ukraine almost as soon as he returned to office. He has cut financial support to Ukraine to almost zero and brokered a deal with European countries to purchase matériel for Ukraine from the United States. He has weakened NATO’s Article 5 commitment. He has diminished Europe’s general capacity to deter Russia and, by adding friction to the trans-Atlantic relationship, has made it harder for Ukraine to defend itself.

The subsequent changes in Europe have been gradual, but dramatic. On one level, the transition is to Mr. Trump’s liking. Germany has led the way in expanding European defense budgets, and with its wealth and technological sophistication Europe is on its way to becoming a defense-industrial powerhouse. But this, in turn, is making Europe less deferential to Washington. Europe and Ukraine have an abundance of agency and no desire to be chess pieces on a board. Mr. Trump has done so much to make this war Europe’s war. Now that it is, the most important question is whether Europe — deeply invested in the precedents that the war will set in Ukraine and elsewhere — can maintain a united front. The United States can be a partner, a nullity or an obstacle, but it cannot undo the evolution that it has provoked.

If it chooses to, the United States could further degrade its relations with Europe and Ukraine. It could terminate all support for Ukraine. It could end targeting and intelligence sharing. Mr. Trump might decide to do this after the midterm elections, when he no longer has to face the American electorate, perhaps out of a personal dislike for President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine or the potential profit in normalizing relations with Russia. But this would probably not be the cause of Ukraine’s defeat.

Mr. Trump can hurt Ukraine, and to a degree he can isolate it diplomatically. He alone cannot decide its future.

Michael Kimmage is the director of the Kennan Institute, a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and the author, most recently, of “Collisions: The Origins of the War in Ukraine and the New Global Instability.”.

New York City Passes Horse Carriage Ban, Ending a Central Park Tradition

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A passenger’s death in June became the impetus for the City Council to ban the practice, but the bill will likely face a court challenge before being implemented in 2028.

By Ed Shanahan and Dana Rubinstein

The New York City Council voted on Thursday to banish horse-drawn carriages from Central Park in two years, setting the stage for the elimination of an attraction as old as the park itself.

The Council vote on the bill imposing the ban was a definitive, if not final, step toward ending a politically contentious debate over the future of the carriage industry, which some people criticize as a form of animal cruelty with no place in a crowded park and others embrace as a vestige of old-world charm.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he supports the initiative, but has not said whether he will sign the bill, which faces a likely court challenge.

The legislation dictates that horse carriages will not be allowed to operate in the city as of June 2028, but it includes few concrete details about how the city will address the economic fallout of eliminating the industry for the roughly 200 owners, drivers and stablehands whose livelihoods are tied to it. The bill is also vague on what will become of the 180 carriage horses.

Officials say that the nearly two years between the bill’s passage and the ban’s effective date give them enough time to hash out those details. Opponents of the ban, including the union that represents the owners, are not reassured.

In a letter sent to city officials on Wednesday, lawyers for the union, Transport Workers Union Local 100, vowed to challenge the legislation in court should the council pass it.

The bill’s passage was a major victory for animal-rights activists, who have waged a yearslong campaign against the carriages. Those efforts, which had previously failed to attract substantial political support, gained momentum this summer with the death of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India.

Mr. Mahajan was in a carriage with his family when the driver stepped out to take their picture. The horse bolted, and the teenager’s mother fell from the carriage. In trying to help her, he fell as well and hit his head on the ground.

Since his death, his parents have been vocal in pushing for a carriage ban, including with an emotional appeal to Council members via videoconference from the couple’s home in India. On Thursday, several family members were in City Council chambers for the vote banning the industry. They have taken steps to file a wrongful-death lawsuit against the city and Con Edison, saying that stray voltage caused the horse to become agitated.

By last week, Julie Menin, the Council speaker, and Mr. Mamdani had agreed on the legislation.

The union argues that not only are the horses well cared for and heavily regulated, but that the bill’s provisions for addressing the economic fallout, which include creating a “horse-drawn-cab-industry transition plan” by next April, amount to empty promises.

John Samuelsen, the T. W. U.’s international president, said on Wednesday that the bill did “not have any protections in it” for workers. The industry employs roughly 150 drivers, a couple of dozen stable hands and farriers who shoe horses, according to the union.

Mr. Samuelsen reiterated his belief that Ms. Menin was using a “contrived public safety crisis” to cater to real estate interests eager to develop Manhattan parcels now occupied by horse stables. Ms. Menin has denied that accusation.

Mr. Samuelsen and other critics have repeatedly noted that Mr. Mahajan’s death, while tragic, was the first known death of a carriage passenger in Central Park in the industry’s history.

Those critics include President Trump, a New York native who lamented the Council’s move in a social media post on Thursday.

“The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience,” Mr. Trump wrote. “So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”

Those who oppose the ban have also said that speeding cyclists, including those on e-bikes and pedicabs, pose far greater hazards. Since Mr. Mahajan’s death in June, a cyclist died after colliding with an unleashed dog, and a pedestrian was killed after being hit by a cyclist.

Jim Gennaro, a councilman and self-described equestrian, has argued that provisions for the care of the horses to be retired are inadequate and that finding appropriate homes for them will not be easy. He estimated the cost of caring for a horse at $25,000 a year.

“Sometimes it takes months to find suitable lifelong accommodation for even one 26-year-old retired horse,” Mr. Gennaro, a Queens Democrat, said in a statement on Wednesday evening.

In their letter to city officials on Wednesday, the union’s lawyers said they had ample grounds for a legal challenge, including the absence of any provision in the bill to compensate those who had spent “many thousands of dollars” to buy carriage medallions from the city.

The 68 medallions have cost owners as much as $400,000 a piece, according to the union. Should the bill pass, the lawyers wrote, the union would seek a court order blocking it “before the ink dries.”

Nicholas Paolucci, a spokesman for the city’s Law Department, said officials were “reviewing the letter.”

“We are confident the legislation is grounded in the law and will be prepared to defend it,” he added.

On Wednesday, Joann Ariola, a Republican councilwoman from Queens who had previously signed on as a sponsor of the bill, said in a statement that she was withdrawing her support. The carriage ban in its current form, she said, did not give adequate “consideration to the hard-working carriage drivers whose livelihoods are at stake.”

“The drivers deserve a meaningful plan, real solutions and a clear path forward before their ability to earn a living is taken away,” Ms. Ariola wrote.

Ms. Menin said on Wednesday that setting the ban’s effective date two years from now gave city officials enough time to help drivers and others employed in the industry to find new jobs and that she was committed to working with the Mamdani administration to achieve that goal.

A spokeswoman for the mayor said the administration “has been working on a detailed plan for the transition of the work force and industry, and we have begun discussion of compensation for medallion owners.”

Ed Shanahan is a rewrite reporter and editor covering breaking news and general assignments on the Metro desk.

Dana Rubinstein covers New York City politics and government for The Times.

Impeachment. It’s Not Just for Presidents.

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By David French

Opinion Columnist

Imagine that it’s January 2027 and Democrats hold both chambers of Congress. They’ve been elected in a wave of public outrage over inflation, the war in Iran, and — crucially — public corruption. In fact, a Fox News poll taken shortly before the election showed that “corruption in government” was the top concern of voters, even greater than inflation.

How should the Democratic majority respond?

Last week Senator Elissa Slotkin, Democrat of Michigan, shared her thoughts about this, and it made parts of the right very, very angry.

During a discussion at the University of Chicago, Slotkin argued that a Democratic-controlled Congress should impose accountability on the Trump administration, but also that it can’t become the “whole personality” of the Congress.

And so, she proposed, Congress should “pick signature cases and you have to go after people and projects that are just super egregious.” She acknowledged the two failed impeachments of President Trump, but said, “The people around Donald Trump who are doing his bidding and enabling this have no such immunity. They have no immunity the way the president does. And to me, he couldn’t do any of this stuff without all those people saluting and supporting it. So you go after the people who did his bidding.”

Here’s the part that made the right truly mad: “I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? That sounds fun. I might get an opportunity.’ I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want. And so let me avoid participating in that.’ I want that deterrence message sent.”

The Chicago Thinker, a self-described conservative and libertarian student-run publication from the University of Chicago, clipped the latter portion of her comments and ignited a firestorm.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board wrote that Slotkin was “essentially promising a scorched-earth lawfare campaign that goes after all and sundry, including what she calls ‘people who enabled’ Mr. Trump.”

A group called the Center to Advance Security in America even went so far as to file an ethics complaint against Senator Slotkin, claiming that she may have been trying to intimidate young Americans from pursuing careers in public service.

Others just lied. Greg Price, a MAGA influencer with a large following on X, said that Slotkin “just said that he [sic] wants to prosecute everyone who works for President Trump.”

Different others threatened her. Mike Davis, a prominent Republican lawyer and former clerk of Justice Neil Gorsuch, posted on X, “Try it, @ElissaSlotkin. Learn about the Second Amendment, sweetheart.”

Jesse Kelly, a talk radio host who also has an immense following on X, wrote, “Elissa Slotkin should be arrested for what she said. These are the kinds of things we have to do to communists in order to stop this from escalating.”

“Crush this before it gets worse,” he said.

The hysteria was so out of proportion to Slotkin’s comments, that it’s worth pondering whether this was Trumpists’ own exercise in “deterrence.” They’re trying to deter accountability for MAGA’s immense corruption.

In reality, however, Slotkin was raising the right question and — by focusing on the “signature” cases — in the right way. How should a Democratic Congress respond to the extraordinary corruption of the Trump White House? And what can it do if President Trump is essentially immune to prosecution and impeaching the president has already failed, twice?

Her top-line answer is sound — pick the most egregious cases and pursue his enablers. But the default method should be impeachment rather than prosecution. Done correctly, impeachment can be more unifying and more effective than a campaign of criminal prosecution.

In fact, a campaign of criminal prosecution may well be impossible. Prepare for Trump to issue a host of pre-emptive pardons, protecting everyone from his family to his cabinet to his most senior advisers from criminal liability for any federal crimes committed in office or near one.

In other words, Trump may use the most misguided provision of the Constitution — the pardon power — to wreck the rule of law. In response, Democrats and Republicans should revive the impeachment power, the most underused portion of the Constitution, to save both the rule of law and the structure of our government.

First, let’s talk a bit about the law. Any efforts to prosecute Trump or his enablers criminally will run up against three roadblocks. Two are obvious, one is less so.

Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the Constitution gives the president the power to “grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.” This power is one of the last vestiges of royalty given to the American president, and its reach is limited only by his or her integrity.

Trump now understands this reality fully, and no one should doubt his willingness to exercise his power to the fullest.

As Joe Biden demonstrated (in one of the worst moves of his presidency) the power to pardon can even be pre-emptive, granting pardons for cases that might be brought. It extends to people inside and outside the government, and it can grant total immunity from legal accountability for even the most heinous of federal crimes.

The second barrier to prosecution is unique to the presidency: Trump v. United States — the most misguided Supreme Court decision of the new century. As I’ve argued before, an otherwise originalist court reached a decidedly un-originalist decision to grant former presidents sweeping immunity for actions undertaken in office. The immunity isn’t absolute, but it’s broad enough to make any post-term prosecution of a president extraordinarily difficult.

The final barrier is both legal and practical. Proving a public corruption case is hard, and it’s getting harder. For example, in a 2016 case, McDonnell v. United States, the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of a former Virginia governor, Bob McDonnell. He and his wife received roughly $175,000 in loans and gifts from a businessman named Jonnie R. Williams Sr.

The court found that the government had not proven that McDonnell had committed any “official acts” in exchange for a financial benefit. McDonnell had set up meetings between Williams and Virginia public officials, had hosted events benefiting Williams’s company at the governor’s mansion, and had contacted other Virginia officials on Williams’s behalf.

Those were not official acts, the court reasoned, because “to qualify as an ‘official act,’ the public official must make a decision or take an action on that ‘question, matter, cause, suit, proceeding or controversy,’ or agree to do so.”

A later case, called Snyder v. United States, reversed the conviction of James Snyder, the former mayor of Portage, Ind. He received a gift of $13,000 from a truck dealer after Snyder spent more than $1 million at the dealership to purchase garbage trucks for the city.

The Supreme Court found that Snyder had received a “gratuity,” not a bribe, and the relevant federal statute criminalized bribery, and did not criminalize granting a gratuity after a favorable decision had been made.

Taken together, these decisions opened up an immense gray zone for financial influence, leaving bribery prosecutions viable in only the most brazen of cases.

I bring up these cases not because they foreclose any prosecution of Trump officials, but rather because they show that simply proving that money changed hands under suspicious or plainly immoral circumstances is not the same thing as proving a crime.

What this means in practice is that public corruption cases should be brought, but they must be brought carefully and selectively, when the law is clear and the evidence is overwhelming.

There could be plenty of those to go around — but only if Trump stays his hand on pardons. And he almost certainly won’t.

But impeachment is different. It’s a political remedy for “high crimes and misdemeanors” that involve violations of the public trust, not just violations of the law. And it has an important prophylactic effect that not even a felony conviction possesses — it can ban a convicted person from “any Office of honor, Trust or Profit under the United States.”

The impeachment power is also broad. It extends to the president, vice president and all “civil officers” of the United States. While the term “civil officer” isn’t defined by the Constitution, it almost certainly extends to cabinet heads, ambassadors, other senior executive branch officials and federal judges.

In fact, a number of federal judges have been impeached, convicted, and removed from office in American history.

While we know that it is highly unlikely that a sufficient number of Republicans will cross the aisle to vote to impeach and convict Trump, would they have the same loyalty to, say, Kimberly Guilfoyle, the recently deposed ambassador to Greece who The Wall Street Journal reported had solicited a substantial gift from a Republican donor before her Senate confirmation?

Does that loyalty extend to Richard Grenell, the special missions envoy who’s worn a number of hats during both Trump administrations and who’s embroiled in his own pay-to-play scandal after Alina Habba Mildon, the president’s former lawyer who went on to work at the Department of Justice, accused him of siphoning off millions of dollars intended for a donation to the Kennedy Center, which he ran at the time? (Grenell denies any wrongdoing.)

Does that loyalty extend to Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, who’d already committed an impeachable offense when he disclosed military plans on unclassified Signal group chats and hasn’t slowed down since?

As I was writing this edition of the newsletter, news broke that Julio Herrera Velutini, a billionaire from Venezuela, retained Mildon last year for a four-year period with a compensation package worth more than $50 million. He received a pardon from Trump shortly afterward. (Mildon, too, denies any wrongdoing.)

Herrera had been charged with felony bribery, but negotiated a plea deal for a misdemeanor campaign finance violation. But even that was too much for him to bear.

These incidents are but the tip of the iceberg of corruption, the real Trump tower. In May, Isaac Saul, the founder of Tangle, an online journal, published a comprehensive piece called “The Everything, Everywhere, All at Once Corruption Story” that attempted to provide a complete account of the Trump administration’s self-dealing.

It’s a sobering read, and it’s already out of date. The scandals just keep coming.

The list of people who’ve committed impeachable offenses may be long, but the number who actually face impeachment should be relatively small. As Slotkin argued, accountability can’t be the whole personality of Congress.

But here is the question: If the Republicans lose their congressional majorities, and if public corruption is a principal concern of the voting public, then why shouldn’t Democrats make Republicans take difficult votes to protect many of the most corrupt and unpopular people in American politics?

And if Republicans do start to regain their senses, then some may find it in their own interests to purge their party of its most corrupt figures, the very people who squandered the Republican Party’s victory in 2024 and put the party on a path to defeat in 2026.

I understand the concerns around what Slotkin said. Her comment about deterring young people from joining the administration — especially taken out of its larger context regarding focusing on “signature” or “egregious” cases — looked like a blanket warning against government service under Trump.

And I am partly persuaded by smart and wise people like my friend Jack Goldsmith, a former senior Justice Department official and Harvard Law professor, who fears an escalating tit-for-tat of political prosecutions. That’s why prosecutions should be selective, undertaken (as I said and as Slotkin did, too) in the most egregious cases with the most obvious facts.

At the same time, however, it is political and moral and cultural malpractice to answer the public’s righteous demand for accountability with silence and inaction.

The fear of mutual escalation cannot be used to turn government service into a law-free zone, where unscrupulous actors can exploit the public trust, enrich themselves and harm the Republic — and then, when their misdeeds are discovered, demand leniency because accountability is somehow just too dangerous and destabilizing.

That’s why impeachment is the ideal response. You are not threatening a person’s liberty. Impeachment doesn’t send anyone to jail. But you are exposing their corruption through both a public investigation and a public trial and imposing the most effective punishment for a democratic government, banning them from federal service.

In addition, impeachment would serve a separate salutary purpose; it would put Congress back in the driver’s seat of the American government.

I don’t want young people deterred from public service. I do want them deterred from public corruption, and I want America spared from Trump’s grotesque rerun of the Gilded Age.

I was traveling last week and missed my Sunday column, but I thought I’d share a great conversation from last Friday. Jill Lepore, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian, hosted a discussion about the state of the media on America’s 250th birthday. I was onstage with Steve Inskeep, host of NPR’s Morning Edition and Up First and Jameel Jaffer, the executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University.

One of the most important questions centered around the state of local journalism. Why are so few people tuning in? Here was my response:

We have a market problem. And the market problem is that people in local communities are more thinking about national news. And so if you offer local news, they’re not as interested.

And this is something like if I had to write my book again where I was talking about solutions to our national polarization, one thing that I urged was people to get more involved locally.

Well, after I wrote the book, there was a big wave of local activism in the South, but it was all over a national issue, which is eliminating, purging, CRT, critical race theory, from its [fictional] prevalence in rural southern school districts.

And so, you began to have a situation where people were using local races to fight national issues and that there was less interest in a local issue or in a local publication unless it had an opinion on a national issue.

You can watch the whole thing here.

Presume for the sake of argument that it would be impossible to impeach and convict Donald Trump or J. D. Vance, but it would be possible to impeach and convict one or more of the most corrupt senior members of the Trump administration. Who should be impeached and why?

Thanks for reading. You will soon start to get my columns emailed to you too.

His most recent book is “Divided We Fall: America’s Secession Threat and How to Restore Our Nation.” You can follow him on Threads (@davidfrenchjag).

Justice Dept. Opens Inquiry Into Corey Lewandowski

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The details of the inquiry remain unclear, but it is one of the rare instances in which a Trump ally or appointee has been investigated for potential wrongdoing during the president’s second term.

By Glenn ThrushTyler Pager and Nicholas Nehamas

The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski over accusations that he personally profited from his role as a top adviser to the Department of Homeland Security, according to two officials with knowledge of the situation.

The inquiry, one of the rare instances in which an ally or appointee of President Trump’s has been investigated for potential wrongdoing during his second term, is in response to a referral from the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general, those officials said.

It was not immediately clear what actions are under investigation.

A lawyer for Mr. Lewandowski forcefully pushed back against any suggestion of criminal activity. “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” the lawyer, Adam Trigg, said in a statement.

The Wall Street Journal earlier reported news of the inquiry.

Mr. Lewandowski, who served as Mr. Trump’s first campaign manager a decade ago, worked closely with Kristi Noem, the former homeland security secretary, but left after she was forced out in March.

After Ms. Noem left the Department of Homeland Security, she took on a role as a special envoy for Western Hemisphere security at the State Department. But her term was not renewed when it ended in September. She now holds a lower-profile role as a senior adviser at the State Department.

The catalyst for Ms. Noem’s firing appeared to be her answers during two congressional hearings, particularly her under-threat-of-perjury statements that Mr. Trump had approved of tens of millions of dollars of government ads in which she was prominently featured.

Mr. Lewandowski wielded power far beyond the scope of his role as an unpaid adviser, serving as Ms. Noem’s top aide and confidant. He often hosted meetings in her office without her present, grilling agency officials and issuing orders as he flexed his vast influence over Mr. Trump’s efforts to detain and deport millions of immigrants.

While he joined the department early last year in what was supposed to be a limited, part-time role, Mr. Lewandowski, a longtime Republican operative, used his perch to build an expansive portfolio in which he had wide influence over personnel, contracts and department operations.

Mr. Lewandowski helped elevate Gregory Bovino, a midlevel leader of the U. S. Border Patrol, to a senior position commanding militarized deportation raids across the United States.

Mr. Bovino was forced out earlier this year after agents under his supervision killed two protesters in Minneapolis during an aggressive immigration sweep that he oversaw.

In the last hours of Ms. Noem’s tenure, her agency delivered a windfall to one of her political donors by buying five airplanes from the man’s firm at a substantial markup.

The Department of Homeland Security agreed to pay the donor’s firm $108 million for a Boeing 737 airliner that had been converted into a huge private jet, complete with a stand-up bar, two bedrooms, marble showers and a table covered in manta ray skin.

The firm, Daedalus Aviation Corporation, had bought the same plane a few months earlier from a seller who had asked for less than $90 million, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

Alan Feuer, Maggie Haberman and Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Nicholas Nehamas is a Washington correspondent for The Times, focusing on the Trump administration and its efforts to transform the federal government.

He’d Be the First Openly Gay Man in the Senate. He Rarely Brings It Up.

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee in New Hampshire, would make history if he won. On the campaign trail, he doesn’t dwell on it.

By Jess Bidgood

Reporting from Rochester and Manchester, N. H.

It was a Friday night in an ornate New Hampshire opera house, and Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic candidate for Senate here, had nearly finished his finely tuned stump speech.

He had slammed Washington corruption, promised to fight for affordable health care and lamented high prices, hewing to the message that Democrats across the country believe will win them back control of the Senate.

Mr. Pappas didn’t mention the man in plaid, standing amid the voters on the creaking wooden floor, who may nevertheless represent the most remarkable aspect of his candidacy: his husband.

Mr. Pappas, 46, is running a closer-than-expected campaign against former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican, a race that both parties view as critical. If he wins, he will be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate — but this is not something he’s made central to his campaign.

“I’m not thinking much about history right now,” Mr. Pappas said in an interview. “I’m really thinking every day about the struggles of New Hampshire.”

His low-key approach to breaking a barrier mirrors that of some other Democratic Senate candidates this year, as a party burned by losses in cycles past backs away from identity politics. Former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska talks little about the fact that she would be the first — or tied for the first — Native American female senator. In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s Muslim faith has become the target of political attacks. But on the trail, he talks more about how he would be the first Democratic doctor elected to the Senate in decades than the fact that he would be the first Muslim in the chamber.

Mr. Pappas’s understated approach to his potential pathbreaking reflects his generation as well as the way that his state, with its libertarian leanings, has become more accepting of gay rights over the course of his decades-long political career. Mr. Sununu has left the matter alone.

But it also comes at a fraught national moment, as some gay rights activists warn of the potential for backsliding. Just last week, Vice President JD Vance made fun of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, by suggesting falsely that he was gay.

“We are seeing some incredibly cynical attacks on the L. G. B. T. Q. community today that have been mainstreamed in our politics, and people in the community are scared for where this country is headed,” Mr. Pappas said in an interview.

Still, he said, his constituents have been broadly accepting.

“Our state motto is ‘Live Free or Die,’ ” he said. “I think people, regardless of their politics, really just want their neighbors to be able to be themselves.”

If there is one thing New Hampshire voters know about Chris Pappas, it’s probably not the fact that he’s gay. It’s the chicken tenders.

He grew up in Manchester, where he was a fixture at the Puritan Backroom, the longstanding Pappas family restaurant where his grandfather is said to have invented the chicken tender. It has been a regular campaign stop for candidates for Congress and the White House for years. (Mr. Pappas is a co-owner of the business today.)

Mr. Pappas, who attended one of the state’s largest public high schools, wasn’t sure he would ever be embraced by his community as a gay man. There was no gay-straight alliance there, nor a single out student, as far as he knew.

“I’m living a reality today that I didn’t think was possible when I was growing up just a few decades ago,” he said.

But he came out at Harvard, and wove his identity into a political career that began when he came home and ran for state representative at the age of 22. “It’s not like I put a bullet point on my palm card, but I was very open about who I was,” Mr. Pappas said. Kathy Sullivan, the former chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, said Mr. Pappas’s sexual orientation has rarely become much of an issue in his campaigns.

“I can’t tell you there was a moment when I went, ‘Oh, Chris Pappas is a gay man,’” she said. “It’s just not a big deal.”

“People who knew, knew,” Mr. Pappas said. “And then I think as the battles kind of raged on issues around equality, I found my voice and was regularly speaking out on those issues.”

Pushing for gay rights became a key theme in his career.

In those years — the mid-aughts — New Hampshire was reckoning with gay marriage, which the highest court in Massachusetts, just over the border, had just deemed legal. Mr. Pappas delivered his first floor speech in 2004, when the state Legislature took up a bill to ban the recognition of those marriages.

“Everyone must see this bill for what it is,” Mr. Pappas said then. “It’s an anti-gay bill, plain and simple. No matter how it’s dressed up. No matter how it’s portrayed. No matter how it’s amended.”

That bill passed. By 2007, though, Gov. John Lynch had signed legislation legalizing civil unions — making New Hampshire the first state to do so without a court order or a pending lawsuit. In 2009, six years before it was legal nationwide, Mr. Lynch signed gay marriage into law in New Hampshire. By then, Mr. Pappas was treasurer of Hillsborough County. He lost re-election in 2010, before he was elected to the state’s Executive Council in 2012 and then to Congress in 2018.

In Washington, where he has served four terms in the House, he became co-chair of the Equality Caucus and has, over the years, sponsored or supported several gay rights measures, including one that would expand federal civil rights protections for gay and transgender Americans, and another that would protect benefits for gay, lesbian or transgender veterans discharged from the military because of their sexual orientation or their gender identity.

He is now running to replace Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the three-term Democrat who is not seeking re-election. His understated style mirrors hers.

In 2020, Mr. Pappas was running for re-election to Congress when his Republican opponent, Matt Mowers, used the debate stage to lob one of the biggest attacks of that campaign: Mr. Pappas, he said, had been dating an Amazon lobbyist while voting on bills that Amazon had lobbied on.

“That’s not true,” Mr. Pappas said, shaking his head.

Mr. Mowers did not mention the fact that the lobbyist in question, Vann Bentley, was a man, but Mr. Pappas and some gay rights organizations suggested the attack was rooted in homophobia.

Six years on, that exchange is a fixture of attack ads by Republicans’ main Senate super PAC against Mr. Pappas in this campaign. At least one ad shows images of Mr. Bentley, who is now Mr. Pappas’s husband; another never makes it clear that Mr. Pappas is in a same-sex relationship.

“My husband’s work has always been separate from mine,” Mr. Pappas said, accusing “dark money groups” of trying to “muddy the waters.”

(There is no evidence that Mr. Pappas lied about the existence of the relationship; the bills in question, which Amazon supported, were sweeping measures like government funding and defense measures, and Mr. Pappas’s votes lined up with much of his caucus’s.)

At times, Mr. Pappas has tried to neutralize personal attacks with wry humor. In September, the National Republican Senatorial Committee included a photo of Mr. Pappas and his cat, Dorothy, in a photo collage it posted on social media that also contained an image of Dr. El-Sayed dressed up as a character from “Blue’s Clues,” and Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, drinking bubble tea.

“How does the left keep finding such normal men?” the post asked.

“I have a cat,” Mr. Pappas responded, “and John Sununu’s name is in the Epstein files.” (In a 2010 email, the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein suggested that an associate meet up with “john sununu, has good stories.” It is unclear whether that was a reference to Mr. Sununu or his father, John H. Sununu, the former New Hampshire governor. Mr. Sununu’s campaign said neither man ever communicated with Mr. Epstein or with the associate.)

Barney Frank of Massachusetts had been in the House of Representatives for six years when, in 1987, he became the first member of Congress to voluntarily come out, shortly after a closeted colleague died of AIDS.

It would be another quarter century before an openly gay candidate was elected to the Senate: Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, in 2012. (Since then, Kyrsten Sinema, who is bisexual, and Laphonza Butler, who is gay, have joined and left the chamber.)

So, to gay rights advocates across the nation, the election of Mr. Pappas would represent a major milestone.

“It feels like something you’d want to sing from the rooftops,” said Mayor Matt Gerding of Somersworth, N. H., who said he is the state’s second out gay mayor. But he said he understood why Mr. Pappas’s campaign doesn’t.

“I think they know that, New Hampshire and many people in New Hampshire, aren’t looking for a candidate to necessarily check boxes and make history,” Mr. Gerding said. “They’re looking for a candidate that is honest, and putting their interests first.”

Mr. Pappas was joined this month on the campaign trail by Pete Buttigieg, who is perhaps the nation’s most prominent gay politician. (The two overlapped at Harvard for two years, although Mr. Buttigieg did not come out until later in life, when he was 33.)

But at a packed campaign office and again at the opera house, they assailed national Republicans while leaving it to young organizers who took the stage before or after them to spell out the history they could make.

“It’s because of Secretary Buttigieg and Congressman Pappas that I came out to my family and friends and discovered that the people around me truly loved me for who I was,” one organizer, Calvin Wood, said in Manchester.

In an interview, Mr. Buttigieg said it would be meaningful if Mr. Pappas breaks a barrier. But it wouldn’t be the point of his campaign.

“I think every campaign is about the voters much more than it’s about the candidate,” Mr. Buttigieg said. “And the most important thing about the candidate is: Are they prepared to stand up for what the voters most want?”

Michael Kruse contributed reporting, and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Jess Bidgood is a managing correspondent for The Times and writes the On Politics newsletter, a guide to this pivotal moment in American politics.

Tom Skerritt Has Died. He Was Viper in ‘Top Gun’ and the Captain in ‘Alien.’

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

His rugged good looks, commanding presence and versatility led to key roles in “M*A*S*H” and “Steel Magnolias,” and he won an Emmy on “Picket Fences.”

By Anita Gates

Tom Skerritt, the affable, generally soft-spoken, simultaneously folksy and commanding Emmy Award-winning actor whose best-known roles were in films as different as “M*A*S*H,” “Alien” and “Steel Magnolias,” died on Wednesday. He was 93.

The family announced the death in a statement but provided no further details.

Mr. Skerritt was a familiar and complex screen presence for almost six decades. In Robert Altman’s “M*A*S*H” (1970), he was Duke Forrest, a boyish, martini-drinking Army surgeon, a laid-back guy, perhaps not as flamboyantly iconoclastic as some of his colleagues. He shared their worldview, however. Watching another character, Maj. Frank Burns, being taken away in a straitjacket, he offered his superior officer a thought: “If I nail Hot Lips and punch Hawkeye, can I go home?”

After that, he tended to play strong authority figures — lawmen, military types, confident fathers — who seemed innately, unrelentingly American. In “Alien” (1979), he was the common-sense spaceship captain, a reluctant hero who did the right thing when a monster was on the loose. In “Top Gun” (1986), he was Viper, the hard-nosed flight instructor who told Tom Cruise’s character, “That’s pretty arrogant,” then added, “I like that in a pilot.” But Viper spoke compassionately to the young man about his dead father.

In “The Turning Point” (1977), he was Shirley MacLaine’s solid, understanding husband — a New York dancer turned Oklahoma City husband, father and ballet teacher. He won the National Board of Review’s best supporting actor award for the role. And in “A River Runs Through It” (1992), he was a stern Presbyterian minister, the father of Brad Pitt’s character, who loved fly-fishing in rural early-20th-century Montana.

Playing a small-town Wisconsin sheriff on the prime-time CBS series “Picket Fences” (1992-96) made Mr. Skerritt a household name and brought him an Emmy for best lead actor in a drama series. Some wondered, however, if drama was the right category. In one unlikely episode of the show, created by David E. Kelley, the pope came to town and witnessed a murder. In others, an obese woman killed her husband by sitting on him, the mayor shot a carjacker, and a cow somehow gave birth to a human baby.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

“It was a wonderful satire, though I don’t know if it was always seen as that,” Mr. Skerritt told Film Comment in 2016.

Thomas Roy Skerritt was born on Aug. 25, 1933, in Detroit, the youngest of three sons of Roy Skerritt, who was described as a salesman in the 1940 census, and Helen (Maybee) Skerritt.

Right after high school, Tom enlisted in the Air Force, where he spent four years. Back in Detroit, with the help of the G. I. Bill, he entered Wayne State University as an English major and took art classes at night. Growing interested in film school and in directing, he transferred to U. C. L. A., where he did theater on and off campus. In his last semester, he was cast in the Korean War combat movie “War Hunt” (1962). The ensemble cast also included Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, unknowns who became stars, close friends and mentors.

During the 1960s, Mr. Skerritt appeared mostly on television series — among them “Combat!” (Mr. Altman directed 10 episodes of the show), “Death Valley Days,” “12 O’Clock High” and “The Virginian.”

Television was a significant part of his career in later years, too. Playing some 40 roles in series, mini-series and TV movies in the 2000s, he was seen as recurring characters on “Cheers” (Kirstie Alley’s debonair, desirable, rich boss) and “Brothers & Sisters” (the dead husband who returned in flashbacks).

“For a long time, I kept resisting acting as a profession,” Mr. Skerritt told Film Comment. “There was something about the totality of visual storytelling that appealed to me,” so he remained more interested in directing and writing.

He developed an ulterior motive. In the same interview, he recalled deciding that acting jobs would be “a great way to learn how to be a director.” Ultimately, he did direct a handful of television series episodes, mostly in the ’90s.

In addition to his most famous portrayals, he appeared in another three dozen or so films, including “Steel Magnolias” (1989), as Julia Roberts’s irreverent Louisiana father; Robert Altman’s “Thieves Like Us” (1974), as Shelley Duvall’s father, a gas-station owner; “The Dead Zone” (1983), as a small-town New England sheriff; and the science fiction drama “Contact” (1997), as a scheming presidential adviser.

Mr. Skerritt married Charlotte Shanks in 1957. They had three children and divorced in 1972. He and his second wife, Susan Ellen Aran, had one child and a 14-year marriage (1976-90). In 1998, he married Julie Tokashiki, and they had one child.

Information about his survivors was not immediately available.

His decades of work in TV and film left him cleareyed about the industry, and the effect that one’s appearance can have on a career.

“Years ago, someone said that I was a character actor locked in a leading man’s body,” he told People magazine in 1993. “I thought that was a wonderful compliment.”

Unsealed O. J. Simpson Records Prompt a Request for a New Investigation

The New York Times October 22, 2026

O. J. Simpson Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Tanya Brown said she believed someone helped O. J. Simpson get rid of the murder weapon. One of Mr. Simpson’s former lawyers called for a special prosecutor.

By Mike Baker and Tim Arango

A sister of Nicole Brown Simpson, the slain ex-wife of O. J. Simpson, said this week that she would like to see law enforcement officials investigate whether multiple people were involved in the 1994 killing.

The sister, Tanya Brown, said she believed someone helped Mr. Simpson get rid of the murder weapon, and highlighted a recent New York Times article that, citing newly unsealed court files and interviews, examined the possibility.

“We deserve answers,” Ms. Brown said.

Ms. Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were found stabbed to death in June 1994, and Mr. Simpson was charged with murder. He was acquitted by a Los Angeles County jury in a high-profile criminal trial but later held liable for the deaths in a civil case.

Ms. Brown said she was wary of anything that would fully reopen the case and the trauma of the 1995 trial. But at the same time, she said she would like to see prosecutors seek to answer whether someone helped Mr. Simpson or assisted in a cover-up.

She wasn’t alone in calling for renewed scrutiny of the case.

Alan Dershowitz, one of the lawyers who represented Mr. Simpson, said that a special prosecutor should be appointed to examine whether an accomplice was involved.

Mr. Dershowitz pointed to the findings of The Times’s report, which included documents detailing how a secret informant told law enforcement about the missing murder weapon and Mr. Simpson’s flight from justice. The informant’s brother told The Times that he saw his brother the night of the killings with what appeared to be bloody hands, and that he disposed of a bag with a heavy object inside at his brother’s request.

“The public, even though it’s been 30 years, is entitled to the best evidence as to what really happened or didn’t happen,” said Mr. Dershowitz, a professor emeritus of law at Harvard University.

Another member of the defense team, Robert Blasier, was wary of the idea, given that Mr. Simpson and the informant are now dead. Mr. Blasier, who believes the theories about an accomplice may be true, said that he doubted the world would ever know what really happened.

There are legal hurdles in revisiting the three-decade-old case. In a statement, the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office noted that a charge of “accessory after the fact,” used when someone assists a criminal after the crime, carries a three-year statute of limitations. “Under California law, the alleged actions, even if provable, could not be prosecuted due to the lapse of time.”

A spokesman for the Los Angeles Police Department has said that the Simpson case remains “open and ongoing” and that cold case detectives continue to make inquiries as new leads emerge.

In California, the state attorney general and district attorneys can hire or appoint special prosecutors. In Los Angeles there is recent precedent. Nathan Hochman, the district attorney, last year appointed a special prosecutor to investigate police misconduct cases.

During the 1995 murder trial, prosecutors focused on Mr. Simpson as being the lone participant in the murder. More than a decade later, in the book “If I Did It,” Mr. Simpson described a “hypothetical” account in which someone was with him at the scene and then helped him get rid of bloody clothes and the murder weapon.

The secret informant described in the Times article, Joseph Ippolito, had been a mafia associate and convicted drug trafficker from New Jersey who escaped from prison a month before the murders. He was also close friends with Al Cowlings, the confidant of Mr. Simpson who drove the white Bronco during the infamous police chase on the day Mr. Simpson was arrested.

Mr. Ippolito was arrested more than a year after the murders and told federal law enforcement then that he had important information about the state case, including details on the location of the weapon. Federal prosecutors considered Mr. Ippolito “extremely reliable” because he was helping them on successful mafia and drug cases.

Mr. Ippolito had been on the radar of law enforcement officials and even Mr. Simpson’s defense team. But prosecutors in Los Angeles did not seek to bring him in or question him at trial.

Mr. Ippolito died in 2006. Mr. Simpson died in 2024. Mr. Cowlings did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Dershowitz said the idea of an accomplice was plausible, as he from the start had wondered about the missing murder weapon.

“I’ve often thought that there might have been an accomplice,” Mr. Dershowitz said.

Laurie Levenson, a professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who commented on the Simpson case at the time, said she doubted a special prosecutor would be appointed and questioned whether it would lead to a break in the case. She is doubtful any new evidence could emerge.

Still, she faulted the authorities in Los Angeles for, in her view, not thoroughly investigating what Mr. Cowlings may have known about the killings.

“I think this is a bit like the Jimmy Hoffa story,” she said. “It will keep going because it was never resolved.”

Mike Baker is a national investigative reporter for The Times, based in Seattle.

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

How a Legal Backlash Against Big Tech Is Forcing Big Changes

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Regulating Social Media

Advertisement

Supported by

A series of lawsuits has created a new de facto regulatory regime as courts order companies like Meta and Google to change their business practices — and pay up.

By Cecilia Kang

Reporting from Washington

For decades, tech giants grew at breakneck speeds as Congress struggled to keep pace with the consequences of the companies’ rapidly booming businesses.

But a new de facto regulatory regime has emerged over the past year as courts clobber the biggest internet companies. And for the first time, their product designs and advertising models — which critics say treat users as products — are costing the companies serious money.

The latest blow came on Wednesday, when a New Mexico judge ordered Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, to pay a record $25 billion penalty for abusing consumer privacy. In a 20-page ruling, the judge scolded the company for deceiving consumers and allowing their data to be harvested by the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica.

“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” wrote Judge Francis J. Mathew of the State District Court in Santa Fe.

The decision, and others like it, amounts to a comeuppance for tech behemoths, whose fortunes have been built on the business model of winning the attention — and data — of users. Now, trials and court decisions have laid bare many of the allegations over deceptive and harmful business practices that critics have said long propelled the companies’ growth.

New consumer guardrails are emerging through the courts’ record financial penalties and orders of changes to designs of the companies’ technologies, legal experts said.

“We’re witnessing an inflection point in the regulation of social media,” said Nora Engstrom, a professor of law at Stanford. “Courts, not Congress, are promoting accountability and forcing concrete change.”

The changes stem from thousands of lawsuits filed against Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon, TikTok and others by individuals, schools, and state and federal officials. Their claims include that the internet giants harmed consumers by creating addictive platforms, abusing their power through their collection of valuable data and deceiving users.

For years, the tech industry successfully fought off many threats by invoking a legal shield known as Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996. The law protects the companies from liability for the content posted on their platforms. The companies have also said that there is plenty of competition, and that they have benefited consumers with free services like search and social media connections.

The arguments have long worked to deter new laws. But courts have recently decided differently.

“The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” Judge Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday. “It relates to the way in which Facebook induces people onto the platform and ultimately keeps them there,” he said, “which in turn is what has allowed Facebook to become as profitable as it is.”

The legal backlash was nearly a decade in the making.

In March 2018, concerns over data privacy boiled over with revelations that Cambridge Analytica, which was based in Britain, obtained large tranches of data on U. S. Facebook users without their consent. Employees said the data had been used to sway voters during the 2016 presidential election.

Mark Zuckerberg, who founded Facebook in 2004, was called to testify on Capitol Hill in two days of marathon hearings on privacy abuses related to the scandal. But Congress did not pass any related legislation.

Executives from Meta, Amazon, Google and others were also called to testify in Congress about how their products and monopolistic power abuses over the years have caused potential harms. Again, there was little effect.

But then the courts slowly rolled into motion. Federal regulators and states filed lawsuits challenging the companies’ dominance, business practices and actions that have caused harm to children. Parents and teenagers challenged the companies under claims of personal liability. And school districts filed lawsuits over shouldering costs for mental health services linked to social media use.

Starting in 2024, courts ruled twice against Google in federal antitrust lawsuits, declaring the company a monopolist in search, then advertising technology. Judges issued court-ordered fixes, although critics said they were weak. Meta avoided a similar fate in an antitrust trial, but Amazon and Apple still face upcoming federal cases.

For the state and user lawsuits — primarily targeting social media — personal injury and consumer protection laws appeared a long shot. The products are not physical like a defective baby crib.

But in March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and YouTube to pay a young woman known as K. G. M. $6 million for personal injuries related to years of mental health problems that she said derived from the addictive designs of Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

The watershed decision was followed in August by the New Mexico judge’s order for Meta to pay $942 million in penalties for harming youths with addictive design features, which were violations of state consumer protection laws.

Then last month, attorneys general for 47 states, the District of Columbia and U. S. territories struck a $17.1 billion settlement with Meta that forced time and other limits for young users to curb addiction to Instagram and Facebook. As part of the agreement, Meta paid nearly all of the states $459.3 million to resolve outstanding state privacy claims from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

“There is now a sense of accountability and a public reckoning of social media,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general of Colorado, who co-led that settlement.

In all of the social media trials this year, the companies faced a jury, highlighting the public anger against tech. And the cases relied on mountains of internal documents showing Meta executives, including Mr. Zuckerberg, and YouTube leaders openly discussing how design decisions like infinite scroll, video autoplay and beauty filters increased use by young users.

In the New Mexico data privacy trial last month, lawyers argued that the company misled the public about the privacy of their platforms and presented email conversations involving Mr. Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg, then Meta’s chief operating officer.

The jurors ultimately found that 26 of the 29 statements made by Meta and its executives were unfair or deceptive. It is unclear if the court decisions will have a lasting effect. The companies have vowed to appeal. The decisions come years after the allegations of harm. And the financial penalties are fractions of the companies’ valuations — still some of the most valuable in the world.

But the losses could be a chink in the armor of the companies, legal experts said. And more trials are coming.

“Congress has held hearing after hearing and have done nothing,” said Tim Wu, a law professor at Columbia University who has written for The New York Times. “But it turns out, you can use old law — ancient laws — to catch up to the social media companies if you are willing to challenge them.”

Hi, I've been writing about tech giants like Google and Meta for more than two decades. Something began happening this year: they were losing in courts — and losing big. So I wanted to step back and assess what was going on. What stood out to me is that past misdeeds have not been forgotten and in some instances stem back from more than a decade ago. And in nearly every case, the private conversations between executives have been used as primary evidence against the companies.

Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy for The Times from Washington. She has written about technology for over two decades.

Home Prices Are Starting to Fall in Some Pockets of the U. S.

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped slightly to 7.32 percent as prospective home buyers continue to struggle with affordability. But home prices are starting to drop in some areas.

By Gregory Schmidt

Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices have pushed many potential buyers to the sidelines, crimping home sales and prompting housing experts to lower their recovery forecasts for the rest of the year.

The mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said Thursday that the most popular home loan in the United States — the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage — slipped to 7.32 percent, the fifth consecutive week that rates have been above 7 percent.

High housing costs have put the market in a deep freeze, but prices are falling in some pockets of the country.

“What we’re seeing is more motivated sellers that are cutting prices,” said Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor. com, a listings website.

Prices on more than 20 percent of listings were reduced September, said Mr. Berner. Some markets that soared during the pandemic are correcting, he added, pointing to cities in Florida and Texas. “What were the hot markets are now the pretty cool markets,” he said.

In Austin, for example, home prices slid more than 8 percent in September from a year earlier, according to a report from Realtor. com, using a metric called price per square foot, which is used to calculate the value of a property relative to its size.

Buyers are more educated now and have more flexibility to wait, said Crystal Olenbush, a real estate agent in Austin. Sellers, on the other hand, are feeling pressure to price their homes more realistically, she said, adding that she is seeing more reductions as the market resets.

“People are negotiating,” she said. “They are getting all kinds of opportunities.”

Still, affordability remains an issue nationwide. The median sales price of U. S. homes rose 1.3 percent in September from a year earlier, to $417,500, the 39th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases, according to a report released last week by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

Prices began to surge during the pandemic, when mortgage rates fell below 3 percent. As the housing market began to heat up, bidding wars broke out, which pushed up home prices around the country.

Since then, homeowners have been unwilling to move, which would mean trading their ultralow rates for higher ones. That created a lock-in effect that has helped keep prices elevated, said Lu Liu, an assistant professor of finance at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

“There could be a behavioral story where people are not willing to take a loss,” she said. “It really depends on whether you’re willing to bite the bullet.”

The higher housing costs have hammered existing-home sales, which fell 2.2 percent in September from the year before, NAR reported. Other key real estate metrics — housing starts, pending home sales and builder confidence — have all slumped recently.

Experts point to elevated inflation as an underlying problem. Higher energy costs are driving inflation higher as the war in Iran chokes the world’s supply of crude oil. Consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher in September than a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. But wages have been relatively flat.

“One of the biggest challenges we’re facing right now, especially for first-time home buyers, is that wage growth is not outpacing inflation,” Mr. Berner said.

The sluggishness is prompting experts to revise their forecasts for a housing market recovery. “We expect housing activity to improve around the end of 2027, when we look for mortgage rates to decline,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote Tuesday in a research note.

Until then, they added, “we think housing activity will be more characterized by gridlock.”

Despite the market downturn, a bright spot has emerged for buyers. Sellers are now reconsidering market conditions, which can give buyers the upper hand.

“The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate better prices,” Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, said last week on a call with reporters.

And builders of new homes are more willing to negotiate to clear inventory.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share since 2020, according to a survey released Monday by the National Association of Home Builders, a trade group.

The average price cut was 6 percent for the seventh consecutive month, the group said. In addition, 65 percent of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month that at least 60 percent of builders have done so.

“Our research shows that new home buyers, who often take advantage of reduced rate offerings from builders, pay as much as a full percentage point less on their mortgage.” Mr. Berner said in a report last year. “New construction should absolutely be on the radar of any prospective home buyer.”

Gregory Schmidt is a senior staff editor who has covered real estate since 2022.

Employers Shift Rising Health Care Costs Onto Millions of Workers

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

New surveys show that increases in premiums and deductibles are forcing people to forgo treatments or doctor’s visits while budgets are strained by higher food and gas prices.

By Reed Abelson

Working families are paying much more for health insurance this year, with many postponing doctor’s visits, treatments or filling prescriptions. The number of uninsured Americans is rising as more people wrestle with unpaid medical bills.

This is the stark picture emerging from two surveys released Thursday that show how millions of people in the United States are struggling to keep up with sharply climbing medical costs in recent years.

As the midterm elections approach, Americans are ranking health care near or at the top of their financial concerns, according to a recent poll from KFF, a nonprofit health research group.

Roughly six in 10 adults reported they were very or somewhat worried about affording care.

The majority of Americans — about 157 million — get insurance through their employer. But as costs for coverage have spiked, with increases in the high single digits, businesses have been shifting much more of the additional expenses onto their workforces.

Employees are paying more for coverage, especially if they work for a small business, according to KFF, which released its annual survey of employers about their health benefits.

Many people are also paying thousands of dollars in medical expenses when they get sick, because companies have increased the plans’ deductibles to offset increases in premiums.

The yearly price, on average, for employees to cover their family is now $7,471 a year, up 9 percent from 2025. The total cost for a family plan, including the amount the employer contributes to the annual premiums, has reached $28,303.

Overall, the average deductible for U. S. workers is approaching $2,000 before insurance kicks in, according to the survey.

“People tell us in polls that their health care costs are their top cost-of-living concern, tied with gas prices. The fact that workers’ share of premiums went up almost three times faster than inflation in 2026 helps explain why,” said Drew Altman, the president and chief executive of KFF, in an email.

Harder hit are employees of small companies, defined as those with fewer than 200 workers, whose paychecks have been shrinking as premiums increase, according to the KFF survey. On average, they are paying $9,687 a year for coverage.

More than a third of people working at a small employer have annual deductibles of $3,000 or more.

Companies are also erecting new hurdles for workers to get care, like cumbersome approval processes for expensive drugs or treatments, the KFF survey found. Another way that businesses are trying to lower costs has been to restrict employees’ choices of doctors or hospitals.

“Employers are paying the equivalent of buying an economy car for each employee who has family health insurance coverage, and in 2026 they offloaded more of that cost to workers,” Mr. Altman said. KFF surveyed more than 1,900 employers with at least 10 workers.

For their part, employers attribute higher costs to several factors, including hospital care, expensive new cancer therapies and expanding coverage of GLP-1 medications for obesity and diabetes.

The rollbacks in government programs like Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act have also left more people without health coverage, according to a separate survey from the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit research foundation that analyzes Americans’ experience with insurance every other year. The fund has been a longtime supporter of the A. C. A. and other efforts to expand coverage.

The share of working-age adults who are uninsured rose to 11.2 percent in 2026 from 8.9 percent in 2024, the Commonwealth study showed. Conducted from early May through mid-July, the study has provided one of the first indications of whether people no longer enrolled in Medicaid and Obamacare found other sources of insurance.

The increase in the uninsured rate over the last two years “was really notable,” said Sara R. Collins, a senior scholar at the fund who led the Commonwealth research.

After Obamacare was enacted in 2010, the number of working-age adults and children without insurance fell from around 46 million to a low of about 25 million three years ago. The government changes and soaring medical costs across the broader health sector have fueled a backslide in coverage, bringing the estimated number this year to 30 million uninsured, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

The Trump administration is expected to release official figures on the number of uninsured Americans next year.

The recent increase is statistically significant, Ms. Collins said, and the previous Commonwealth estimates of the uninsured rate have been lower than the official government figures and generally tracked in the same direction.

The Commonwealth survey also noted that about 12 percent of working-age adults reported a gap or lapse in their insurance, the same share as in 2022.

The increase in the uninsured rate was not unexpected, with some estimates showing that nearly five million people dropped their individual coverage. Many were no longer able to afford their Obamacare insurance after President Trump and Republican lawmakers declined to extend pandemic-era subsidies that had helped defray the cost of a typical plan.

Enrollment in Medicaid, the federal-state program for the poor, has also been declining, although the bulk of the cuts to that program as part of Mr. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act do not take place until next year. Over the last four years, the share of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid dropped from 15.5 percent to 13 percent, according to Commonwealth.

But the Commonwealth survey, which was based on telephone and online interviews among a sample of 9,360 adults, also underscored how financially insecure people have become about their ability to pay for medical care. The number of people who said they had delayed or skipped care altogether because of the expense increased to 50 percent this year from 46 percent in 2022, according to the survey.

“These reports show the reason why health care costs are at the top of voter concern and outrage,” said Anthony Wright, the executive director of Families USA, a left-leaning consumer advocacy group.

The deepening strains on household budgets are also evident as the rate of medical debt or unpaid bills keeps rising, affecting even those who are insured. About a third of adults with individual policies and those with coverage from an employer reported they were paying off medical bills or medical debt they had already incurred, according to the Commonwealth Fund.

People without insurance tend to have lower levels of medical debt, Ms. Collins of Commonwealth said. “You just use less care if you don’t have insurance coverage.”

The survey found that most Americans believed the federal government had a responsibility to ensure that people had coverage, although Democrats and independents expressed that belief more strongly than Republicans.

“They are mad at hospitals and drug companies and insurers for charging so much,” said Mr. Wright of Families USA. “They are furious at Congress for not reining them in.”

Employers and insurers “have never addressed, not in a significant way, the drivers of health care costs,” Ms. Collins said. “Health care costs are the thing that drives premiums and deductibles.”

Thanks to everyone who’s commented so far — many people are clearly feeling the squeeze. If you’ve had to delay care or look for cheaper options and are open to telling me more about it, feel free to drop me a note at abelson@nytimes. com.

Reed Abelson covers the business of health care, focusing on how financial incentives are affecting the delivery of care, from the costs to consumers to the profits to providers.
