Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

A young family thought they had escaped the toxic legacy of Love Canal with a dream house near a creek in the suburbs. Then the men in the hazmat suits showed up.

Bailee and her mother, Lexi Hawk, look at the yard where Bailee is no longer allowed to play. Credit...

Supported by

By Christopher Maag

Photographs by Brendan Bannon

Christopher Maag spent five days reporting in and around Niagara Falls, N. Y. He and Brendan Bannon visited at least six “red hot” zones on radiation maps.

The first time Lexi Hawk sensed something was wrong, she was playing in her backyard with her toddler, Bailee. Ms. Hawk heard a plane that sounded as if it was right on top of them. She looked and there it was, flying super slow and right above the treetops. It passed over her house again and again.

“I was like, ‘What’s going on?’” she remembers thinking. “‘Are we getting attacked?’”

That was the summer of 2024. A year later, Ms. Hawk and Bailee were outside again when three men pulled up to their house in a truck. One got out and started sweeping a Geiger counter along the grass.

“They told me not to worry, it was probably just a rock,” she said. Some rocks, they explained, could have natural, low-level radioactivity. “I was a little concerned.”

Then, this summer, after finishing her shift at a hair salon, she drove home to find a crew of men on her property wearing head-to-toe protective suits. One used a little yellow backhoe to dig holes in the yard.

“It was like a horror movie scene,” said Ms. Hawk. “It was like driving into a nightmare.”

The little blue ranch house in Niagara, N. Y., was supposed to be a suburban oasis for Ms. Hawk, 24, and her partner, Trevor Bradley, 26. They had lived much of their lives in the toxic minefield of nearby Niagara Falls, a small city where Love Canal — the site of perhaps America’s most infamous environmental disaster — ranks as only the most well-known of dozens of local landfills.

Then this spring, the government contacted people living across a 60-mile swath of western New York, from the suburbs of Niagara Falls to a constellation of farm towns south of Buffalo, with an alarming request: Could officials test their property for radioactivity?

Out of 1,400 households that received the requests, 38 may need extensive cleanups. Four were so radioactive that the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers offered to relocate families immediately. This was how Ms. Hawk and Mr. Bradley learned that they had been letting their 3-year-old daughter play in a yard contaminated by Thorium-232 and other radioactive isotopes.

Ms. Hawk and Mr. Bradley now keep a map that government workers gave them that shows the radioactivity on their property. It is covered with hundreds of dots, each representing a Geiger counter reading. Blue dots, like those in the driveway, indicated low radioactive risk. Yellow dots — elevated risk — crisscrossed the lawn.

Red dots — radiation that government agents described as “red hot” — covered the woods and followed a trail leading to a creek, ending at a swing that Mr. Bradley built for his daughter. It’s Bailee’s favorite place to play.

“Why am I still living here?” Mr. Bradley said, minutes after he was given the map. “And how do I keep my daughter safe?”

Lexi Hawk spent much of her childhood living with her grandparents in a house near Military Road in Niagara. They had an aboveground pool that she swam in all summer with her eight cousins, who visited often. They would play on the swing set and stomp around Gill Creek. When they felt adventurous, the cousins would cross the creek and explore the abandoned drive-in theater on the other side.

“We were catching little crawfish, and the little minnows that swim by, and frogs,” Ms. Hawk said. “It was so fun.”

Her grandparents’ house was a refuge from a chaotic home life. Her father was in the navy and would be absent for months at a time, and her mother struggled with opioids and was in and out of jail. Seven members of her family contracted cancer, she said, and six of them died, including her grandmother.

“So that kind of messed with me as a teenager,” Ms. Hawk said. “I started acting out, smoking weed.”

Trevor, too, had a difficult childhood. As a boy he lived five blocks from Love Canal, a neighborhood that had been evacuated in the 1970s after residents learned the toxic waste dump beneath their homes had most likely caused hundreds of birth defects, rare diseases and early deaths.

Even decades after the toxic landfill at Love Canal was capped and supposedly contained, Mr. Bradley said his family’s basement reeked of chemicals. He reports a litany of health disasters. His aunt got sick in her 20s with a mysterious illness that plagued her until her death at age 53. His grandmother died at age 34, of leukemia. She was the eighth person on the block to die of leukemia, he said; the youngest was 12 years old.

Ms. Hawk met Mr. Bradley when they were in high school; Lexi was 15, Trevor 16. After they dated for a week, Trevor moved in with Lexi and her family.

“We’ve just dealt with a lot of death,” Ms. Hawk said. “So we were both just like, ‘We have nobody but each other.’”

Ms. Hawk became a hairdresser, and by age 18 she was managing a Supercuts salon. In a year she had saved enough money to buy a house of her own — the blue ranch right behind her grandparents’ place, for $129,000. It was in a good school district, at the end of a quiet street bordered by woods and her beloved Gill Creek.

Mr. Bradley, a carpenter, gut-renovated the home with Ms. Hawk’s help. For four happy years they believed they had escaped Love Canal and the legacy of toxic dumping around Niagara Falls.

“I thought we were in the good area,” Ms. Hawk said.

Then the men in white protective suits arrived with their backhoe.

On a sunny afternoon this August, Bailee stood at the sliding glass door in her parents’ bedroom. She looked to her mother, who was in the kitchen, then back outside. This is Bailee’s new ritual, Ms. Hawk said, and she does it throughout the day. Ms. Hawk relented.

“You’re allowed to go on your trampoline,” she said.

Bailee smiled. She stepped onto the back deck, climbed onto the trampoline and started to hop. Moments later, her mother saw that she had moved. Ms. Hawk hustled outside and found Bailee sitting in the yard with one hand in her mouth.

“Bailee!” Ms. Hawk called from the deck. “Get up here! Are you trying to eat grass? Let’s not do that. Can you not eat that?”

Bailee stood and followed her mother. She pouted, but did not cry. Safely back indoors, Ms. Hawk quizzed her daughter, who is 3.

“Bailee, what’s happening in the backyard?” Ms. Hawk said.

“Poison,” Bailee said.

“What kind of poison?” Ms. Hawk said.

“Radioactivity,” said Bailee.

The poison is the legacy of decades of corporate greed and government indifference. According to the state Department of Environmental Conservation, at least some of the nuclear waste buried around Niagara Falls was generated by the Manhattan Project, when chemical companies there were part of the effort to build the first atomic bomb. But most of it was created by private companies processing naturally radioactive ores into commercial products.

In both cases, leftovers that resembled ordinary gravel or dirt were given for free or at reduced cost to local contractors. It was used for road beds, for instance, or as fill in residential yards, possibly including Ms. Hawk’s.

By 1981, reports by federal and state agencies confirmed that radioactive waste was buried in unregulated dumps around Niagara Falls, and that a thorough regional study was required to find it all. Locals have long traded rumors about unregulated dumping, and Ms. Hawk grew up hearing her grandfather’s stories about his bosses at a local chemical factory ordering him to dump barrels of waste into sewers or even the Niagara River.

“Hey, this is western New York,” a Niagara Falls city planner told The Buffalo News in 2018. “You dig in something that was put down in the 1940s or 1950s, you might find something you didn’t expect. This stuff turns up everywhere.”

The government’s systemic study did not begin until 2023, when the Environmental Protection Agency began its low-altitude aerial surveys. So far, according to Amanda Lefton, commissioner of the Environmental Conservation Department under Gov. Kathy Hochul, it appears that the waste came from the manufacturing of chemical products and not nuclear weapons.

“What we’re finding here,” Ms. Lefton said, “are levels that are worrisome for long-term exposure.”

The testing happening now is proof that the government is getting ahead of the problem, said Ms. Lefton, adding that state and federal agencies “launched this effort together to proactively look for radiological wastes that shouldn’t be there.”

But to Ms. Hawk, the government’s decision to look now does not absolve it of the greater sin: doing nothing for nearly 50 years.

“They knew,” she said. “And they let me live here.”

Ms. Hawk and Mr. Bradley understood they would have to relocate, but they were finding it painful to relinquish their dream home. For weeks this summer, Mr. Bradley resisted the urge to mow his yard or weed his garden for fear of what lurked beneath.

By August, he could no longer stand the mess. He finally cut the grass (but didn’t bag the potentially radioactive clippings). A few days later he went to the garden and began pulling weeds with his bare hands. On the government’s map, both areas are blanketed in red dots.

“I wanted something that I could be proud of,” he said. “I wanted to have little trails through the woods, have flowers and plants and a little bridge over the creek. I had visions of living here till the day I died.”

So far, at least, Ms. Hawk and Mr. Bradley say they have avoided the illnesses that have plagued their families. But they are worried. When government workers arrived to test Ms. Hawk’s grandfather’s yard, they walked in circles around the pool with a Geiger counter. They huddled quietly for a few minutes, then approached Ms. Hawk and asked if she ever used the pool. They suggested she avoid it.

“I was like, ‘What do you mean?’” Ms. Hawk said. “I went in that pool all the time when I was pregnant and when Bailee was an infant.”

One day, Ms. Hawk strapped Bailee in her car seat and headed to the grocery store to buy bottled water — the family’s preferred source of drinking water since they got the news about their yard.

“We go through a case every three days,” Ms. Hawk said as she left. “It’s crazy.”

Mr. Bradley stayed behind on the couch. With his partner and daughter gone, the smile fell from his face. Ms. Hawk is so busy now — organizing protests, rallying supporters on Facebook, haranguing government employees on the phone, working scattered shifts at the hair salon — that Mr. Bradley does not want to burden her any further. He keeps his feelings to himself.

“I go to work, come home, put a smile on my face,” he said. “I’ve got to act like it’s all OK. And, like, I’m terrified.”

Mr. Bradley has fought the government over toxic waste before. When he was 12, his mother filed a lawsuit against the city of Niagara Falls and local chemical companies, arguing that Love Canal’s containment system had failed, allowing toxic chemicals to seep into their house. He remembers his brother became sick and got terrible headaches every time he went into the basement.

Trevor was a named plaintiff in the case. As a child and young adult, he sat for hours of depositions about toxic waste. As the case progressed, he watched, powerless, as members of his family died strange, early deaths. The case was dismissed on technical grounds in 2023.

When his partner organized the neighborhood’s first news conference about radioactive waste this July, Mr. Bradley stayed home.

“I dealt with this for so long, I don’t want any part of it,” Mr. Bradley remembers telling Ms. Hawk. “Do you think you’re going to get any further than my mom did?”

Mr. Bradley worried about removing Bailee “from her safe space, the only home she knows.” He didn’t know where the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers would find them a house to stay in, or how long his family would need to live there while the E. P. A. removed waste from his yard. If his family ever moves back home, he worries they might never be safe from environmental hazards. Whatever happens, he said, the house he loves is now worthless.

“No one’s going to buy this house,” he said. “Are you kidding me? Everyone in Niagara and Erie County’s seen our house on the TV, next to radiation. So we’ve just got to eat that loss.”

He looked from the couch to the front door. Beside it sits an overstuffed chair that Bailee likes to climb to look out the window. Just outside lies the garden, a cluster of red dots on the government map. Mr. Bradley fell quiet, wondering how much radioactive bombardment Bailee took before the family ever learned it was there. He began to cry.

“I just want to know if my daughter is going to be OK,” he said. “And I know they’ll probably never be able to answer that.”

For nearly 50 years, the government has known that radioactive waste — some of it from the Manhattan Project nuclear weapons program — was scattered around Niagara Falls and nearby towns. Some homeowners are still wondering what may be buried in their yards.

@Christopher Maag thank you for following our story! It means a lot to us. Most people are blissfully unaware of how much toxic waste is buried around Niagara. I think it’s extremely important to expose the truth with one story at a time!

Christopher Maag is a reporter covering the New York City region for The Times.

Ebola Outbreak in Africa Reaches Widest Expansion Ever

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Ebola Outbreak

Advertisement

Supported by

Health officials are urgently seeking answers about the origins of a case newly identified in Nigeria, the first in that West African nation.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

The Ebola epidemic that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo earlier this year has achieved a grim new milestone, turning up in a third region of the African continent, the widest footprint of any Ebola outbreak to date.

This week, health officials identified a new case in Abuja, Nigeria, more than 2,000 miles west of the outbreak’s epicenter in Central Africa. The news came the same day as the announcement of a ninth case of Ebola in the East African country of Kenya.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said in an interview on Wednesday that he was calling for a meeting of all African health ministers on Oct. 28. If they cannot come up with ways to stamp out the outbreak, he said, “the whole continent can be affected.”

Since the first case was identified in May, Congo has recorded more than 9,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,600 deaths, making the outbreak the fastest growing Ebola epidemic ever. Within Congo, the disease has spread to eight provinces, and about 70 percent of new cases occur in the community, suggesting widespread undetected transmission.

Clinical trials of vaccines against Bundibugyo, the type of Ebola in this outbreak, are underway, but the shots are not expected to be available for many more months. And they leave out children under 5, who account for nearly one in four cases and one in three deaths.

Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and Abuja, its capital, is a hub for global travel, with thousands of international passengers each month.

The patient in Nigeria had recently returned from a trip to Uganda, raising questions about whether that country, too, has active cases again. Uganda confirmed 20 cases and two deaths earlier this year, but the World Health Organization declared in August that Uganda’s outbreak had ended.

Regardless of its origin, “I see the Nigeria case as a reflection of how uncontrolled the growth has become,” said Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the director of Boston University’s Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases.

Dr. Bhadelia said she was more worried about Ebola spreading undetected in African countries that may share borders with affected countries than about it moving to other continents. “I worry about South Sudan every day,” she said.

Some public health experts were alarmed by a lack of clarity about the Nigerian case. The patient is a Ugandan national who lives with her husband, a Swiss diplomat, in Abuja.

The Ugandan health ministry has said the woman traveled to Congo on business and passed through Uganda on her way back home to Nigeria. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here,” the ministry said.

But according to Dr. Kaseya, the woman told health officials she did not travel to Congo and had been in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, on a two-week holiday.

“This is what she said, but we need to continue investigation because for sure she got Ebola somewhere,” he said.

Referring to the possibility of ongoing cases in Uganda, he added: “It’s so difficult to comment and to have a conclusion on that if we don’t know the full story from the lady.”

The dates of the patient’s travel are also unclear. The World Health Organization’s Africa office said she developed symptoms on Oct. 7, four days after returning to Abuja. But an official from the Nigeria C. D. C. has said she arrived in Abuja on Oct. 5, two days before symptoms emerged.

She sought care for malaria-like symptoms Oct. 11, but doctors did not suspect Ebola as the cause of her illness for more than a week. She was diagnosed as being infected with Bundibugyo on Oct. 20. During that time, according to Nigerian officials, she came into contact with at least 44 people, including many health care workers, who are now being closely monitored for signs of illness. But that number is likely to grow as officials learn more about her whereabouts before she was diagnosed, experts said.

In Kenya, eight new cases identified so far are all contacts of the first, a Congolese patient who traveled through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. The patient was diagnosed on Oct. 5 and died the same night.

“One imported case can be contained by quickly tracing contacts,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization. “The real danger is sustained spread within communities.”

Nigeria contended with an imported case of Ebola during the 2014 outbreak, but was able to snuff out the resulting cluster of cases within a couple of months, in part by relying on its infrastructure for polio eradication.

Dr. Bhadelia said she was hopeful Nigeria would once again be able to contain Ebola quickly. She said she was more concerned about the lack of information from the Ugandan government on the potential trails of infection left behind by the patients who traveled to Kenya and Nigeria.

“We’re not hearing enough about the contact tracing, or active investigations to look for any chains of transmission that may have resulted around these two cases,” she said.

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

He Told Us About an O. J. Accomplice. Then He Said He’d Lied. What Next?

The New York Times October 22, 2026

O. J. Simpson Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Insider

A source said his brother had been with O. J. Simpson the night of the murders in 1994. But when we refused to pay, he retracted his story.

By Mike Baker

Mike Baker is an investigative reporter for The Times.

It was the kind of text message that every reporter dreads receiving: An important source did not want to talk further unless I paid him for the privilege.

“if you’re willing to pay me send me an offer and I’ll think about it,” Sam Ippolito messaged me in June.

A few months prior, Mr. Ippolito had confided to me, on the record, that his deceased brother Joey had been with O. J. Simpson on the night of the 1994 murders for which Mr. Simpson had been charged and acquitted. Sam Ippolito knew this, he said, because the brothers had been staying together in the same West Hollywood, Calif., apartment at the time.

We were discussing a plan to publish his account, along with other details, when I went back to Sam to vet his story a bit more. His request for compensation, however, complicated things. I explained that the ethics rules at The New York Times prohibit reporters from paying for interviews.

“In part, the fear is that paying someone for an interview gives the world a strong reason not to trust what the person had to say,” I told him. He had not asked for compensation during our initial interview and, in fact, said at the time that he was not looking for money.

But now, Sam said he had been offered money to tell his story elsewhere, which is legal and permitted by other news organizations. When I declined to bid, he attempted to retract what he had previously told me.

“non of what i told you was true sorry,” he wrote.

Even though he had no legal right to take back what he said, the message caused us some chaos. Was he telling the truth then or now? We decided to keep hunting for information that could corroborate whether Joey Ippolito had some personal knowledge or involvement in the case.

Investigative reporting can often be frustrating. Sources can be skittish, deflecting or contradictory. Public records requests get denied. People shut doors in your face. Everything takes longer than you (and certainly your editors) expect.

There had long been theories in Los Angeles about people who might have been with O. J. Simpson on the night of the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. Mr. Simpson himself had stoked that premise. In 2006, he had prepared a “hypothetical” account — later published in the book “If I Did It” — that described how a friend had joined him at the crime scene. The friend had been horrified by the bloodshed, Mr. Simpson wrote, but by the time he and the friend had returned to Mr. Simpson’s home, the friend had agreed to help him get rid of Mr. Simpson’s bloody clothes and the murder weapon.

Could that be true? A few years ago, a legal battle was brewing about a screenplay that explored that exact idea. I decided to take a closer look.

I went to Los Angeles to meet with one source who had hours of secret audiotapes of a man, Charlie Ehrlich, who had implied in the recordings that he was the one with Mr. Simpson that night. The idea had a sense of credibility: Mr. Ehrlich was in Mr. Simpson’s circle of allies; he had been charged with Mr. Simpson in a robbery case in Las Vegas in 2007. And “If I Did It” had given Mr. Simpson’s accomplice the pseudonym name of Charlie.

But nobody who we interviewed from Mr. Simpson’s 1994 orbit knew if Mr. Ehrlich was in the L. A. area at that time. When I tried to meet Mr. Ehrlich in Florida, he told me that the things he had said on the audiotapes were lies, that he had played along with the idea of being the accomplice to make money and that he had not met Mr. Simpson until years after the murders.

But another name that Mr. Ehrlich had mentioned on the tapes and in conversation, and one already on our radar, was Joey Ippolito, a former mafia associate and drug trafficker. People could place him in Los Angeles in the early 1990s, and my colleague Tim Arango was able to dig through boxes of court archives that showed he had been close friends with Al Cowlings, a confidante of Mr. Simpson who was driving the white Bronco during the case’s infamous police chase. Not to mention: A month before the murders, Mr. Ippolito had escaped from federal prison.

In the process of vetting Sam Ippolito’s story about his brother, we got archival records from when Joey Ippolito was finally caught in August 1995 and prosecuted in New York. But there was a problem: Some of the records were missing, still under seal, and so it was not clear why Joey Ippolito had received such leniency when he was sentenced in 1996.

I decided to send a note to the federal judge who had overseen the case.

“Mr. Ippolito had a lengthy and well-connected history that I believe is in the public interest, and the records can illuminate the process by which he received a plea arrangement,” I explained. “I do not believe there is any substantive need in keeping the records sealed, as Mr. Ippolito reportedly died twenty years ago.”

A couple weeks later, the judge phoned me. She agreed to make the records public.

When the records arrived, Tim and I were shocked at how much prosecutors had praised the cooperation of Mr. Ippolito. He had become a key informant on drug cases and the mafia. He was also dishing about what he knew about Mr. Simpson and the murder weapon, and Mr. Simpson’s attempts to escape justice. The prosecution deemed Mr. Ippolito an “extremely reliable” source, and the records suggested that Mr. Ippolito did, in fact, carry insights about the missing murder weapon — although in a way different than what Sam Ippolito had described.

Then there was Fat Joe.

The rapper who always seems to be in the right place at the right time did a video podcast episode in 2025 in which he spoke of Mr. Simpson and an Italian friend named “Joe.” Watching the podcast, it became clear to me that Fat Joe was talking about Joey Ippolito.

The tale he told added yet another layer of intrigue. Fat Joe said that Mr. Ippolito had once told him that when Mr. Simpson and Mr. Cowlings were in the Bronco during the infamous chase, Mr. Ippolito had been at the airport with a private jet, ready to help them escape.

So there it was, three versions of the Ippolito story: In one, he was passing along information to federal law enforcement about Mr. Simpson and the murder weapon. In another, he told a friend how he had been poised to help Mr. Simpson flee Los Angeles. In a third, as told and later retracted by his brother, he was with Mr. Simpson on the night of the murders.

We began trying to weave those stories together into a coherent tale. We knocked on the doors of former mobsters. We dug through thousands of pages of records in a storage shed in Florida. We talked to federal investigators who kept in touch with Mr. Ippolito up until his death in 2006.

All of it combined — the documents, the interviews, the timeline of events — shows that at the very least, Joey Ippolito had been a secret informant never before revealed to the public. And there was a possibility, given his brother’s account, that he was even more.

So, finally, we published.

Mike Baker is a national investigative reporter for The Times, based in Seattle.

From Kenya to Japan, Rush to Fix Security Flaw Takes Sites Briefly Offline

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Governments and businesses around the world scrambled to prevent hackers from exploiting a vulnerability in PHP, a popular programming language.

By Lynsey ChutelAmelia Nierenberg and Brian O. Otieno

Lynsey Chutel and Amelia Nierenberg reported from London. Brian O. Otieno reported from Nairobi, Kenya.

Japan’s prime minister. A hospital in Germany. Taxpayers in France. An I. T. firm in Kenya.

People’s online routines were disrupted around the globe on Wednesday and Thursday as governments and companies rushed to protect their websites, after security researchers found major flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.

Many took their websites down as an emergency precaution while they fixed the flaw, which was identified using artificial intelligence. A fix was quickly available, and software developers and tech departments from Helsinki to New York scrambled to apply it, meaning that in many cases the outages lasted less than a day.

But the flaw and the temporary shutdowns it provoked showed how far-reaching potential cyberattacks could be — and how deeply the internet has embedded itself into our lives.

In Finland, one of the most digitized countries in the world, the government’s public websites were temporarily shut down, forcing even basic tasks to pause.

“It’s in the fabric of our society, a lot of these services,” said Kalle Pusa, 33, a software developer who is involved in Helsinki city politics. “And I think yesterday and today, a lot of the fabric was a bit ripped apart.”

Mr. Pusa was trying to arrange for the local garbage department to pick up an old couch. But that had to wait until the site was back online.

“It had very strange consequences,” he said.

The British government said that 32 of its services went down as a precautionary measure. In Germany, the websites of states and major cities like Berlin and Munich were affected. The Hannover Medical School assured users that its hospital had not been hacked.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi encouraged businesses to take down their sites, saying on social media that access to her official website had been briefly suspended until updates were installed.

In the Netherlands, several official websites were offline on Wednesday and into Thursday, including the country’s digital ID site, a portal that gives citizens access to government services, and a crime tip website.

While recent data suggests that the use of PHP is waning, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use it, by some estimates.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of Cloudflare, a company that helps websites secure and manage their internet traffic, said that it saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the flaw in the hours before it was publicly announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Mr. Prince said in a social media post.

Security researchers using OpenAI’s advanced A. I. models found the vulnerability, which could allow hackers to take control of servers, steal private data and deface websites, experts said.

PHP, a decades-old language, is a critical ingredient in popular services like WordPress and Drupal. The nonprofit PHP Foundation released a patch Wednesday morning, and security experts said that correctly applying it should protect websites from harm.

But fast-moving hackers could exploit the flaws if they are not fixed quickly enough.

“Any machine running this software — and there’s a lot of machines running this software — is vulnerable,” said Seth Kaufman, a software developer based in the New York area.

Mr. Kaufman, who develops open-source software for museums and cultural organizations, said he used PHP because it is a simple, free coding language. It’s been around forever, he said, and some people in the coding community think it’s clunky. But mostly, he said, it works.

“It does what it’s supposed to do,” he said. “It’s effective. So that’s why it’s still used everywhere.”

That much was evident in the diversity of websites that were taken down as businesses and authorities rushed to fix the flaw.

Anthony Wambua, who runs an I. T. firm in Nairobi, woke up early to do so. He worried that PHP was now “synonymous with serious vulnerabilities.”

In Kenya, which prides itself on its embrace of online services, Mr. Wambua and others worried that the government’s response was sluggish. “I am scared that given the slow speed at which our government moves some of their sites might still be hit,” he said.

In Britain, fans of the reality television show “The Traitors” were briefly met with a cutesy error message with a picture of knitted mice. In France, services on the official tax website had not yet been fully restored as of Thursday evening.

While the temporary outage turned out to be a “road hump” for institutions with large I. T. departments, small businesses went dark for up to seven hours, said Alistair Gleaves, who provides communication services for small businesses.

Mr. Gleaves, who is based in Exeter, in southwest England, quickly warned his clients when news of the flaw broke late Wednesday. His own business suffered when third-party payment services went offline.

He saw a glimmer of hope: A. I. models had helped uncover the flaw. There has been a lot of concern that A. I. is “going to take over the world, it’s going to kill us all,” he said.

But here, he added, “it found the problem.”

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

What Is PHP? Why Are Government and Business Websites Going Offline?

The New York Times October 22, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

A critical security flaw in the programming language underpinning much of the web has prompted a global rush to patch vulnerable systems.

By Karla Adam and Dustin Volz

Governments and companies around the world are racing to patch their websites — or taking them offline until they can be fixed — after the discovery of major security flaws in PHP, a piece of software that underpins much of the internet.

OpenAI, whose artificial intelligence models were used to find the bugs, said in a blog post that it was “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory” given PHP’s widespread use.

PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is a decades-old, open-source programming language that is used to build and run web applications. By some estimates, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use the software.

Services in which PHP is a core ingredient include content management systems like WordPress and Drupal, which help people run websites. Because PHP is a sort of foundational code baked into so many platforms — think of it as invisible digital infrastructure — many businesses may not even realize they rely on PHP.

Security researchers discovered issues in the programming language that could be exploited by an outside attacker.

The bug, which has been hidden in the software for years, was identified by researchers at Calif, a small, U. S.-based cybersecurity company, using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Researchers from Wiz, an Israeli-American security firm owned by Google, also independently reported the vulnerabilities.

The flaw is the latest to be discovered using advanced A. I. tools, which cybersecurity experts have warned are dangerously effective at finding bugs and weaponizing them. In its blog post, OpenAI said that the discovery of the PHP vulnerability highlighted “how A. I. can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The company added that, as far as it was aware, “frontier A. I. found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”

Given that PHP powers much of the web, security professionals are concerned that hackers could move quickly against unpatched systems, manipulating how they operate and stealing the private data they contain. Experts also cautioned that because the technical details are now public, malicious actors can reverse-engineer a patch to rapidly increase their attempts exploit the vulnerability.

That creates an unusually urgent race to update systems. While A. I. models can help spot vulnerabilities, it can also be used to target many victims at once.

The PHP disclosure was further complicated by a leak before the patch. On Tuesday, details of the bugs were mentioned in a post on a hacker forum, which prompted the nonprofit foundation that oversees the software to release a fix a day earlier than planned.

The defenders and hackers began racing to protect or compromise systems on Wednesday when the patch was released. But there were signs of an earlier leak from the group of security researchers working to create the fix.

Late Wednesday, Amazon revealed in a blog post that it had data showing that an unknown actor had used the PHP attack four days before the patch’s release against a honeypot network, or a decoy system, that the company maintains. (A honeypot network tries to catch cybercriminals in the act of doing something nefarious.)

The identity of the attacker was unknown, but the early activity suggested that hackers could have been readying attacks for days before a fix was released.

“It remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” C. J. Moses, the chief information security officer at Amazon, said in the blog post.

Sites that rely on PHP are vulnerable, which means a good chunk of the internet.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of CloudFlare, which helps websites secure and manage internet traffic, said in a social media post on Wednesday that the company “saw thousands of attempts to exploit” the flaw in the hours before it was publicly announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Mr. Prince added.

Several government websites in Europe and Asia went offline as a precautionary measure.

The Dutch cybersecurity agency, Internet Archive and the operator of Wikipedia took down a number of its systems. In Britain, the prime minister’s office said some government services might be offline on Friday.

On Thursday morning, the website of Finland’s government displayed a message to users: “The websites of the government are fully or partially unavailable. We are currently resolving the issue. Please try again in a moment.”

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan urged operators whose sites rely on PHP to apply the patch as soon as possible. For those unable to do so immediately, she wrote on social media, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures could be effective in reducing risk.

Because PHP is so pervasive, the collateral damage could fall on everyday users whose personal data and essential online services depend on sites staying secure. Consumers could experience online disruptions in the coming days with certain businesses or government services.

Aaron Krolik contributed reporting.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Reliably Red Iowa in Play as Economic Woes Mount

The New York Times October 22, 2026

The Trump administration’s policies could cost Republicans in a state that is being hit hard by expensive diesel prices and uncertainty over trade.

Make sense of the day’s news and ideas.

Catch up on big news, and wind down to end your day.

The Trump administration’s policies could cost Republicans in a state that is being hit hard by expensive diesel prices and uncertainty over trade.

Iowa farmers like Jolene Riessen are struggling with the elevated cost of fuel. Credit...

Supported by

By Alan Rappeport and Bayliss Wagner

Visuals by Rebecca Gratz

Alan Rappeport reported from Ida Grove and Primghar, Iowa. Bayliss Wagner reported from Sioux City, Clarion and Des Moines.

The diesel fuel that powers the tractors and combines on Kelly Nieuwenhuis’s 3,000-acre Iowa farm costs almost double what it did earlier this year because of the war in Iran. Fertilizer prices are also rising, as Russia’s war in Ukraine drags on. And sales of the corn and soybeans that he grows have been depressed amid trade fights with China, Canada and Mexico.

Mr. Nieuwenhuis, a registered Republican, voted for Donald J. Trump in 2016 and 2020, but not in 2024. He is frustrated with Mr. Trump’s policies as president, and plans to split his ticket in the midterm elections. He will support Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor, but is backing Ashley Hinson, the Republican running for Senate.

“It’s the economy, stupid,” said Mr. Nieuwenhuis, echoing a political slogan that has doomed Republicans in the past.

He recalled spending $16,000 to fill up the fuel tanks on his farm in Primghar, Iowa, this fall. “Every election it comes down to the economy, and this policy is not working,” he said. “The Iran war, all the energy costs, the inflation — everything has gone up in price drastically.”

The country’s economic crosscurrents are cascading across Iowa. High gas prices, elevated interest rates and Mr. Trump’s unpredictable economic policies, including tariffs, have been battering rural America over the last year. Iowa’s economy contracted in 2025 and notched the weakest annual growth rate in the country, according to the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Polls suggest that the state that helped propel Mr. Trump’s political rise could flip in favor of Democrats when voters cast their ballots next month.

The stakes are so high that Mr. Trump will head to Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday to try and convince a once-stalwart Republican base to keep his party in control of Congress. He is expected to promote the $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel prices that he announced on Monday night. It was the second time in two years that the president authorized billions of dollars in bailout money for farmers harmed by his administration’s policies.

The payouts are papering over a painful economic problem for Iowa’s farmers, who were hurt by international backlash to Mr. Trump’s tariffs in his first term and never fully recovered. Farmland values in the state have been tepid in recent years, and farm bankruptcies were up by 220 percent last year.

The economic doldrums in the state have spread, with big companies such as John Deere, Wells Fargo and Whirlpool announcing job cuts in Iowa in recent months.

Mr. Trump’s argument to let Republicans keep political power in Washington and Iowa could be a tough sell.

The Iowa Farmers Union, one of the state’s oldest farm organizations, backed the entire Democratic congressional slate this cycle, breaking a decades-long streak of abstaining from federal endorsements.

Matt Russell, a farmer and the group’s executive director, said that its members had been frustrated with Mr. Trump and the state’s Republican congressional delegation long before the war. He cited cuts to federal programs benefiting farmers, cancellations of promised grants and the expiration of Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies.

The Iran war and trade tensions have only added to the strain farmers were feeling, he said, as rising costs have eaten into their slim margins.

“Republican leadership at the federal level has not been standing up to this administration and has not been actually delivering the investments that we were counting on,” Mr. Russell said.

Some top Republicans, including Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, have pleaded with the Trump administration to do more to help the state’s economy. Last year, Mr. Grassley called on Mr. Trump to exempt potash, an ingredient in fertilizer, from the tariffs the president imposed on Canada. He recently called on the White House to temporarily ban diesel fuel exports, saying it would “help family farmers.”

Peter Orazem, an economist at Iowa State University, said that economic output in Iowa had been far slower than most other states over the previous five years, recording an average annual growth rate of just 1 percent since 2021.

The state is not just vulnerable to dramatic changes in the agricultural sector. Tariffs have increased manufacturing production costs in the state, and Mr. Trump’s immigration policies have made labor costs more expensive. The president’s aversion to wind and solar has also weighed on Iowa’s renewable energy sector.

“Iowa is basically lagging the rest of the U. S. pretty much across the board,” Mr. Orazem said. “I believe that there are few states that have been more disadvantaged by Trump policies than Iowa.”

The agricultural concerns in Iowa also go beyond corn and soybeans.

The Iowa Cattlemen’s Association, which represents beef producers, has also expressed frustration about some of Mr. Trump’s trade policies. In August, the group criticized his decision to cut tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of ground beef, saying the move to sell meat below market rate would hurt struggling ranchers.

Economists said the imports would not significantly affect consumer prices. But they caused cattle futures to drop by hundreds of dollars, influencing the prices cattle ranchers could negotiate for at market. Numerous Midwestern Republican lawmakers, including Ms. Hinson, pushed back against the imports.

The executive director of the Iowa Cattlemen’s Association, Bryan Whaley, said that some of the Trump administration’s policies, and Mr. Trump’s comments, had driven market volatility, which he called the main challenge facing cattle ranchers in Iowa. But he said that ups and downs were part of working with any president.

“As in every administration, you’re always going to have things that you appreciate and some things that are done that you may not necessarily agree with,” Mr. Whaley, a rancher, said when asked about Mr. Trump’s performance.

Mr. Whaley added that the state’s congressional delegation had been “extremely receptive” to the group’s concerns.

The political arm of the Iowa Farm Bureau, the state’s largest grass roots farm organization, endorsed Ms. Hinson and all four Republican House nominees. But the group’s political action committee, which has historically supported Republicans at the top of the ticket, declined to endorse in the governor’s race. The group did not respond to a request for comment on the decision. The Democratic nominee, Mr. Sand, has appealed to Republicans and swing voters with a centrist message.

The backlash to Mr. Trump’s policies has Democrats feeling emboldened.

Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has slammed Republicans over high diesel prices and Mr. Trump’s tariffs on potash, which is largely imported from Canada. Last week, Mr. Turek visited the farm of a three-time Trump voter, Marcus Tomlonovic, to drive the point home.

Mr. Tomlonovic, a 30-year-old corn and soybean farmer in Colfax, Iowa, said he was planning to vote for Mr. Turek and other Democrats because he was frustrated that Mr. Trump had entered a foreign war after promising to stay out of them.

“I feel like we’ve been betrayed,” Mr. Tomlonovic said in a phone interview, adding that diesel had cost him an additional $1,000 each week. “How much more are we going to take before small farmers can’t hang on?”

Derek Eadon, a Democratic strategist from West Des Moines, said he was “cautiously optimistic” that Mr. Trump’s unpopularity would help Democrats perform well in November.

“The Iowa Republican Party has been in lock step with Trump the entire way since he’s been in office,” Mr. Eadon said. “And I don’t think there’s any getting away from that at the very end with a tweet or a vote here or there.”

In a state Republicans have dominated since 2016, when Mr. Trump flipped it after Barack Obama twice won it, major races have become unexpectedly competitive. Mr. Sand has led the Republican nominee, Zach Lahn, in every major nonpartisan poll this year.

Ms. Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, is neck-and-neck with Mr. Turek, a state representative. And Republican candidates in three of the state’s four congressional districts have struggled to establish clear leads over Democratic opponents.

“We do need to find ways to provide relief to our farmers who are at the fields every single day in the middle of harvest,” Ms. Hinson told reporters at an event this week in Des Moines, where she discussed pausing the diesel gas tax. “I think long term we need to be focusing on more refining capacity here in the United States.”

This week, the main super PAC supporting House Republicans canceled its ad reservations in the swing district held by Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican, signaling that the party no longer saw a path for the second-term lawmaker. Senate Republicans’ top super PAC has spent more than $40 million on advertising in Iowa to support Ms. Hinson, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, a staggering sum in a state that Mr. Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

The political environment is “brutal” for Republicans in Iowa, said Alex Conant, a Republican consultant who has worked on Senate and presidential campaigns in the state.

“If the economy is the number one issue everywhere,” Mr. Conant said, “it’s the only issue in Iowa.”

Some Republican farmers are still planning to stick with their party.

Jolene Riessen, who grows corn and soybeans on her family farm in Ida Grove, is spending $6,000 every week to 10 days to fill fuel tanks with diesel. She has had to sell a dry spreader truck and a tractor to save money to offset the higher costs.

But she does not blame Mr. Trump for invading Iran, and thinks that oil companies are using that as an excuse to hike prices on consumers. She will continue to back Republican candidates even though inflation is making her life harder.

“I haven’t really seen the Democrats do me a lot of favors,” Ms. Riessen said. “I mean, I just go back to the Biden administration. What do they do for the farmer?”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure

Wired October 21, 2026

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.

In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores

Wired October 21, 2026

Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves.

“As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.”

“Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied. “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.”

A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.”

Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out.

“The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.”

Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.”

Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.”

If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike.

“Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”

Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.)

“First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said, though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans.

Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “health hazards,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage”—were invoked by several hosts. But these policy adjustments, seemingly, will not change how any of these things are treated.

Airbnb already has its own ground rules that all guests must agree to. The general credo is to "treat your host’s home like your own," which translates to things like putting trash in the trash can and not leaving moldy dishes.

If a host finds that anything was damaged or went missing during a stay, guests are expected to pay a “reasonable” amount to repair or replace it. Hosts are also protected through the platform’s protection program, AirCover, which will reimburse up to $3 million for certain property damage caused by guests, including furniture, cars, and other belongings.

Additional cleaning costs, such as performing "smoke odor removal" or handling "pet accidents” are also covered by AirCover. Airbnb notes that the cleaning fees hosts are allowed to set are only meant to cover standard guest turnover tasks like laundry and vacuuming. Hosts can’t “charge guest fees for failing to perform specific cleaning or checkout tasks,” though they can still leave guest reviews “based on cleanliness.”

In the Airbnb Hosts subreddit, a few lurking guests were quick to bring up the cleaning fees, which are famously the subject of their ire. One self-described “mostly guest” said they’re not opposed to running the dishwasher or stripping the bed. “Just don’t charge me a cleaning fee over $100 then,” they said.

“Truth nuke,” another person replied. “Why would I have to pre-game the cleaners?”

‘It’s the President’s Fault’: The White House Blame Game Starts Early Ahead of the Midterms

Wired October 21, 2026

Trump White House aides have started to cast about for a scapegoat to offer the president in the event of bad midterm election losses, as Republicans stare down brutal predictions in key House and Senate races, sources familiar with the matter say.

Republican political operatives say privately that the real blame lies with Trump for starting the Iran war in an election year, causing higher prices across the board and prompting a nationwide voter backlash, the sources say.

“Clearly it's the president's fault,” one operative tells Inner Loop.

But Trump aides also know, for obvious reasons, they cannot say publicly or tell the president behind closed doors that his own policy decisions are at fault as they contemplate losing not just the House majority, but possibly the Senate.

The result has been an unusually early effort to find a scapegoat, and sources say eyes have fallen on deputy chief of staff and political strategist James Blair, who organized the Trump 2024 campaign's turnout strategy and returned to the role for this midterm cycle.

Blair's efforts included a marquee plan for certain states to redraw congressional maps early, which looked likely—though not certain—to yield favorable House seats for Republicans, so long as the coalition that Trump turned out in 2024 came out to support Republicans in 2026.

Even accounting for the Iran war, the redistricting gambit was supposed to bring roughly 10 to 15 pickups for Republicans in the House. After Virginia's top court blocked Democrats from redrawing maps to keep pace in the redistricting battle, Blair wrote on X: “Lord grant me humility.”

But in a remarkable backfire five months later, election forecasters have found that some of the redistricted seats now favor Democrats.

The redrawn map for Florida's 25th congressional district just south of Fort Lauderdale, for instance, is now characterized as "Lean Democrat," and the outlook is so bad that the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican–aligned group, has pulled money out of the race.

Maps that were drawn for Republicans in ruby-red Texas are suddenly also vulnerable, even in seats where the party has incumbents. In Texas' 15th congressional district, GOP candidate Monica De La Cruz's race is now rated a "tossup" by the Cook Political Report.

Blair's allies inside and outside the West Wing say the criticism directed at him is grossly unfair because he could not have foreseen the effects of the Iran war and scandals involving Trump officials undoing his planning.

Blair is also viewed as retaining the confidence of Trump and the White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and he traveled on Air Force One to two rallies within the past week, suggesting any blame that ultimately comes his way could be just symbolic.

After all, when Blair left the White House earlier this year to run Trump's midterm strategy from the outside, the president announced the move as only temporary and said that Blair would return after the election.

Responding to the reporting in this story, Blair said in a statement, “the President, our partners in the House and Senate, and I remain focused on winning in November. All Republicans should be spending themselves equally in our worthy cause.”

“The anonymous ‘sources’ peddling this nonsense are self-serving opportunists focused on themselves. We’re focused on the President and the American people,” White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez added in a statement.

As for Wiles herself, despite reporting that she has been under fire, sources inside Trump's orbit are adamant that if Wiles leaves after the midterms, it will be purely of her own volition.

Trump aides acknowledge that much of the palace intrigue scapegoating is preemptive. Expectations are so low that if Republicans take some wins—like holding on to the Senate—Blair will be “seen as a savior,” one of the sources added.

But they also say that in many ways Blair has perhaps made it too easy for them to single him out. He explicitly owned the House midterm strategy, and now he may be walked to the gallows with that same rope.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Bose Is Buying Skullcandy. It’s Not as Weird as It Sounds

Wired October 21, 2026

Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park City, Utah.

The acquisition isn't out of left field. Bose has lent its audio expertise to Skullcandy over the past year under its Sound by Bose licensing program. Skullcandy designs the headphones and then works with Bose on the audio front. The relationship began with the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025 and more recently, with the Crusher 1080 ANC headphones in July.

When WIRED spoke with Skullcandy CEO Brian Garofalow in July about the partnership, Garofalow highlighted the 23-year-old company's ability to build community and culture, specifically around the board sports community (the first Skullcandy product was designed on a ski chairlift). But he admitted the company wasn't “the greatest at the engineering part of innovation with products.”

This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). Bose acquired McIntosh Group, owners of luxury audio brands McIntosh Laboratory and Sonus Faber, back in 2024. But Bose seems to be after Skullcandy's connection to its community.

“What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren’t reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand.”

That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. “We want to make sure we’re right at the heart of it, as they always have been,” she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.

As WIRED's headphone reviewer, I find Bose and Skullcandy an odd pairing. In consumer audio, Bose pioneered active noise-cancelation (ANC) in headphones, and maintains that legacy with ANC-leading products like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen). Skullcandy, on the other hand, has often been viewed as the butt of the joke when it comes to audio quality. It has had a reputation for middling sound, bass-over-everything headphones, and a loud, bold aesthetic.

Recent collaborations have started to change those perceptions—WIRED rated the Method 360 ANC earbuds an 8/10, noting good sound quality and ANC for the money. Snyder says those buds and the recent Crusher collab are just the tip of the iceberg. “It’s the beginning of what we think we can do together,” she says.

I’m very curious about what comes next from Skullcandy, headphones or otherwise. Either way, we’ll see if Bose's acoustic muscle can give the lifestyle brand the permanent glow-up it’s been chasing.

One of My Favorite Eufy Security Cameras Is on Sale

Wired October 21, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

While security cameras are ostensibly for, well, security, they can also be super handy for making sure your kids came home at the right time, checking up on your pets when you’re away, and investigating that weird sound in the middle of the night without having to get out of your toasty bed.

I’ve tested so very, very many security cameras, and there are a few reasons I think you should snap up this particular Eufy Security Wall Light Cam S4 deal at $80 off. I’m also going to highlight a couple of other Eufy options currently on sale.

Eufy

Amazon

Shop

The Eufy Wall Light Cam S4 looks and acts as a modern, motion-activated wall light, perfect for illuminating a driveway, porch, or back gate, which is where I have mine (no more stubbed toes when I take out the trash at night). Eufy has also packed in a 4K camera that you can swivel to get the right angle, offering a wide, crisp view of your chosen spot. It records locally, with 32 GB of storage built in, and it's subscription free, including the on-device AI detection, which can accurately distinguish between people, vehicles, and pets. Installation is quick and easy, and it connects directly to your Wi-Fi. You’ll just need a decent signal at your chosen spot.

To sweeten the deal, there’s a solar panel to keep the battery topped off. It sits neatly on top, but you can detach it for better placement to catch the sun’s rays. Despite being in a busy spot, mine has stayed charged for the last couple of months, though I suspect that may change as we head into winter.

What I like best about this security camera is the wall light functionality. You can set the brightness and color temperature (I like a warm light). You can also schedule it to only trigger between specific hours or set it to be activated from sunset to sunrise based on your location. I also love that it doesn’t scream outdoor security camera; you only notice it if you look closely.

Some downsides: the frame rate is just 15 fps, so fast-moving subjects can appear blurry, particularly in the dark (though the light helps with that). Some folks will also need to top off the battery on occasion, so you’ll want to keep it somewhere within reach. I also feel it’s overpriced at the original $250, but at $170 ($80 off), that's less of an issue.

Eufy

Amazon

Shop

Eufy

If you need an indoor camera, the Eufy S350 is also on sale right now at $100 ($40 off), and it’s a wonderfully versatile, feature-packed, dual-lens camera. It even has automatic tracking, making it ideal for checking in on your cat or dog throughout the day. It regularly dips down to this price, so you might want to wait for Black Friday, when I predict it will drop another $20.

The EufyCam C35 2-Cam Kit at $130 ($70 off) is also worth considering right now. These cameras work inside or out with an easy magnetic mount and come with a handy HomeBase Mini for local recording and onboard AI that includes facial recognition. This is a common discount, but it's still a great deal for a two-camera kit with hub.

Fall is also hosting season, which means making your place more presentable for the holidays. Maybe you’ve moved, as many do at this time of year, and are still furnishing your new space. Fortunately, home goods sales are plentiful right now.

Ruggable’s October Hosting Sale is one of my favorite excuses to redecorate, with up to 30 percent off select styles. It runs through October 25, so your window is closing as I type. Keep reading for more reasons I love Ruggable, plus a few of my favorites currently on sale.

I adore Ruggable. The entire WIRED Reviews team adores Ruggable. I have the Pamir Moroccan Flatwoven runner under my kitchen sink, and it's gorgeous, but I don’t panic when spills and stains happen. In fact, I welcome them. The beauty of a washable rug is that you can actually live on it, which feels almost radical when so much home decor seems designed for childless, pet-free people who never eat or drink.

WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz has a toddler and a cat, both of whom have peed on his hallway rug. Both times, he was grateful he could toss it in the washing machine and dryer and move on. Commerce executive director Cooper Fleishman was debating between the Wendel Ochre Rug by Anthropologie, the bohemian Yara Navy & Bronze Rug, and the Berber-inspired Enya Multicolor Rug for his office. Reviewer Simon Hill has the Santiago Persian Tufted Rug in his home in Scotland (yes, they ship to the UK and Europe) and recommends the Mandalore Tufted Rug for any Star Wars fans out there.

Ruggable

Ruggable (6 x 9)

Ruggable

Ruggable (6 x 9)

Ruggable has thousands of designs to choose from—2,122 to date. It’s a blessing and a curse. The brand also regularly offers alternatives to discontinued styles, so all is not lost if you were eyeing a piece you can no longer find. Note that the sale does exclude the new Easy Care Wool collection, along with gift cards, spot cleaner, and rug pads. Read the terms and conditions before you buy, and don’t delay; the sale ends October 25.

Is Ruggable Worth It?

While we stan Ruggable, it’s not without its shortcomings. WIRED editor Kat Merck has the Jonathan Adler Venom Flatwoven Rug in her kitchen; the edges curl up, and it drives her nuts. I will say my Ruggable’s nonslip pad has betrayed me more than once. It shifts around the kitchen and is the occasional tripping hazard. Aligning a rug onto the pad is also a two-person job, but it’s not impossible if you live alone. Customers online have also reported issues with prints fading over time, but that’s practically a given with high-traffic, machine-washable rugs.

We also like Revival, which has an assortment of hand-knotted and woven imported wool rugs at reasonable prices. Plus, the company is having its own 20-percent-off sitewide sale that ends on Sunday.

GM Wants Your Car to Do Your Chores

Wired October 21, 2026

Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.

But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.

It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.

GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.

GM also says it will use AI to speed up new-vehicle development, eventually cutting its four- to five-year development time in half—the speed at which Chinese carmakers create new vehicles today.

The automaker plans to expand its “eyes-off” highway driving technology to its most popular cars, inching closer to its years-old promise of making a personal self-driving car. It previously said the system was coming to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. Today, the company’s Super Cruise feature lets drivers take their hands off their steering wheels on hundreds of thousands of miles of pre-mapped highways. Reaching true autonomy will take time, but GM isn’t ready to talk about that publicly. “This industry is rife with promises that were not fulfilled. I am not keen on making them,” Anderson says.

But GM is taking a different approach from, say, Tesla. The electric carmaker sells a driver-assistance feature called “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” that can navigate many highways and local roads but requires drivers to stay alert and ready to take over at any moment. That kind of system “presents the illusion of autonomy without its benefits,” Anderson says, who for a time led Tesla’s Autopilot program. If drivers can’t do other things while their car is doing most of the driving, it’s less useful and “comes with the direct expense of the safety of your vehicle and the people around you,” he says. “That would not be a responsible way to operate.”

GM’s method, by contrast, is to slowly expand “eyes-off” capabilities to more sorts of roads, letting drivers text or eat or watch YouTube first on some highways, and then on more highways, and then on local roads, and then maybe everywhere.

That’s when the automaker's vision gets bigger and blurrier. The cabin, the company says in a blog post, can become a space to “relax, work, and unwind. … In time, this will pave the way for a future where your car can take on everyday errands,” the company says. The personal self-driving car will pick up groceries, drop off children, and then maybe even find a parking spot at the end.

Urban planners and infrastructure experts have worried about this vision. If you lower the price of a car trip, in money and time spent driving, won’t everyone send their cars out for every task? Won’t the roads be crowded with pods full of people sleeping, emailing, and YouTubing while their vehicles slowly pilot them onward—or worse, cars with no one in them? Won’t cities become sprawlier?

Anderson says yes. If you have cheap, personal driving robots, “you will very likely incur more of those robots on the roads. And so there's a lot of societal and infrastructural considerations to make here,” he says. But he argues we have time, and that cities take time to sprawl. “I wouldn't call this an imminent thing, but it certainly is something we should be thinking about.”
